#3461. Grey's Anatomy's Downfall Can Be Traced Back To One Moment

"Grey's Anatomy" has been on the air since 2005, which is to say that it's experienced a handful of high highs and very low lows. Shonda Rhimes' medical drama, which premiered as a humble mid-season replacement and became one of the longest-running shows in the history of its medium, stars Ellen Pompeo as surgical intern turned award-winning general surgery attending and hospital owner Dr. Meredith Grey, who lives, loves, and learns alongside her colleagues and who has a knack for picking up cases that connect to her personal life in some way (as all of the doctors do, honestly).

(I say it "stars" Pompeo, but there's a technicality here; Pompeo technically left "Grey's Anatomy" as a series regular in Season 19 in 2022, but still provides voiceover and appears on the show often enough that she's still the main character for all intents and purposes.)

There are, if I'm being honest, many parts of "Grey's Anatomy" that one could identify as a major series downfall, like the time Dr. Isobel "Izzie" Stevens (Katherine Heigl) has ghostly physical intimacy with her dead fiancé before figuring out it's a brain tumor, the time a plane crash kills most of the show's surgeons, or every time a wedding is interrupted by a dramatic, ridiculous problem. The issue? Many of those lows are followed by highs (as Heigl's Izzie leaves the series, there's a hospital merger followed by a two-part finale in Season 6 that's a legitimate series highlight). That's why I'm pointing to a true point of no return for "Grey's Anatomy," and I am truly sorry to say that, despite my respect for the show's commitment to "realism" during a terrifying time for the entire world, the 17th season of the medical drama, also known as the "COVID season," is its downfall.

At face value, it makes total sense for a show like "Grey's Anatomy" to address the very real COVID-19 pandemic head-on; because the characters also dressed in protective medical gear, there was an air of practicality to the whole thing to boot. Here's the problem: the way they addressed it was straight-up bonkers. Partway through Season 17, Meredith develops a pretty serious case of COVID-19, which sidelines her (and, to an extent, Ellen Pompeo) for the remainder of the season's run, giving her a truly bizarre storyline where she sees dead loved ones in dreams in a random seaside location that fans like me simply refer to as the "coma beach."

Instead, fans of the series couldn't escape the pandemic surrounding them, and to make things worse, the show's best quality — its genuinely funny and smart dialogue — fell by the wayside in the process. Meredith may have eventually recovered from her severe case of COVID-19 and left the coma beach behind after Season 17, but the show wasn't able to pull off the same feat ... and as it continues, you can feel the slip in quality with each passing season.

I know better than most people that "Grey's Anatomy" has its fair share of detractors; I've been watching this damn show since it premiered, and it's one of the longest relationships of my life without comparison. I'll be among the first to admit that a lot of it is heightened and silly — and I got the chance to interview a friend who's a real doctor for this very site, who confirmed that it's the least realistic televised medical drama by a country mile.

Still, I'll go to the mat for a lot of seasons and episodes of "Grey's Anatomy." Shonda Rhimes, while she was still hands-on with the series, was a masterful dialogue writer and gave actors like Sandra Oh (who left the series after the Season 10 finale) unbelievably sharp monologues with regularity. The chemistry between most of the original actors was undeniably great, its jokes often hit their mark beautifully, and remember that two-part Season 6 finale I mentioned? "Sanctuary" and "Death and All His Friends," which chronicles a devastating mass shooting within the walls of the central hospital, is one of my favorite TV episodes ever ... and I'd stack it against plenty of prestige dramas any day.

That's what makes the fall of "Grey's Anatomy" particularly painful for me. I'm committed to the proverbial bit by still watching it, but it's painful. Instead of quippy dialogue that feels like a tennis match, characters over-explain everything in the preachiest way possible (like a female doctor explaining to a male counterpart that women get Brazilian butt lifts because society influences them into it). "Grey's Anatomy" is a pale shadow of what it once was, and it all started in Season 17.

#3460. GTA 6 Trophy Count and Full Completion Time Leaks in New Reports

Completionists are going to spend months in Leonida

Millions of players will start their adventure in Leonida with the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6 later this week. They're currently preparing themselves and completing the games they've left unfinished so they can dedicate all of their time to GTA 6 soon — especially gamers who have asked for time off from work to play it. But the question on many players' minds is how much time they will need to finish the story and 100% complete it.

As it turns out, a week off from work might not be enough. After gathering information from various people who've played the game, Insider Gaming has reported that it should take around 50 hours to get through Grand Theft Auto 6's campaign. The story is reportedly spread across five chapters and consists of nearly 100 missions.

Besides the main story, players can go for GTA 6's Platinum Trophy or the Mythic achievement. However, according to Insider Gaming, that should push their total playtime to at least 200 hours. Besides earning a gold medal on story missions, it's expected that players will have to study all 170 animal species, just like in Red Dead Redemption 2. Additionally, Henderson believes that there will be certain trophies that will depend on RNG — likely related to the casino and gambling. So, are you ready to spend hours at the slot machines?

According to one unconfirmed report, GTA 6 will have 55 achievements for players to complete.

As shown in several interviews, teasers, and the extended trailer, there's plenty of side content and optional exploration you can do — even if it's just grabbing a bite to eat, looking at the intricate cloud system, or taking the bus until the end of the line. Therefore, we can conclude that besides the main story and the completionist trophies, players will likely spend far more than 200 hours in Vice City and greater Leonida.

Grand Theft Auto 6 will be released on Nov. 19 for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X.

For years, Johnny Galecki was one of network television's biggest stars. His long-running sitcom, The Big Bang Theory was a hit, and hits bring fame and big paydays. Galecki could have taken his money and retired to a quiet life, and it turns out he wrestled with that decision between then and his latest gig as I just found out.

After seven years, Galecki is returning to acting by way of a theatrical production of Kowalski, and ahead of that, he talked to BroadwayWorld.com about why he chose this project. It's a fair question considering Big Bang spinoff series Stuart Fails to Save the Universe was part of the 2026 TV schedule, and I'm sure the creative team would've loved to have had him in Season 1. It turns out Galecki's decision to take this role was about more than just having a job, but wanting to see if he still had a passion for acting:

I knew I was in a position where I needed to learn if I still loved this work or not, honestly. I was beyond confused, I was concerned that this very first love of mine, and for a very long time my only love, seemed to have left me. And I was very content, but it was a bit of an identity crisis, I suppose. Or lack of knowing where I fit in the world, all of a sudden. I’d been doing theatre since I was seven and acting in various mediums since. And so, I just couldn’t figure it out, why I was entirely bereft of any interest in it any longer.

Galecki did indeed have options considering how much money he made from The Big Bang Theory. He reportedly makes a good deal more via reruns as well, so it's not like he needed to return to acting. And yet, as someone who has been working as an actor since childhood, it was a major part of his identity. Taking on this role was a test to see if he still loved being a performer, or if he needed to figure out what the next chapter of his life looked like.

And, with that, we now have him playing Tennessee Williams in Kowalski. It's not just a role, as Johnny Galecki pointed out, but one that will challenge his abilities as an actor:

I knew it needed to be something that would challenge me, something that I couldn’t hide behind, something that I couldn’t blame on it being underwritten, or a thankless role if it failed.

It's interesting to read that comment, and I do wonder if that's meant to be a pointed jab at what roles could've been waiting for him. It's easy to imagine that Stuart Fails to Save the Universe would love to bring in Johnny Galecki to reprise Leonard Hofstadter eventually, likely for one of the cameo roles we've seen others like Kaley Cuoco play. Is this a hint that co-creator Chuck Lorre shouldn't hold his breath about the Leonard actor reprising the role?

Should that be the case, he's not the only star with a stance on that. Sheldon Cooper actor Jim Parsons openly stated that he's done playing the character, which could put the Chuck Lorre series in a sticky situation. Stuart and friends need to find one of Leonard, Sheldon, or Howard to help set the universe right, and now it's looking like they may have to wait for a while.

All this to say, Johnny Galecki didn't openly besmirch his time working on Big Bang Theory. It's just hard not to think about that when it was the last role that he played before this big return to acting. It could be that this statement had nothing to do with his work on TBBT at all, but I can't help but wonder. Regardless of that, I'm glad he's found a role that he finds both challenging and exciting.

Catch episodes of TBBT by streaming them with an HBO Max subscription, or find them in syndication on various networks. Now that Johnny Galecki is acting again, I'll be curious to see if he starts to pick up more work! I guess it depends on how this acting stint goes.

#3458. Five Creative Ways to Spend Your FSA Funds Before the End of the Year

If you have a flexible spending account (FSA), you know the drill: Use the funds before the end of the year, or lose them. Unfortunately, chances are slim you can pack the rest of the year with doctor's appointments. Does that mean your hard-earned funds go to waste? Definitely not. You can spend your remaining FSA funds on other qualifying healthcare costs. And what counts as "qualifying" might surprise you—for instance, you can use your FSA or HSA funds to get yourself a sweet new fitness tracker or smartwatch.

As the end of the year approaches, here are all the ways you can spend any leftover money in your FSA balance.

Many over-the-counter medications and health items are FSA-eligible, including pain relievers, cold medicine, bandages, dental care products, menstrual products, and more. Scan your medicine cabinet and make a list of anything you need to stock up on.

FSA/HSA eligibility for smartwatches and other fitness wearables is real, but the main “catch" (as I’ve previously explained) is proving the device is in fact necessary, which requires you to obtain a Letter of Medical Necessity (LMN).

Screenless recovery trackers like Whoop, Amazfit Helio Strap, and the Oura Ring can usually be justified as HSA/FSA eligible around sleep quality, HRV-based stress monitoring, or recovery tracking tied to a chronic condition. Similarly, smartwatches can qualify the same way a basic tracker does, as long as you can link a relevant documented health concern. For instance, Coros offers FSA/HSA eligibility for all its watches and heart rate monitors through its partnership with Truemed. Amazfit similarly lets you filter by HSA/FSA eligibility for its smartwatches.

If you want to get creative with it, the official FSA store lets you filter by "surprisingly eligible." Similar to the section above, for some of these items, you'll want to brush up on how exactly to get an LMN to justify certain tech as FSA-eligible for you personally. In the meantime, go crazy and snag yourself Epsom salt for $8.99, Supergoop! sunscreen for $38.00, or perhaps a snazzy massage gun for $349.99.

Knee braces, wrist splints, compression socks, and other orthopedic items can help relieve chronic pain issues. Rather than wait for these issues to rear their heads down the line, use FSA money to offset the costs of these fixes now. If you use eyeglasses or contacts, consider using your FSA dollars to update or refresh your prescriptions. Don't forget to stock up on eye drops and lens solution, too.

If you have medical procedures scheduled for early next year, many healthcare providers will allow you to pre-pay the estimated costs this calendar year using FSA funds. This includes dental work, physical therapy, chiropractic visits, Lasik eye surgery, and more.

However you choose to spend your FSA funds, don’t let that money go to waste. After all, it came out of your paycheck. Check in with your employer’s rules for any balance remaining on Dec. 31 this year, so you aren’t left forfeiting your hard-earned funds. You can find a complete list at the FSA store here.

#3457. Michael Bay And David Fincher Worked Together On An Unexpected Project That Still Holds Up Today

It's a rare thing when two equally well-known artists collaborate behind the camera. An auteur director team-up doesn't happen often, but it's certainly not unheard of. This year alone, we've seen the news that Steven Soderbergh is helping out Matt Reeves with "The Batman Part II," while Quentin Tarantino has handed the "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" character of Cliff Booth over to David Fincher for the upcoming Netflix spin-off. That latter director, as it happens, isn't a stranger to blending his creative DNA with another filmmaker. Famously, Fincher took over the troubled "Alien 3" after it had been developed for years, and inherited a script structure from director Vincent Ward that he isn't thrilled with to this day.

Around the same time, the budding film auteur (who was then still primarily known as a music video director) was approached to make a video for the rock star Meat Loaf's 1993 single "I'd Do Anything for Love (But I Won't Do That)." According to Craig Marks and Rob Tannenbaum's 2011 book "I Want My MTV: The Uncensored Story of the Music Video Revolution," Fincher and Meat Loaf's vision was pretty much what the finished video became, a Gothic riff on "Beauty and the Beast." However, Fincher's price tag caused Meat Loaf to look elsewhere for the video's director, turning to none other than an up-and-coming Michael Bay. (That's one version of the story, at least; more on that later.) Though the two didn't directly work together on it, the final video is, in its own weird way, a collaboration between the pair.

Although Michael Bay and David Fincher technically worked together at the production company Propaganda Films, their relationship was definitely more complex than just coworkers or collaborators. As various colleagues and other luminaries who worked at or with Propaganda detail in "I Want My MTV," Fincher was already a star internally given his extensive work on numerous successful music videos, and this was something that the young Bay was all too aware of. Employees told Craig Marks and Rob Tannenbaum that Bay would follow Fincher around the Propaganda offices constantly, with some people already considering him a younger version of Fincher.

This comparison came to a head when Meat Loaf approached Fincher with the gig for "I'd Do Anything for Love." According to Meat Loaf, the musician pitched Fincher with a "Beauty and the Beast" premise for the video, which Fincher allegedly loved. However, Fincher supposedly gave Meat Loaf a quote of $2.3 million, which Loaf balked at. He continued:

"So he came back a few days later and gave me a budget of $1.7 million. I said, 'David, we don't have that kind of money.' And Fincher said, 'Well then, get Michael Bay.' That's the last time Michael Bay was the cheaper option."

So, in Meat Loaf's version of the tale, the vision for the music video was the singer's idea, Fincher couldn't make the budget work, and the then-cheaper Bay got a hand-me-down project which he spun into a hit video.

In Meat Loaf's version of what happened with the "I'd Do Anything for Love (But I Won't Do That)" music video, the video was an idea had by the singer which changed hands from David Fincher to Michael Bay. However, according to Propaganda Films producer Joni Sighvatsson, it was his idea to pass the torch from Fincher to Bay, and as such, the video ended up being the one and only collaboration between the two filmmakers. As he recalled:

"Fincher was very expensive. He and the label were at an impasse over the Meat Loaf video, so I said, 'Why don't we just give this to Michael Bay?' Fincher gave it to Bay, we ended up spending $750,000, and it was a seminal video. Michael directed, and it was David's concept. That was the first and last time Fincher and Bay collaborated."

It's very possible that Sighvatsson is merely aggrandizing the story of the "I'd Do Anything for Love" video, making it sound like it's the result of two now-famous auteurs rather than just one. Or it's possible that he and Meat Loaf have hazy memories of what went down and how. All we really have to go on is the video itself, which remains one of the most visually rapturous short films of the 1990s. It's the most perfect visual encapsulation of Meat Loaf's sound, all theatricality and opera. It's got Bay's fingerprints all over it, of course, from a fetishization of hardware and sunsets to the way every woman is shot like a supermodel. Yet the video's Gothic flavor and trappings feel more Fincheresque. However it happened, the video is a gift, and we should probably thank all three men for it.

#3456. iOS 27.2 adds new features in six iPhone apps, details here

iOS 27.2 recently launched with new features for iPhone users, including improvements across six Apple apps. Here’s what’s new.

One of my favorite additions to Messages this year, Suggested Actions, debuts in iOS 27.2.

Suggested Actions appear underneath messages in a conversation when relevant. They can suggest creating a calendar event or reminder, adding to a note, and more based on the context of the message.

The feature was originally part of the iOS 27 beta this summer, but didn’t make the public build. Now it’s back in iOS 27.2, new and improved. There’s also an option to fine-tune which types of suggestions you’ll see.

Read more: iOS 27.2 adds new Messages feature that’s already a favorite

Every major streaming service has its own profiles feature, letting users on the same account keep their viewing history and recommendations separate. Apple TV has long offered such a feature in tvOS, but now with iOS 27.2 and iPadOS 27.2 it’s coming to iPhone and iPad too.

When you launch the TV app in iOS 27.2, you’ll be greeted by a new profile selection screen. You can easily disable it if you don’t want to see if again. But if you ever share your iPhone with kids, the new profiles feature should come in handy.

Read more: iOS 27.2 gives Apple TV a new profiles feature on iPhone

Dual Capture is one of FaceTime’s best new features in years. Added in iOS 27, on compatible iPhones it lets you keep your front and rear cameras both active at the same time while on a FaceTime call.

iOS 27.2 brings a key upgrade to Dual Capture: it’s now available for Group FaceTime calls.

To use the feature, just hit the flip camera button like usual, and by default on iPhone 17 and newer you’ll stream both camera feeds simultaneously.

Read more: iOS 27.2 makes FaceTime’s best new feature even better

Timed with its new Home products push, Apple adds a pair of new Home app features in iOS 27.2 for compatible smart locks.

‘Lock After Closing’ is a new automation setting that lets you choose how long after a door is closed that it should lock automatically. Previously you could only set a duration based on the time since a door was unlocked, not closed.

‘Door Left Open’ tackles a related, but distinct problem: a door being left open too long. With compatible locks, you can configure the Home app to automatically notify you if a door has been left open for a certain period of time.

Read more: iOS 27.2 has three new changes just added this week

Apple Podcasts keeps getting better, with AI-powered automatic chapters and transcripts some of my favorite features. And in iOS 27.2, Apple has a welcome change to the Up Next queue on the Home tab.

Up Next is now split into two separate queues: New Episodes and Continue Playing.

Without the redesigned Health app, none of the new features appeal to me all that much. But performance improvements, bug fixes, and security fixes are always welcomed. What most of really wants is faster and more reliable Siri AI, along with support for a wider range of personal data, such as PDF documents on the iCloud Drive.

New Episodes contains only the latest episodes from shows you follow, while Continue Playing is a hub for all the episodes you’ve previously started but haven’t yet finished.

Apple’s Games app introduces some small updates in iOS 27.2 as well.

The Home tab now shows you recently downloaded games that you haven’t yet played. Previously, you would only see games with some play activity. And Apple says achievement progress and leaderboard scores have been updated in the Home tab to be easier to track. Finally, the Friends tab “provides context on friend suggestions and shows recent games played on friends’ player pages” per Apple.

Which new iOS 27.2 features are you most excited about? Let us know in the comments.

#3455. These 10 New Features Are Coming to iOS 27.3

Apple dropped the first developer beta for iOS 27.3 on Tuesday. While this update isn't as large as iOS 27 proper, it's surprisingly feature-filled for a 0.3 update. This is only a beta, so anything could (and likely will) change before Apple officially launches the update. But, as it stands, iOS 27.3 tests 10 new features—including one feature the company trialed in the previous beta.

Technically, anyone with a compatible iPhone can try out iOS 27.3 right now—assuming you enroll your Apple Account in the developer program. But a word of warning: Betas can be temperamental, and could be risky. As such, I'd recommend avoiding the beta until Apple releases the public beta, which comes after a bit more testing to iron out larger issues. Either way, make sure to make a full backup of your iPhone to a Mac or PC first, as issues with the beta could result in permanent data loss.

With watchOS 27, Apple released "Audio Intelligence," a new set of features for Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. Audio Intelligence uses the watches' new S11 chip, along with on-device AI and cloud-based AI, to run new features, like Sound Recognition and Shazam (music recognition).

With iOS 27.3, however, the company is now officially testing the other two Audio Intelligence features it originally announced with watchOS 27. First, there's Live Rewind: By double-clicking the watch crown, you can pull up a transcript of the last 15 seconds of a conversation. Siri Recap, on the other hand, displays summaries of conversations you had that day, in case you need a refresher on any chats you might have otherwise forgotten about,

The company generated some controversy when it first announced these two Audio Intelligence features, since, on the surface, it sounds like these new Apple Watches are essentially spying on people all day long. According to Apple, however, that isn't really the case. The company says Audio Intelligence is private, and never records or stores any audio. No speakers are ever identified, and text results (both transcripts and summaries) are deleted automatically after a set period of time unless the user saves them to the Siri app. You can read more about how Audio Intelligence works here.

Despite their claims, I'm sure there will still be strong feelings surrounding these Audio Intelligence features. We'll have to see whether Apple can prove Live Rewind and Siri Recap aren't all that creepy throughout the iOS 27.3 beta process.

iOS 27.3 also introduces app actions for Siri AI. Apple is testing new abilities for Siri AI, including organizing files, planning events, or adding photos to albums. You could ask Siri to organize your Downloads folder, or delete files that haven't been opened in more than a year. You could ask Siri to find a coffee shop you went to last week, or to save an article to your Reading List in Safari. You could ask Siri to check your calendar and set up a time for an event based on when you're free. You can even ask the assistant to schedule, edit, or unsend messages.

For example, you could ask Siri AI to help you plan a trip with your friends. You could ask the AI to put together a themed playlist in Apple Music, schedule a message to a group about an upcoming trip, organize the websites you've been visiting in Safari into a tab group, and, after the trip, ask Siri to move your best photos to your favorites album. These new actions work in the following apps: Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. Developers can also add Siri AI app actions support to their own apps.

Apple started testing its new Health app with the iOS 27.2 beta, but pulled the redesign before the official release. Now, with iOS 27.3, the new app is back. The new Health app has a health dashboard for the first time, as well as new features like Health Age and movement assessments. It seems to be pulling from some popular competitor services, hopefully, for the better. For more on the new Health app, check out Lifehacker health editor Beth Skwarecki's explainer.

Continuing on the Health track, iOS 27.3 also introduces "Gym Strength." This is a new Fitness+ feature that offers a personalized four-week strength-training plan. You can customize these plans to meet your goals, experience level, and schedule, and they adapt as you progress. You'll get recommendations based on your experience with exercises, reps, and sets, including video demos for exercises. You can access Gym Strength on both iPhone and iPad, and Apple Watches are optional—though you can log your progress with the wearable if you have it.

Vertical tabs have been a favorite among browser aficionados, as they give you more screen real estate in your browser while keeping your tabs off the side. Apple hasn't made the jump—until now. This feature works with iPads running iPadOS 27.3 as well as Macs running macOS 27.3.

Another new Safari feature in testing is "Adaptive Dark Mode." This feature forces websites into a dark theme, if they don't have a native theme of their own. There are third-party apps that can do this, but this is the first time Apple has offered this feature built into Safari.

Apple is also testing new StandBy experiences with iOS 27.3, which were previously only available on the iPhone Duo. When you turn your iPhone sideways while plugged in, you'll find new Analog and Digital Clock faces with new customization options. There's also a new Photos face, with the option to pull images from Shared Albums.

"Reachability" pulls your iPhone's display down towards the bottom of the screen, so you can access items towards the top of the display with one hand. It's a useful feature for those of us with big iPhones, and now, there's no iPhone bigger than the Duo. With iOS 27.3, Apple is testing Reachability for its first foldable phone. It's a bit like the inverse of how Reachability currently works: You can swipe on the left or right side of your Duo's display to shift the other side of the screen towards your current position. If you're holding your Duo in your left hand, a swipe of the left side will pull the right side over to the left, and vice versa.

Apple is also rolling out new languages for Siri AI in iOS 27.3. Now, Apple's smart assistant supports Traditional Chinese, Vietnamese, Turkish, and Norwegian.

If you have an Apple Intelligence-compatible iPad running iPadOS 27.3, you now have access to Siri Mode in Camera. As with iOS, you can open the Camera app on iPadOS to access Siri Mode, and ask Siri about your surroundings.

For a number of families, the Christmas Season is all about Santa Claus and his gift-giving, but in Hollywood, Santa comes in the shape of Tom Cruise and his famous Christmas cake. Even Oprah Winfrey spends the holiday season waiting around for the legendary coconut cake to arrive on her doorstep. However, that seems to be changing this year now that Oprah has discovered the cake isn’t as exclusive as she thought.

That’s right: the Queen of Favorite Things and one of the most influential pop culture figures in the world used to wait all year for the infamous cake, just like Top Gun: Maverick co-star Glen Powell, longtime cake recipient Kristen Dunst, and, most recently, Digger scene partner Riz Ahmed. It’s hard to imagine any celebrity sitting around waiting for a cake to be delivered to them, especially Oprah, who has the ability to get whatever she wants. Yet that’s how all these stars have been spending their holiday season for several decades. Winfrey recently said:

In our house, we’d be like ‘Has the Tom Cruise cake come yet? Has the Tom Cruise cake come?’ And all these years, up until this year, I thought that Tom had the cake specially made for Tom, okay. Then I realized Tom has a bakery.

Now, I don’t think anyone thought Cruise was baking the Christmas coconut cakes himself. While he’s a talented actor and impressive stuntman, baking is time-consuming, and his schedule is usually packed. The identity of the bakery that prepares the cakes isn't a total secret, but now, Oprah has let that cat out of the bag on a grand scale.

During a podcast taping (shared on Instagram) where she had several caregivers in attendance, Winfrey revealed that Doan’s Family Bakery in Los Angeles was the one responsible for the Hollywood Christmas tradition and that anyone, including us normal people, can order the cake.

The Emmy-Award-winning host rejoiced at being able to order the cake whenever she wants. And in true Oprah fashion, her first instinct was to share the good news with those in her life:

I can get the cake! And so I started sending it to people, saying, ‘It’s the Tom Cruise cake.’

I'm wondering how Cruise will feel knowing that Winfrey has further emphasized the source of his famous gift With this, might he consider changing up his yuletide tradition and switch to something? It's hard to say, but even if he did, I'm sure he'd think of something just as special. After all, the Mission Impossible star is known for his generosity, like never forgetting to call Rosie O’Donnell for her birthday.

Winfrey shares the same generosity gene with Cruise, of course, so it’s no surprise that she instantly felt the need to share the cake with not only her friends and family, but also the caregivers in attendance for the podcast taping. Yep, everyone in the audience was promised a delicious coconut cake would be delivered to their door courtesy of Goldbelly. Check out the full clip below:

A post shared by The Oprah Podcast (@oprahpodcast)

I would be insanely jealous, but of course, the good news is that anyone can order the cake from Goldbelly right now. It’s not exactly cheap, but it might be worth it to say that I’ve tried the infamous “Tom Cruise Cake,” thanks to Oprah.

#3453. 25 Years Later, Dumbledore's Best Sorcerer's Stone Line Is Still The Greatest Harry Potter Quote

In the wizarding world of Harry Potter, Albus Dumbledore is often referred to as one of the wisest and most powerful wizards in history ... so, it's lucky for the titular boy wizard that Dumbledore just happens to be the headmaster of his magical academy. In the original Harry Potter film franchise (which is getting a new life, in a way, with the forthcoming HBO Harry Potter TV show), Harry Potter, as played by Daniel Radcliffe (who may not watch the HBO reboot series), leaves his humdrum life with his mean non-magical relatives behind and starts attending Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry, run by Dumbledore (Richard Harris in the first two movies before the legendary actor passed away in 2002, at which point Michael Gambon took over). There, he meets his best friends Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger (Rupert Grint and Emma Watson), learns how to cast magic spells, and has his first encounter, so to speak, with the Dark Lord Voldemort who tried to kill him as a baby.

Let's all be honest: Dumbledore sort of gets all the best quotes in the Harry Potter franchise. After all, his entire purpose is to dispense wisdom, so he drops a lot of stone-cold bangers. But what's his most memorable quote from the first movie, "Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone" (which hit theaters on November 16, 2001)? We think we've pinpointed the perfect Dumbledore line from this film 25 years after its release.

During his first Christmas at Hogwarts, Harry receives the Cloak of Invisibility from an anonymous friend who leaves him a note telling Harry it belonged to his late father James. Emboldened by this gift, Harry starts exploring the halls of Hogwarts by night, and one evening, he stumbles upon a room containing a mirror that shows him not only James but his late mother, Lily, and even the extended family he never got a chance to meet. Understandably, the orphaned Harry becomes obsessed with visiting the mirror every night, and despite his confusion when Ron sees something completely different in said mirror, he returns until he finds Dumbledore waiting in the mirror's little room.

Dumbledore explains that it's called the Mirror of Erised, and it shows you your deepest desire. That's why Harry sees the family he never knew, and it's also why Dumbledore tells Harry, "It does not do to dwell on dreams, Harry, and forget to live." Dumbledore is right: Harry's devotion to seeing his family every night in the mirror is a short-term comfort that's terrible for the child's overall mental health, and even though Dumbledore tells him the mirror is moving to a different location anyway, Harry does promise not to look for it again.

Not only that, but in the third act of "Sorcerer's Stone" (as Harry looks for the titular object), we learn that the mirror is part of the defense system that keeps the Stone safe when Harry stares into it and receives the stone not to use but to have. In this way, Harry isn't dwelling on dreams, he's utilizing the mirror to achieve a vital goal.

#3450. How To Rob A Bank Pays Tribute To A Bruce Willis Movie With A Clever Easter Egg

There's something of a paradox when it comes to making legitimately good crime action movies. On the one hand, most filmmakers want the action to be as accurate and based in reality as possible, whether it be robbing a bank, taking down a security truck, or whatnot. On the other hand, they don't necessarily wish to inspire criminals who would copycat a crime they happened to see in a movie, especially as that's an instance where all publicity doesn't necessarily equal good publicity. (Remember the brouhaha over a crime allegedly inspired by 1995's "Money Train," a case which only just reached a resolution a few years ago?)

The irony of the new crime action film "How to Rob a Bank" is that it intentionally wishes to exist on the edge separating these two sides. The film, written by Mark Bianculli and directed by David Leitch, concerns a group of friends who, upon becoming radicalized by the various injustices of the current U.S. wealth gap, decide to become bank robbers. Their gimmick is hiding their crimes in plain sight, filming themselves in the act and detailing exactly how they did it for their YouTube channel (all while hiding their identities, naturally).

Thus, Leitch and Bianculli have to include a bunch of real-world tactics and hardware without going too far. To help accomplish this, they have their bandits (who've dubbed themselves the Wolf Pack) borrow a technique from the sequel to the bonafide action classic that is "Die Hard," i.e. 1990's "Die Hard 2." And while the characters never mention the movie on-screen, the inclusion of a trick used by that film's villains works as both an Easter egg homage to that movie as well as a bit of real-world verisimilitude, as this particular tactic does sound like it could actually work.

In "Die Hard 2," the terrorists holding Washington Dulles International Airport hostage around Christmas are former U.S. Army soldiers who've been corrupted by a military drug lord. After Bruce Willis' John McClane their plans while getting a quip or two in, the airport brass call in a military counter-terrorism unit. Then, during the subsequent firefights between the counter-terrorism unit and the terrorists, each group makes a point of switching to clips for their machine guns labeled with blue instead of red stripes. Eventually, McClane discovers this code means blue for blank rounds and red for live rounds, revealing that both units are working together.

While the terrorists in "Die Hard 2" have devised a fairly elaborate scheme, the blank-vs-live rounds element seems fairly simple and self-explanatory. In other words, it has an authenticity about it, which is why its use in "How to Rob a Bank" feels smooth rather than belabored. The Wolf Pack want to make their robberies feel threatening to the authorities they encounter and only elect to use live rounds to save their own skins. As such, adopting the blue and red labeled gun clips makes for an easy to understand visual code, so much so that the characters in the film barely have to explain it to the audience.

For those who know "Die Hard 2," this is a cute Easter egg calling back to that film's intuitive code system. Yet, for those who don't know, the element still completely works, and its realism adds to the movie's credibility. Who knows if anyone has used it (or will) in real life, but it helps "How to Rob a Bank" exist on that edge.

The Harry Potter film series may have ended in 2011, but its lead, Daniel Radcliffe, remains a household name. He’s made a splash not only by taking on so many “weird” film projects, but he's also made a mark in TV and on Broadway. If you can believe it, the British actor himself said people told him he would have career troubles after his Wizarding World days. However, Radcliffe ultimately succeeded, and he recently recalled how all that happened..

After Daniel Radcliffe nailed his adorable, precious Harry Potter audition when he was 11, his life would change forever. However, the David Copperfield actor opened on The Old Man and the Three about how challenging it was for him in transitioning to life post-Potter. And I didn’t expect such a brutally honest take:

The thing I always say about Potter and what it did for me in terms of like — towards the end of the films I started getting all of us started getting the question a lot from journalists of like, ‘What are you going to do after this?’.... The implication was always like, ‘Well, you're fucked now aren't you? What are you going to do after this? There's nothing left.’ And you know, actually as I look back and I'm like, I can't believe people were saying that kind of stuff to a teenager. It's a really crazy thing to say to a young person.

It's a real shame that people suggested that to Radcliffe and put so much pressure on him at a young age. From the outside looking in, it almost seemed like he was being set up to fail. I can understand that there are many actors out there who are forever remembered for one role. However, that didn't necessarily mean the December Boys actor would be one of them. Radcliffe continued to explain on the podcast that he didn’t let anyone’s negativity bother him:

So I think there's a thing that happens when part of growing up famous is that as you are trying to figure out who you are, you are getting this perceived version of yourself reflected back at you from like a million places and a million people all the time. And so you have to figure out what of that is not real and what you actually are and what you actually want.

After Radcliffe spent so many years playing The Boy Who Lived, I can really understand why he'd go down a path of self-discovery. Even his Harry Potter co-star, Alan Rickman, advised him and other alumni to try theater. And lo and behold, Radcliffe would eventually star in the Broadway show Merrily We Roll Along, which made tons of money and landed him his first Tony Award.

Plus, we can’t forget that Radcliffe got into “deeply fucking weird” stuff in film projects that would come after Potter. To name a few examples, he played a farting corpse in Swiss Army Man, sported pistols for hands in Guns Akimbo, and showed his dark side while growing horns from his head in, well, Horns. Plus, we can’t forget when he put the weird in Weird: The Al Yankovic, which he described as his favorite film he did post-Potter.

It goes without saying that Daniel Radcliffe has been quite fortunate, and he can openly admit he hasn't done it alone. He also credits the creatives he's worked with for hiring him:

So a lot of people were asking us like, ‘What are you going to do after this, and are you going to be typecast?’ And I think there has — I'm sure there is an element of there are some directors out there who particularly in the first few years after Potter didn't want me in their movie because they're like, ‘Everyone will just be seeing Harry Potter when they look at him.’ But for every one of those directors, there was also a director that went, ‘Oh, I would like him in my movie because I want to be the person that reinvents him or that can show an audience this actor that they think they know in a different light.’

Well, there you go. It appears that directors wanted the credit to be able to help show Radcliffe’s versatility outside of playing a wizard. Of course, many filmmakers naturally become impressed when an actor knows how to step outside of his comfort zone and take on different roles. To that point, Radcliffe’s former Harry Potter director, Chris Columbus, was definitely impressed with the talented actor’s career moves when the franchise ended, saying his projects showed how “fearless” he was.

Even though Radcliffe received a lot of negativity that his career would end once Harry Potter did, I’m so happy they were proven wrong. And, with that, the public at large has been able to enjoy watching the actor take on a plethora of roles. While the fantasy franchise will always be a career-defining moment, I’m glad that Radcliffe is thriving and continuing to test himself as an actor.

Fans can still revisit the films that first brought fame to the English actor, though as the Harry Potter movies are streaming now with an HBO Max subscription. And don’t forget that the book-adapted TV series will head arrive on that same streamer as part of the streaming schedule on Christmas Day.

Just your average South Floridian cinephile who believes the pen is mightier than the sword.

#3448. Patrick Stewart Had A Small But Important Role In One Of The Best Animated Movies Of The '90s

It feels impossible to do justice to the late Sir Patrick Stewart with mere words, but we can attempt it. One part of his incredible legacy is voice acting; how could he not try his hand there when he had such a magnificent voice? Stewart's defining voice role is probably the eccentric CIA Deputy Director Avery Bullock on "American Dad." Casting him against type there is the whole joke. Patrick Stewart, famous for playing dignified, fatherly authority figures like Captain Jean-Luc Picard and Professor Charles Xavier, is the one saying all of Bullock's ridiculous, profane, and unhinged lines, which become even funnier read in his baritone voice.

The folks behind the biblical epic "The Prince of Egypt" also knew the weight Stewart's voice carried. At Steven Spielberg's suggestion, DreamWorks Animation adapted the first stretch of the Book of Exodus, or how the prophet Moses (Val Kilmer) — raised as an Egyptian prince — discovered his true heritage and led his people out of bondage. Patrick Stewart plays Pharaoh Seti, adoptive father of Moses and the man who ordered the massacre of Hebrew babies that made Moses' mother send him away. Stewart/Seti has only a few scant scenes in the movie's first act, but he casts a shadow as wide as any pyramid over the rest of the film.

As with later DreamWorks pictures, "The Prince of Egypt" employs celebrity voice casting: Kilmer as Moses, Ralph Fiennes as Moses' brother/Seti's son Pharaoh Rameses, etc. But here, it mostly works — mostly. Jeff Goldblum as Moses' brother Aaron is a distracting bit of casting where you hear the actor first, not the character. "Prince of Egypt" doesn't disguise Stewart's voice either (you probably couldn't with a voice of such power), but it complements his character to a chilling effect.

In "The Prince of Egypt," Seti first appears admonishing his two sons for being reckless in a chariot race. He's especially harsh on his heir, Rameses, explaining that "one weak link can break the chain of a mighty dynasty." When Moses asks his father to go easier on Rameses, Seti offers understanding (and pure dramatic irony): "Moses, you will never have to carry a burden like the crown I will pass to Rameses."

Pretty typical Patrick Stewart, right? Seti is stern but reasonable, some of the same qualities that made Captain Picard such a respected leader. His respect-commanding voice is even more effective as a disappointed father, too; would you want to hear "I'm disappointed in you" from that voice?

But then Moses learns the truth about where he came from, and how. Seeing his son in despair, Seti is gentle but also doesn't deny he had a generation of Hebrew babies murdered as population control. The animation and Stewart's performance work in perfect sync. In Seti's whispered tone, he sounds genuinely pained. Even if his claim "sometimes, for the greater good, sacrifices must be made," rings hollow here, Seti's thousand yard stare tells us that maybe he does feel the weight of what he did and realizes he's damned for it.

But then the kicker comes: He tries to "comfort" Moses that the babies cast into the Nile "were only slaves." The dissonance of Seti loving his own family and also being a genocidal enslaver is potent, but sadly believable. Fittingly, this is also the last time we see him in the film, because the bond he shared with Moses has been severed.

"The Prince of Egypt" is one of the most gorgeously animated films ever made, and it's not only the animation that's beautifully crafted. The storytelling is sharp and mature. It sits at the very fine line of being simple enough for kids and complex enough for adults; Moses and Rameses being turned from beloved brothers to enemies by forces much bigger than themselves is painful to watch.

Right off, "The Prince of Egypt" is an unconventional title for the Exodus story; after all, the whole story is about Moses rejecting that life for his people by birth. (Compare it to the 1956 biblical epic titled "The Ten Commandments.") But the movie paints Moses' deliverance of his people as bittersweet, since it cost him the brother he loved.

Though not nearly as controversial as Nikos Kazantzakis's book (and later Martin Scorsese's film) "The Last Temptation of Christ," "The Prince of Egypt" similarly invents human drama from scripture. "Last Temptation" works from the tenet that Jesus was both fully divine but also fully human. So, then, wouldn't he be afflicted by man's foibles and doubts? The Book of Exodus holds that Moses was raised as an Egyptian in the Pharaoh's own family. Wouldn't Moses, then, feel pained about having to turn his back on the home where he was raised, even if he recognized the necessity of God's plan for him?

Part of the tragedy is that this only flows one way. After Moses learns the truth, he can't look at the enslaved Hebrew workers without thinking their birthright is also his. Conversely, neither Seti nor Rameses clock that the son/brother they love would've been just another of those slaves. It's an excellent use of Patrick Stewart, twisting our relationship to his fatherly presence and providing an undercurrent of darkness to it.

#3447. Nintendo Switch 2 Is Finally Getting Capcom’s Fastest-Selling Game Ever

Who needs GTA 6 when you can battle a dragon instead?

With the success of Resident Evil Requiem, Pragmata, and Onimusha: Way of the Sword, it's safe to say that Capcom has had a fantastic 2026. And the venerable developer's 2025 wasn't too shabby either. Last February, it released Monster Hunter Wilds for PlayStation 5, Windows PC, and Xbox Series X. It went on to sell a whopping eight million copies in just three days, making it the company's fastest-selling game of all time. As of September 2026, Monster Hunter Wilds has sold 12.2 million copies, making it Capcom's 11th-best-selling game of all time. That number is set to go up significantly after Dec. 4, when it finally launches for Nintendo Switch 2.

Monster Hunter Wilds is the first game in the series to let players bring two weapons into the field — you can swap your loadout on the go thanks to your helpful bird friend known as a Seikret. It also adds pop-up camps to allow for a more seamless experience with less backtracking. The new wound system allows players to target a beast's weak points and dole out even bigger damage. You can play with couch co-op, or online with up to three buddies. Best of all, it doesn't matter which console they have — Monster Hunter Wilds supports cross-platform play between all versions, including Nintendo Switch 2,

Folks who pre-order the game ahead of the Dec. 4 launch, will also get a substantial discount. Through Dec. 3, Monster Hunter Wilds is on sale through the Nintendo eShop for $29.99, a 25% discount from its MSRP of $39.99. If you want to try before you buy, there's also a demo featuring the game's prologue available now on all platforms. Save data from the demo will transfer over to the full game if you decide to make a purchase.

If you're a die-hard Monster Hunter fan, the Gold Edition includes an extensive collection of more than 170 DLC cosmetics to customize your character. The Gold Edition isn't currently on sale, and retails for $79.99. That said, the DLC bundle on its own retails for a cool $59.99, so The Gold Edition is slightly cheaper than purchasing the DLC later.

Capcom also has big plans for Monster Hunter Wilds in 2027. The upcoming Ascendance DLC is billed by Capcom as a "massive expansion," which will add a new location called the Skybound Eyrie, which is a network of ancient floating island ruins. It will also introduce challenging Master Rank quests and new monster types. Back in February, series director Ryōzō Tsujimoto said Ascendance will be comparable in scope to previous paid expansions, like Monster Hunter World's massive Iceborne DLC.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

#3445. My Favorite Sony Headphones Are Over $80 Off Right Now

One of the best headphone deals right now is for my favorite headphones: Sony's 1000X series has been around since 2016, with each new model improving on the previous iteration, the latest being the Sony WH-1000XM6, released in 2025. These are the best over-ear headphones I tested in 2025 (or ever, really). Right now, you can get the WH-1000XM6 headphones for $378 (originally $459.99), their lowest price ever, according to price-tracking tools.

The XM6 headphones improve on what were already excellent headphones. Sony upped the count of microphones from eight to 12 when compared to the XM5, which improves more than just how well you sound to someone on a phone call. The microphones are used in almost all of its features, like ANC, Adaptive Sound Control, and the headphones' Ambient Sound mode. They hear your surroundings to adapt their features accordingly. If you switch from a noisy room to a quiet one, the XM6 can switch from ANC to aware mode (if you have Adaptive Sound Control on).

These headphones have a lot more features that you can nerd out on in their companion app. The audio quality is second to none, with the fully customizable EQ giving you plenty of options to get the sound how you like it. I really like being able to see what codec you're listening to in the app's main menu. That way, there's no guessing if you're getting the best audio quality or not. They will give you 30 hours of battery life with ANC on and 40 hours of juice with ANC off. There's an AUX (3.5mm) jack for wired listening, which is a nice touch for audiophiles who still rock iPod Classics (or is that just me?).

The XM6s were not just the best headphones of 2025, but are still the best ones of 2026 and likely to be the best ones for years to come. For $378, you'll be securing the best for a record-low price.

As Sydney Sweeney continues to generate buzz due to her acting career, buzzy lingerie line, those splashy ads and more business ventures, there’s been a continued focus on her personal life. That includes her relationship with Scooter Braun, who has reportedly been helping her make career decisions. As rumors continue to swirl around their relationship, it’s been alleged that Sweeney wants to move to the UK. Now, there’s apparently more evidence that she’s planning a move like Meghan Markle and Prince Harry’s.

Not only has it been alleged that the Euphoria alum is looking for a new residence in the UK, and this claim has sparked a bit of speculation. A recent report from The Sun sheds more light on the purported matter and, according to the outlet, Sweeney recently viewed a property in the village of Little Tew. Per a source, the actress has allegedly informed her people in her inner circle that she’s aiming to split her time between the UK and her multiple properties in the United States. A source for the tabloid also said this:

Sydney has ­visited the Cotswolds twice in the past ten months, and absolutely loves it. She viewed property there within the past three months.

If Sweeney were to make the move, she would actually become just another one of the famous people who live in the area. Among the celebrities who live in the area are David and Victoria Beckham, Ellen DeGeneres and her wife, Portia de Rossi (whose house was thought to have flooded in 2024) and Jeremy Clarkson. The Sun’s insider went on to allege that due to the presence of multiple stars, Sweeney wouldn’t have to worry about residents making a fuss over her, and there’s apparently another benefit:

She doesn’t get bothered by locals, who are all well-used to seeing A-listers, and finds village life incredibly cute and quaint. It’s also a huge change of pace from LA and all the vultures circling. And she can lead a more peaceful life in the countryside. Pinewood Studios are also only about an hour away, meaning she could easily stay at home while filming should she land the gig.

This should all be taken with a grain of salt, considering that no one from Sydney Sweeney’s camp has confirmed or denied that she’s planning to make a new home across the pond. Still, this news comes at an interesting time, considering what’s been going on with the Duke and Duchess of Sussex as of late.

It was reported this past August that Markle and Prince Harry were moving back to the UK alongside their two kids, Archie and Lilibet. For the past six years, the pair lived in Montecito, California, as they relocated to the state after stepping back from roles as senior members of the British Royal Family. Harry and Markle reportedly used a private jet to return to the UK, and the trip allegedly cost them $120,000 in total.

Since returning to the country, the Duke and Duchess’ family has reportedly stayed with friends in the aforementioned Cotswolds. Earlier this month, though, it was reported that the pair had already slightly relocated. Apparently Markle, Harry and their brood moved to the “main house” on the estate after having lived in a “property on the estate.” As for the couple’s attempts to find a place of their own, it’s been alleged that their search has been stalled due to their “champagne tastes” purportedly not matching their financial portfolio.

The public at large will just have to wait and see whether the Duke and Duchess manage to land on a new property in the Cotswolds or somewhere else in the UK. In the meantime, those interested in updates on Sydney Sweeney may continue to watch for any further evidence of a reported move.

#3443. I Ain't Got No Body: The Various Non-Corporeal Aliens In Star Trek Explained

Welcome to Trekspertise, a series where we break down the technology, history, details, and decisions that make the Star Trek universe so complex — and so fun.

One of the primary features of "Star Trek" is theoretical biology. Given the wide panoply of alien species on display throughout the franchise, audiences have been invited to ponder alternate evolutionary paths besides the one that happened to bring us into being on Earth. What kind of planetary conditions would be required to form, say, a hyper-intelligent crystalline being? How did a horta evolve? What will we evolve into in the future? Will our brains adapt to become psychic over time? According to the "Star Trek: Voyager" episode "Threshold" (one of the show's most outraging to fans), it was revealed that humans will eventually evolve into giant salamanders.

This leads to a few logical evolutionary extremes, like the fact that some species on "Star Trek" have evolved into beings of pure energy. "Star Trek" has many examples of non-corporeal aliens who can only be perceived as light, as a psychic presence, as a sound, or as a vision beamed directly into our inferior, corporeal brains. To cite a notable example: In the original series episode "Is There In Truth No Beauty?," audiences were introduced to the Medusans, a highly intelligent, telepathic, and empathic species whose light-constructed bodies are so wildly complex that any human looking at them would instantly go mad. Only a mentally disciplined species like the Vulcans could look at a Medusan, and even then required a special filtered visor (pictured above).

These kinds of aliens expand the audience's mind as to what can be considered life.

In looking at fictional non-corporeal species, "Star Trek" expands our horizons. We're invited to ponder new perspectives about basic concepts like evolution, time, the nature of consciousness, and, perhaps, our own relationship to the cosmos. Non-corporeal entities are one of the coolest ideas "Star Trek" has to offer, and their recurring nature is a constant reminder that life is more complex, and the cosmos more ineffable, than we could ever hope to imagine.

On "Star Trek," non-corporeal aliens tend to appear as lights or clouds or glowing mists of energy. One might recall the smoke-like alien that made Kirk nervous in the episode "Obsession," one of the more underrated episodes of the show. Others might immediately think of Zefram Cochrane's glowing, cloud-like "companion" in the episode "Metamorphosis." That entity had the ability to sort of intuitively communicate with Cochrane (Glenn Corbett), and could also heal diseases and sustain human life beyond its usual biological barriers. A common theme of non-corporeal entities on "Star Trek" is that they are godlike and powerful, able to tap into the powers of the universe in ways we don't understand.

The Medusans may be one of the most popular non-corporeal entities on "Star Trek," but fans of "Deep Space Nine" would surely want me to acknowledge the wormhole aliens, a.k.a. The Prophets. In that show's pilot episode, "Emissary," Benjamin Sisko (Avery Brooks) travels into a stable wormhole and encounters bodiless creatures who can only communicate with him by appearing as people from his memories.

The wormhole aliens from "Deep Space Nine" are so, well, alien, they don't understand concepts like linguistic communication or linear time. They don't see cause leading to effect, but rather a widespread series of events that happen all at once. Sisko has to do the impossible, and explain the human habit of seeing time as a straight line.

And, of course, there are many species of godlike beings on "Star Trek" who often take the form of humans, despite not having physical bodies. Q (John de Lancie) from "Star Trek: The Next Generation" is one of these beings, as is Trelane (William Campbell) from the original series. Those two beings tend to see corporeal humans as lesser species and amuse themselves by taunting and playing with them. Less whimsical is Kevin Uxbridge (John Anderson), a member of a powerful energy species called the Douwd. Kevin took the form of a human, married, and witnessed his wife killed, leading him to, in a moment of ill-temper, commit instant galaxy-wide genocide of a single species. He's the deadliest character in all of "Star Trek."

The list goes on. Q tormented the Calamarain, which exist as ionized gas. There are the Organians, the Lights of Zetar, and the godlike Metrons, the latter of whom oversaw the fight between Kirk (William Shatner) and the Gorn in the episode "Arena," and plenty of other examples. In most cases, non-corporeal entities are so far beyond human experience, it's difficult to communicate with them, much less come to some kind of diplomatic understanding.

But sometimes non-corporeal entities do become our friends. On "Star Trek: Prodigy," the character of Zero (Angus Imrie) is a Medusan who managed to construct a robot-like vehicle for themselves, allowing them to interact with us flesh-beings without exposing themselves. Sometimes the ineffability of the cosmos works in our favor.

#3442. This Bose Portable Bluetooth Speaker Is 33% Off Right Now

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. A price drop always stands out more when the product in question already has a reputation for delivering above its size, and that’s the case with the Bose SoundLink Plus. It hasn’t been on the market for long, but it’s already earned strong reviews—CNET labeled it “the Goldilocks of Bose Bluetooth speakers.” And right now, ahead of Black Friday, it’s down to $179 from $269, which price trackers show is the lowest it’s ever been.

Bose positions it right in the middle of the SoundLink lineup, and you feel that balance in how it’s built. It’s compact enough to clip onto a backpack using its built-in nylon strap, and tough enough to handle getting knocked around, and sealed against dust and full water submersion with an IP67 rating. Battery life can last up to 20 hours, depending on the volume, which is sufficient for full-day outings. On the connectivity side, there’s Bluetooth 5.4 with AAC and AptX Adaptive support, as well as the ability to keep two devices paired for smoother switching. What you don’t get is a microphone, an aux port, or any voice assistant support, which is worth considering if you prefer wired options or use speakers for calls.

As for its sound profile, it leans into mid- and high-bass, which gives electronic and pop tracks a lively pulse, though at higher volumes, you may notice some compression (which is common in speakers this size). It also doesn’t reach into true low-bass territory, so anyone who wants thumping sub-bass may not get it here, but the punch it does deliver feels clean for its size, notes this PCMag review. And while you won't get the width and separation of a stereo mix since the SoundLink Plus plays audio in mono, its directivity is good—meaning its sound remains clear from different listening positions, so you don't have to sit directly in front of it to get a good experience.

#3441. Spotify’s AI DJ adds nine voices and a setting to reduce interruptions

Spotify today expanded customization options for its AI DJ, allowing users to choose between different voices and personalities, as well as control how much the DJ talks between songs. Here are the details.

If you’re not familiar with Spotify’s AI DJ feature, the company describes it as “a personalized mix of music and commentary to help you discover new favorites and connect more deeply with the artists you love,” adding that it takes your listening history into account to “[bring] together your favorite tracks, songs you haven’t heard in years, and new releases to keep things feeling fresh.”

Spotify first introduced the interactive version of DJ in May 2025, and soon expanded its capabilities to Spanish-speaking users. Then, last May, Spotify expanded availability to more than 75 countries, alongside support for French, German, Italian, and Brazilian Portuguese.

Now, as spotted by TechCrunch, Spotify is introducing more customization options, including new voices and personalities, as well as the ability to reduce commentary between songs.

In a new post published on Spotify’s For the Record blog, the company announced today that “Spotify Premium listeners in markets where DJ is available can choose from an expanded selection of DJ voices in English and Spanish,” with seven new English options spanning British, American, Irish, Australian, and Indian accents, along with two new Spanish voices.

Additionally, Spotify now lets users choose whether they want commentary between sets of songs through a toggle that reduces the DJ’s interruptions to brief acknowledgments when starting a session or requesting different music.

#3440. Eight 'Winter Arc' Rules That Will Actually Deliver Results

There are a lot of terrible social media trends out there aimed at self-improvement, yet even though everybody has been making fun of the "Winter Arc" craze, I actually think it’s a good one. During your Winter Arc, you promise yourself you’ll stick to your fitness and self-care routines during (and despite) the end-of-year chaos. It's a good goal, with one caveat: Make sure you choose rules that will actually improve your life and deliver results.

Think of the “arc” in the sense of a “story arc.” The Winter Arc is a self-improvement journey that unfolds over the last few months of the calendar year. The most hardcore #gymtok-ers will tell you the Winter Arc officially begins on Oct. 1, but others start in early November, or whenever they get around to it. The "when" isn't critical, though—whenever you read this is a fine time to start. The close of the Winter Arc is fixed, however: It ends Jan. 1, just as everybody who is less dedicated than you is waking from their holiday food comas and resolving to get in shape.

You get to choose your own terms for your Winter Arc. The general vibe is one of locking in, committing to your goals, and actually doing the things you’re always saying you’ll do. TikToker @carlyupgraded has said that her own mental image of someone nailing their Winter Arc is “hood up, headphones on, getting ready to go for a run in the rain at 5 a.m.”

It turns out I’ve accidentally been Winter-Arc-ing for years; I just didn’t know it had a catchy name. Why save your gym routine for New Year’s when you’ll have the place to yourself all December? We’re even gifted with an extra hour in the mornings to fill with something productive.

I really love the mindset shift involved. Commonly, people are active in the summer (great time for outdoor fun), may or may not stick with their routines in the fall, and let everything fall apart as the holidays approach. Who has time to go to the gym when you’re planning Thanksgiving, attending holiday parties, studying for final exams, or whatever else the end of the year throws in front of you?

But that’s the exact reason why this time of year is the best to start (or restart) a fitness routine, or really any kind of routine. When you start a routine during a busy time of year, you’ll be forced to make it sustainable. The gym routine you can stick with amid the chaos isn’t going to be one you drop after a few months. You’re already training yourself to work around obstacles as they come up, which is a key component of self-efficacy. And when the chaos clears on Jan. 1, your routine will be even easier to stick to.

Of course, there are ways to lean in too hard: Choosing unsustainable habits, falling for bad diet advice, mistaking not masturbating for some kind of health hack, the usual suspects. There’s also the pitfall of focusing too much on the vibes and too little on what you’re actually going to do or how you’ll benefit.

And then there’s the framing: You were working on yourself all year, but you’re in danger of letting up on the gas, but you’re committed to locking in so that you’re a step ahead of everybody who takes this time to slack off. I really don’t love this tack. Self-improvement is not a competition. There’s a difference between being consistent in your training and healthy eating (good) and seeing the pursuit of health and fitness as something where you always have to work harder because you’re at risk of getting left behind.

I also don’t love how gendered the Winter Arc TikToks tend to be. When you search for Winter Arc content, the first few suggestions include “winter arc for women” and “winter arc for men.” When I first started looking at the Winter Arc trend a few years ago, the women’s versions were more likely to include restrictive dieting or to focus on how the Winter Arc will finally (sigh) snatch your waist. These days, the focus is more on personal goal setting: Lots of the girlies filming their Winter Arc rules are doing so in a notebook and talking about journaling exercises that will help you identify what you need to work on to get to your "best self." Sometimes this is all monetized; training plans and journaling prompts can, of course, be purchased at the link in bio.

I do like that many of the women’s versions emphasize sustainability and setting your own goals rather than copying somebody else's. I don't love the enormity of the mental burden you're supposed to shoulder before even beginning. Should I really have to file an in-depth written report with myself before revamping every area of my life with a 100% commitment to multiple goals?

The men’s versions tend to go off the rails in another direction, with rules like “no girls” or “go ghost.” No distractions! Here, I've seen a shift over the years as well: at first there was overly serious content, followed quickly by satire (yelling at the viewer to get divorced and go work out in the dark). Now the men's videos tend to be more vibes-based, featuring images of pre-dawn workouts and plates full of salad with motivational quotes playing in the background. When the men give their rules, they tend to be simpler than the women's—no journaling exercises—but they often boil down to the same overly strict routines. (And then, of course, they'll offer to sell you a 90-day or 60-day plan.)

If you’re going to do a Winter Arc (or if you’re already doing one), make sure to structure it in a way that benefits you. Choosing 10 overly ambitious goals and setting yourself up for failure is not a healthy way to approach self-improvement, OK? Pick goals that are meaningful, achievable without divine intervention, and trackable with tools you already have at hand (for example, tracking your steps with a Fitbit or your running mileage with a Garmin watch).

It’s also helpful to think of developing yourself over this arc, rather than taking it as a three-month (or two-month) challenge where you have to do everything right all the time. If you currently wake up at 8 a.m. and want to wake up at 5 a.m., you don’t have to set your alarm for 5 a.m. tomorrow. It’s OK to aim for 7:30 a.m., make that a habit, then try for 7:00 a.m., and so on.

With that in mind, here are some "rules" I've seen from creators that I'm actually on board with (so long as you don't overwhelm yourself with them):

Wake up earlier. A great goal, especially if you take advantage of the time change to make things easier on your body.

Get to bed on time. Never a bad idea. Cultivating good sleep habits in general is always worthwhile.

Get your steps in. Be thoughtful about what your target is: 10,000 is not for everybody. Better to choose a number that would be a modest improvement on what you already do.

Exercise X times per week. Pick a number that works for you, and get into it. Be realistic about your goal, and for the best results, be consistent even if you’re sore at first.

Eat healthy. This is a great goal, with the major caveat that there are a lot of ways to eat healthy. You don’t need to cut out sugar or pretend that there’s something evil about seed oils. Do get more protein and veggies.

Be more thoughtful about using social media. I’m not going to tell you to delete all your apps (“except TikTok,” as the TikTokers say). But it’s fair to consider whether you might want to delete a few apps, turn off some notifications, or put your phone on Do Not Disturb for more hours of the day.

Journal or read more. Journaling can be great for working through your feelings or cultivating a creative habit. Reading can be entertainment or a great way to learn. Choose whichever you need most.

Learn a new skill. I’ve mostly seen this one in the men’s TikToks, and I love it. They’re often thinking of “skills” that will help in some kind of entrepreneurship grift they’re about to sell you, but there are tons of skills that will come in handy in life, or that are at least fun to learn. Practice a language, get better at cooking, make some art. Skills are, as I’ve noted, a multi-layered exercise for your brain. And they may come in handy someday.

This year I've slacked off on my fitness routine as I've gotten more involved in other hobbies, but I'm actually looking forward to being more consistent. My winter goals include exercising early in the day when possible and reading 20 minutes each day. (I'm even tracking the second one with a sticker chart.)

Ever since the Scrubs revival made its way onto the 2026 TV schedule, I’ve been tuning in, and it really hasn’t disappointed. Last season was good, but I think Season 2 has been especially stellar, and that has a lot to do with what subject matter is getting the spotlight. The new season reeled me in with Dr. Cox’s health developments, but now I’m really hooked thanks to what’s going on with J.D. and Elliot’s relationship. And, I think it’s time I discuss it.

When Scrubs returned to TV, I was instantly taken aback by the choice to make J.D. and Elliot exes. Bill Lawrence defended the decision to CinemaBlend months ago, saying that the couple just couldn’t go a few episodes without “being a horrible couple,” so he wanted to be realistic.

While it bummed me out at first, I’m starting to really appreciate the sort of nuanced conversations that come with J.D. and Elliot no longer being together. They’re both still co-workers and co-parents, so they have to make it work as friends, but I just don’t feel like I see enough relationships like this on TV. My own parents have been divorced for awhile, and I’ve watched their relationship evolve in a new way amidst still being my parents. I know it’s quite common, and yet, for many TV couples it’s either them being together or not.

On that topic, the episode from a couple of weeks ago, “My Story,” really threw me for a loop in the best way. In it, we’re led to believe that J.D. and Elliot end up going to dinner together and deciding to try to make things work again. We learned more about why things fell apart between them, too. But ultimately, we learn the whole scenario is happening in J.D.’s head, and he decides not to pursue their relationship in fear of hurting her once again.

I’m all for love, and a part of me wants to see these two back together, but I'm also really enjoying seeing this unique dynamic on Scrubs. There’s clearly a lot of real love between them, but they were also famously on-again-off again throughout the original run of Scrubs. It feels like we’re getting to watch these two attempt to heal in real time and decide how to go forward in their lives, between being busy medical professionals and being parents, too.

I guess for the time being I’m not thinking about whether I want them together ultimately or not, I just want to continue to see this difficult dynamic between them be explored. I think Scrubs is one of those few shows that can simultaneously be hilarious and emotional, and I think what’s going on between J.D. and Elliot is something worth stretching out for a while.
