#3380. Denzel Washington’s New Crime Thriller Officially Casts a Major ‘Sinners’ Star

Denzel Washington may not be done with the Equalizer franchise, but he's still looking towards the future and other thriller projects to apply his Academy Award-winning talents to. Early next year, he'll appear in The Take, a heist flick on Netflix that has him at the center of a star-studded cast, including Robert Pattinson and Daisy Edgar-Jones. News also broke last month confirming a new team-up with another action veteran, Mission: Impossible director Christopher McQuarrie, for a yet-untitled crime thriller under Amazon MGM Studios. With a release date of October 1, 2027, progress is moving quickly on the project, and the cast is coming together in short order.

The film already has one key role filled by The Marvels star Teyonah Parris, who is set to play Washington's estranged daughter. The story revolves around a former police detective in prison on a life sentence until it's discovered he only has six months to live with terminal brain cancer. He's granted compassionate release and chooses to use that time to reconnect with his daughter and make up for lost time before it's too late. However, what he's not prepared for is the fact that he has a grandson he never knew about and that his dark past hasn't left him behind. Washington's on-screen family is now officially being rounded out with the breakout star of Ryan Coogler's Oscar-winning horror flick, Sinners.

Miles Caton, who earned a Critics' Choice Award and dozens of nominations for his acting debut as Sammie Moore in the Michael B. Jordan vampire joint, will play Washington's grandson in the unnamed thriller. It officially marks the musician's first role booked since opening eyes as the young blues guitarist cousin of the Smokestack Twins. The son of gospel legend Timiney Figueroa, Caton came virtually out of nowhere as a 21-year-old star, having spent his entire career to this point on music, between playing background for H.E.R. and launching his bid as a solo artist with singles like "This Ain't It" and "Lean On" and, as of this year, a deal with Columbia Records. He was critical to Sinners' Grammy-winning soundtrack, even performing "I Lied to You" at the Oscars earlier this year.

For McQuarrie, working with Washington will bring him back to his crime thriller roots that launched him to stardom. Before shooting some of Tom Cruise's most daring stunt work for the big screen, he earned an Academy Award for his work penning the acclaimed 1995 mob movie The Usual Suspects. Scott Barkan and Gregg Zehentner wrote his latest effort, having previously worked together on Into the Dark and Edge of Fear. The production will be a collaboration between Amazon MGM and Scott Stuber's United Artists banner.

Washington and McQuarrie's new crime thriller releases in theaters on October 1, 2027. Stay tuned here at Collider for more on the film as it comes together.

#3379. If you bought an iPhone Duo, have you kept or returned it? [Poll]

When Apple announced the iPhone Duo back in September, the company called it “the most transformational change to iPhone since the original,” and there’s no doubt that it generated a huge amount of excitement.

But a new report suggests that for some buyers the novelty quickly wore off, and they ended up returning their devices. Is this just a handful of people, or is it more common … ?

It’s been a very long time since any smartphone launch has generated quite so much buzz. Apple called it a breakthrough in iPhone design.

iPhone Duo features a breakthrough foldable design that’s beautiful, versatile, and durable, opening up possibilities that feel entirely new yet remarkably familiar […]

“iPhone Duo is the most transformational change to iPhone since the original. With an entirely new design and intuitive experiences, it shows what’s possible when hardware and software are engineered together and redefines what it means to use a foldable phone,” said John Ternus.

Despite not really being the target market for the phone, I was still wowed by the launch video and remained incredibly impressed when I got some hands-on time with one.

Many couldn’t resist buying one despite the price – but The Verge notes that not everyone has ending up keeping the device. Apple allows you to return any product within 14 days for a full refund without having to give any reason. That window has come to an end for some of the first buyers and the site’s Alison Johnson spoke with some of those who’d decided to take advantage of it.

The iPhone Duo replaced both my iPhone 15 Pro Max and my iPad Mini 6. It now is my phone and iPad mini in my pocket. This is the dream phone I never knew I wanted.

And for the lack of Face ID, Touch ID works perfect with my Apple Watch. And even without wearing it, I don’t see the big deal of the ‘huge’ effort of bringing my finger to a button.

For the lacking 5x zoom that I had on my Pro Max, I haven’t had a moment yet that I wanted to use it to be honest. Those moments will definitely arise, but the lack of that camera cannot go up against the amazing overall experience of the iPhone Duo.

But the more fundamental reason for some is that it hasn’t really lived up to their hopes for a multifunctional device.

“If I can have an iPad in my pocket, that would be great.” So thought Ben Seligson, a content creator, photographer, and now former iPhone Duo owner […] “Usually I’d throw a YouTube video on the iPad or throw a podcast up. And then I start cooking dinner and leave my iPad in one spot, but I’d have my phone in my pocket if I got a text, or I needed to set a timer or something like that.” With the Duo, the phone was also the iPad on the counter, so a quick reply became much more of an interruption.

I’m curious as to whether this is just a small minority of buyers or a more common phenomenon. If you bought a Duo early enough to have hit the end of the return window, please take our poll to let us know whether you decided to keep it or return it – and do share your reasons in the comments (which are now back).

Oh, and the good news for anyone buying one now is that you’ll have a lot longer to make up your mind, with the extended return window for the holidays in place. You can now return anything bought today through January 8.

If you’re browsing home security options, Ring has one of the best early Black Friday deals that should be on your radar. Right now, you can add an indoor camera and another one at your front door for less than $65. The Ring Indoor Cam 2K is 58% off at $24.99 (originally $59.99), while the Ring Battery Doorbell 2K is 60% off at $39.99 (originally $99.99)—both at their lowest-ever price.

#3377. Russell Brand Was Sentenced for Rape and Sexual Assault on Monday. By Friday, Netflix Had a Sleazy Doc Ready to Go

The term that comes to mind most is “ambulance-chasing.” Earlier this week, just one week after Russell Brand was convicted of rape and sexual assault and two days after he was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison for his crimes, word spread that Netflix was prepping a documentary on the comedian-turned-criminal.

Olivia Isaacs’ documentary has been in the works for a while. Deadline’s initial story on the project even noted that it “was referenced during the trial” and that while “giving evidence at London’s Southwark Crown Court, Mark Pinheiro, a former friend of Brand, said he had been approached by a producer about the Netflix show.” Related Stories ‘Fatherland’ Wins Golden Frog at ToruńCAMERIMAGE 2026 — Full Winners List After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies

But that the project — “Russell Brand: Open Secret,” a slim and unfocused documentary feature that clocks in at just under 90 minutes — was being dropped on the streamer to ride the wave of interest after Brand’s conviction and sentencing felt distasteful. How essential, after all, could this be? And what could it tell us about Brand’s actual trial, sentencing, and conviction?

Turns out, not much. Isaacs’ film doesn’t get into the trial until its final five minutes (counting its end credits to boot), when it uses title cards to share the conviction news, note that all of the allegations contained in the film itself “pre-date” those that led to the conviction, and make clear that Brand’s legal team was contacted after the Monday conviction and chose not to respond. That’s perhaps the most interesting part of the film’s literally tacked-on final moments: a desire to show its work when it comes to the journalism and attendant standards behind Brand’s long-simmering takedown.

Other elements are far less successful, as Isaacs’ film leans hard on tired tropes and cloying conventions. Captions frequently mention “[unsettling music playing]” or “[dramatic music playing]” during the most benign moments. Old footage of Brand, from home video to early stand-up gigs, is played slowly, all the better to maximize the sense that something is wrong with this man. Far more effective are interviews with those who were allegedly victimized by Brand, but those are often drowned out by played-out techniques.

The film opens with a typical “rise and fall” style montage, charting Brand’s humble beginnings, meteoric rise to fame, profound injection into the cultural consciousness (he met the queen! and also Tom Cruise!), stumble into right-wing ideology, and eventual criminal convictions for horrific acts the film posits everyone knew about forever.

It is, after all, called “Russell Brand: Open Secret.”

Isaacs’ film lacks a thesis beyond the general idea that everyone knew Brand was a creep from the jump. She assembles a hodgepodge of talking heads to hammer that home, including fellow comedians, some genuinely freaked out ex-girlfriends, a handful of accusers (including one who, reticent to appear on camera, is replaced with an actress, one of the film’s most thoughtful choices), and some bizarrely starry-eyed commentators (journalist George Monbiot comes across particularly badly here, zipping from talking about his early delight in Brand and his now-held belief that Brand’s far-right switch is the most horrifying aspect of all of this, oof).

Most compelling are Times journalists Rosamund Urwin and Charlotte Wace, who worked tirelessly to investigate myriad accusations against Brand for years (Urwin first began to look into Brand in January of 2019). Even smushed up against a herky-jerky timeline and a loose sense of purpose, the way that Urwin and Wace talk about the precise nature of their work, what they can and cannot report, the women they spoke to, and the ways in which they were nearly shut down (and, in fact, many other investigations of its ilk were allegedly turned off) is both gripping and necessary.

With more time and better access, the film could have focused more on the police and legal minds that helped build the case against Brand, but in the rush to get this out in the world, that was surely not a major aim.

By its midpoint, Isaacs’ film turns its lens on the culture that helped give rise to Brand, the wild “noughties” when “ladette culture” ruled and being overtly sexy and crude was de rigueur. Women were into Brand! Being ruthlessly unfunny and breathlessly boorish was hot! Also, his dad was mean to him! Diddy and David Walliams jump scares! These are some of the insights on offer in “Open Secret,” and the only thing truly revealing about them is how huge of a mistake it was to let someone as outwardly disgusting and deeply unwitty as Brand get into a place where he could pick and choose his “damsels” or his “whores,” depending on who is talking about them.

The film speed-runs through the last few years of Brand’s life and career, as he pivots into far-right shock politics and Christianity just as the walls are starting to close in on him. Brand may have alleged that his former cadre of famous friends and stalwarts won’t “touch him with a barge pole” these days, but the film’s distinct lack of bigger talking heads stands out. That could stand some further interrogation, too, but there’s simply no time for that. (Well, there is, but not if you want to be a part of this news cycle.)

The four-day gap between Brand’s conviction and the film’s release is zippy, even for Netflix, which has gotten progressively speedier with its true crime joints. In July of 2024, it was announced that Netflix would release a multi-part Karen Read documentary, just days after her first murder trial ended in a mistrial due to a hung jury on July 1, 2024. Three episodes dropped earlier this month.

In January of 2026, the streamer announced a Lucy Letby project with “unprecedented access” after the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) announced it would bring no further criminal charges against the former nurse, who was sentenced to life imprisonment for a slew of charges of murder and attempted murder of infants in her care following a review of additional allegations. “The Truth and Tragedy of Moriah Wilson” was first publicly announced in February of 2026, almost three years after Kaitlin Armstrong was convicted of first-degree murder of the cyclist in November of 2023.

“Russell Brand: Open Secret” will surely capture lots of eyeballs as this part of the news cycle winds down, but what the film trades for immediacy, it more than loses in actual insight. Part two can’t be far behind. Let’s just hope it takes far more time to make and far more consideration to craft.

“Russell Brand: Open Secret” is now streaming on Netflix.

#3375. Apple Won't Make a Small Phone so This Company Is Stepping In

Big smartphones have long been the norm. It seems many, if not most, of us prefer our smartphones to be akin to tiny tablets. Even Apple's smallest iPhone isn't that small, with a 6.1-inch display. (Compare that to the 5.4-inch iPhone mini it used to sell.) But just because a lot of us like it that way doesn't mean all of us do.

Despite what companies like Apple would lead you to believe, there are plenty of people out there who want their smartphones to be smaller. For some, the iPhone mini was perfect, featuring a design that most could use comfortably with one hand. While the sales might not have been steady enough for Apple to continue producing the mini line, anecdotally, I know quite a few people who would happily keep using iPhones this small, if only Apple would make more of them. Perhaps you know people like this too; maybe you're one of them.

While the rumor mill does not suggest that Apple plans to make a new iPhone mini, that doesn't mean the dream of the tiny smartphone is dead. Enter "Enough Phone," a new device with a humble goal: to create a "small, modern smartphone that's enough."

Enough Phone really does seem small. The company says its upcoming device is 133mm by 64mm, and less than 12mm thick. That's the equivalent of 5.24 inches by 2.52 inches, and less than 0.47 inches thick. It's remarkably similar to the iPhone 13 mini, at 5.18 by 2.53 inches, and 0.3 inches thick. While the Enough Phone might be a tad larger overall, and perhaps noticeably thicker, it's still reminiscent of that "mini" footprint.

The Enough Phone's 5.3-inch display isn't particularly modern, however. While we don't know the display type, we do know that it has a resolution of 1520 x 720, which may look less sharp to anyone coming from the 2340 x 1080 resolution of the iPhone 13 mini. I'd wager that most people interested in a device like this aren't looking for an ultra-sharp OLED display anyway, but it's worth noting here.

As for the Enough Phone's other specs, the company says it plans to pack in a 2.4GHz MediaTek Dimensity 7500 chip with 8GB of RAM, 128GB of built-in storage, though you can expand that with a microSD card (something you don't see on many smartphones these days). The current plan is to ship with a single 50MP Sony IMX766 rear camera, and a 32MP selfie cam, which would be amongst the highest-resolution front-facing cameras on any smartphone. It supports 5G, Wi-Fi 6, and eSIM, with the option to use a physical SIM as well.

Enough is also aiming to make its smartphone more repairable than the competition. While smartphone OEMs have made slight improvements to repairability in recent years, few phones are made to be opened up by the user, and their components replaced. While Enough Phone isn't fully modular, it is designed with easy-to-open screws, and comes with a fully replaceable 3,500 mAh battery. Combined with promised software support through 2032, Enough says this device "should last you into the next decade."

Now, all of these specs are targets, as the phone is currently in the prototype stage. Enough says that final details may change "slightly" during testing. I would at least hope that the dimensions, particularly the screen size, remain the same by launch. What will likely stay the same, however, are the ringtones: Enough says they hired composer Brian Squillance of LAANDS to produce the jingles for its phone, which is a neat touch.

Unfortunately for Apple fans, however, Enough Phone isn't an iPhone. That said, it doesn't have to be an Android phone, either. While you can buy the phone with Android 17 installed, you can also choose to run OdysseyOS, a minimalist "de-Googled" operating system made by SLEKE. Enough says OdysseyOS is meant for "intentional phone use," which might appeal to anyone looking for a phone that's "dumb" as well as small.

Of course, neither operating system is iOS. Unfortunately for Apple users, the only true iPhone options here are to continue using an old iPhone mini, which Apple does still support, or to opt for an iPhone 17e, the smallest iPhone the company currently makes. It's pretty easy to find a used and refurbished iPhone 13 mini for reasonable price; but while they can still run the latest version of iOS, you won't be able to take advantage of all of Apple's newest features. Plus, while there's no telling how long Apple plans to support the 13 line for, it won't support it forever—by iOS 28 or iOS 29, your phone might lose support entirely.

If the promise of a modern mini smartphone entices you, you can back the Enough Phone on Kickstarter today. While the company's $399 "Super Early Bird" reward is already sold out, as of this article, the "Early Bird" reward is still up. That reward costs $449, and includes a glass screen protector pre-installed, a protective case, a USB-C cable, a USB-C to 3.5mm headphone adapter, a hex screwdriver, and green "Founders' Edition" backplate screws. Enough says that the retail price for its phone will be $599 after the campaign, so you can save $150 by backing the phone today—if you're serious about small phones. The Enough Phone is slated for a May 2027 launch.

#3374. 7 Pointless Sci-Fi Movie Remakes That Were Worse Than The Original

The science fiction genre has been particularly afflicted with movie remakes that couldn’t hold a candle to the original. Sci-fi has always been one of cinema's most imaginative genres, exploring technological breakthroughs, alien civilizations, dystopian futures, and the potential extinction of humanity. Sci-fi's greatest stories are often remarkably adaptable, with ideas that remain relevant across generations. Naturally, Hollywood has repeatedly returned to successful science-fiction movies, hoping to introduce familiar stories to new audiences with bigger budgets, modern special effects, and contemporary interpretations.

Unfortunately, updating a classic doesn't necessarily improve it. Some older science-fiction movies were products of particularly inventive film-making, using practical effects, intelligent writing, and ambitious social commentary to create worlds that audiences hadn't experienced before. Reproducing their basic premises with more sophisticated technology can leave remakes looking considerably less impressive, especially when the original's most interesting ideas are diluted in favor of generic action and spectacle.

Hollywood has produced plenty of successful sci-fi reimaginings, but there are also several examples that struggle to justify their existence. Whether they misunderstand the original's central themes, replace distinctive characters with forgettable alternatives, or simply fail to capture the same imaginative spirit, these remakes demonstrate that some classics really are better left alone.

The Day the Earth Stood Still (1951) is one of science fiction's greatest films, using an extraterrestrial visitor's warning to dissect Cold War paranoia, nuclear proliferation, and humanity's capacity for self-destruction. Scott Derrickson's 2008 remake, starring Keanu Reeves as the alien Klaatu, attempts to modernize that message by replacing the original's anxieties about nuclear warfare with environmental destruction.

Unfortunately, the updated version sacrifices much of the intelligence that made its predecessor so effective. The remake certainly has impressive visual effects, particularly when Gort unleashes a swarm of microscopic machines capable of consuming everything in their path.

However, its environmental message is surprisingly muddled, with the remake struggling to reconcile its ecological concerns with conventional disaster-movie spectacle. The original’s memorable philosophical exchanges and restrained tension are replaced by an overreliance on destruction and spectacle. As a result, it lost all its charm and was left feeling notably hollow.

Paul Verhoeven's Total Recall (1990) is gloriously excessive science fiction. It combines Arnold Schwarzenegger's unmistakable action-hero charisma with grotesque practical effects, absurd humour, and an increasingly complicated mystery surrounding Douglas Quaid's identity. Len Wiseman's 2012 Total Recall, starring Colin Farrell, is considerably more interested in looking futuristic than recreating the original's wonderfully strange personality.

Both films follow an ordinary construction worker who visits Rekall, a company promising to implant artificial memories of an exciting adventure. However, the remake abandons Mars entirely, relocating the action to a dystopian Earth divided between the wealthy United Federation of Britain and the impoverished Colony.

The production design is undeniably impressive, particularly the enormous futuristic cities and the Fall, an underground transportation system connecting the two territories. Unfortunately, Total Recall's visual similarities to Blade Runner are distracting, and its elaborate action sequences lack the personality of Verhoeven's original. There's also no equivalent to Schwarzenegger's outrageous one-liners, the bizarre Martian mutants, or the unforgettable practical effects that made the 1990 film so distinctive.

H.G. Wells' The Time Machine has inspired numerous adaptations, but George Pal's 1960 film is particularly memorable for its imaginative depiction of a distant future divided between the peaceful Eloi and the subterranean Morlocks. Simon Wells, the author's great-grandson, directed a new adaptation in 2002, starring Guy Pearce as Alexander Hartdegen.

Despite its impressive production design, the remake struggles to recreate the sense of wonder that made its predecessor so effective. The biggest change is the addition of a romantic motivation for Hartdegen's time-traveling adventures. After his fiancée Emma (Sienna Guillory) is killed during a robbery, the scientist becomes obsessed with traveling backwards through time to prevent her death. His repeated failures eventually lead him 800,000 years into the future.

The revised motivation makes the story considerably more personal, but it also reduces the intellectual curiosity that drives Wells' original novel. Instead of exploring the consequences of humanity's social and evolutionary divisions, The Time Machine resembles a conventional adventure about a man attempting to rescue a romantic interest. Jeremy Irons' sinister Uber-Morlock provides an entertaining antagonist, but the character feels more like a generic blockbuster villain than an interesting development of Wells' ideas. It lost all sense of wonder and replaced it with bland action.

Frank Oz remake of The Stepford Wives transformed an unsettling satire on technology and social conformity into an underwhelming comedy vehicle. Bryan Forbes' 1975 adaptation of Ira Levin's novel follows Joanna Eberhart (Katharine Ross), a photographer who moves with her family to a seemingly idyllic Connecticut suburb. She gradually discovers that the town's husbands are replacing their wives with obedient robotic duplicates, creating a nightmare vision of patriarchal control.

The 2004 remake, starring Nicole Kidman and Matthew Broderick, retains the basic premise but dramatically changes its tone. The light-hearted interpretation certainly features some funny jokes but completely undermines the message of the original. The critique of patriarchal control becomes a star-studded farce – cheapening its central message.

It feels a lot like the original movie itself has been replaced by a compliant robotic duplicate designed to perpetuate the status quo. The 1975 Stepford Wives presented the idea of men literally engineering their ideal wives as frightening, the modern remake decided it was funny.

Rollerball (1975) imagined a future in which multinational corporations controlled society and maintained public order through a violent spectator sport. Starring James Caan as Jonathan E, the original used its fictional competition as an allegory for corporate power, consumerism, and the suppression of individual freedom. The 2002 Rollerball remake, starring Chris Klein, largely abandons that political sophistication in favor of chaotic sporting violence.

The new version relocates the action to Central Asia, where Rollerball has become a hugely popular extreme sport. Jonathan and his friend Marcus (LL Cool J) become involved in the competition, only to discover that promoter Alexi Petrovich (Jean Reno) deliberately engineers increasingly dangerous matches to improve television ratings.

There is certainly potential in updating the original's criticism of corporate entertainment for an era dominated by reality television and sensationalist broadcasting. However, the is much more interested in showing people crashing into one another than examining why audiences enjoy watching them suffer. Furthermore, Rollerball's heavily edited matches are frequently difficult to follow, while Klein lacks the commanding presence Caan brought to the original.

Paul Verhoeven's RoboCop (1987) is a particularly effective fusion of science-fiction action, political satire, and grotesque violence. Peter Weller plays Alex Murphy, a Detroit police officer murdered by a gang of criminals before being resurrected as a technologically enhanced law-enforcement machine. His gradual rediscovery of his humanity provides the emotional foundation for a film that simultaneously ridicules corporate greed, privatized policing, and sensationalist television.

José Padilha's 2014 remake updates that premise for an era of military drones, surveillance technology, and sophisticated robotics. Consequently, it should have had so much more to play with. Indeed, there are interesting ideas here, particularly through Gary Oldman's Dr. Dennett Norton, who becomes uncomfortable with the corporation's manipulation of Murphy's memories and emotions. However, the remake's more restrained approach to violence removes an essential ingredient of Verhoeven's satire.

The original Robocop's exaggerated corporate advertisements, grotesque news broadcasts, and outrageous action sequences made its criticism of 1980s capitalism considerably more effective. Padilha's version is slicker and more technologically sophisticated, but its conventional action-movie structure simply cannot match the original's personality.

The original Death Race, directed by Paul Bartel and produced by Roger Corman, starred David Carradine as Frankenstein, a masked driver competing in a cross-country race where contestants earned points for running down pedestrians. Its deliberately outrageous premise provided the foundation for a gleefully tasteless satire of authoritarian entertainment and America's obsession with violence.

Paul W.S. Anderson's version replaces the original's bizarre road-racing competition with a prison-based televised spectacle. Generic muscle man Jason Statham plays Jensen Ames, a former racing driver framed for murder and imprisoned in a privately operated facility run by the calculating Warden Hennessey (Joan Allen). She offers him a chance to regain his freedom by taking the place of the masked racer Frankenstein, competing in heavily armed vehicles against other prisoners.

The remake delivers plenty of entertaining automotive carnage, with its armored cars, mounted machine guns, and elaborate stunt driving providing some impressive action. However, Death Race loses much of the original's darkly comic premise. The 1975 film's scoring system, which rewarded drivers for killing pedestrians, was an absurd extension of its dystopian satire; Anderson instead turns the concept into a fairly conventional prison-break adventure. It’s not a remake in the conventional sense, but a reimagining based on the least important parts of the iconic sci-fi original.

CNET says that in the 45-minute stress test they “stream videos, make a video call, play games and scroll social media.” So it’s an attempt at replicating normal use.

#3370. Will ‘Dune’ and ‘Avengers’ Drown Out Everything Else at the Box Office This Christmas?

Look, it’s only November, but we know we’re not the only people getting excited about Christmas already. In fact, we know that some studio executives have been thinking about the holiday season a lot for a while now. That’s because they know as well as anyone that they have two juggernauts to contend with: “Dune: Part Three” and “Avengers: Doomsday,” which open on Dec. 18 in true clash of the titans fashion.

There’s a question that if those movies take up so much oxygen, will there be room for anything else? The last “Dune” movie surpassed $700 million globally at the box office, and “Avengers: Doomsday” has already sold over $60 million in pre-sales. Those top two titles create enormous competition for everything opening on Christmas weekend itself. Those include the Dwayne Johnson threequel “Jumanji: Open World” from Sony, the football biopic “Mr. Irrelevant” from Paramount, Robert Eggers’ horror film “Werwulf” from Focus, and Luca Guadagnino’s “Artificial” from Neon. Paramount’s “The Angry Birds Movie 3” is also opening on December 23 just ahead of the rest. Related Stories ‘Fatherland’ Wins Golden Frog at ToruńCAMERIMAGE 2026 — Full Winners List After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies

Anyone will tell you the Christmas holiday is always crowded at the movies. And there’s usually room for multiple blockbusters to draw crowds. Despite the onslaught of new titles, U.S, distributors are confident they’ll be able to secure the screens they need to be successful. For instance, “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” this year opened at the end of July to $360 million domestic, and “The Odyssey” in its third week in theaters still made $50 million. Even during the “Barbenheimer” weekend, “Sound of Freedom” in its third week managed to bring in another $19.8 million. There’s always opportunity if the demand is there.

Recent Christmases have been similarly crowded. Last year had “Avatar: Fire and Ash,” “The Housemaid,” a new “Spongebob,” and “Marty Supreme” open the weekend before Christmas, then “Anaconda” and “Song Sung Blue” over the holiday itself. 2024 had “Mufasa: The Lion King,” “Nosferatu,” “Sonic the Hedgehog 3,” “A Complete Unknown,” “Babygirl,” and “The Fire Inside” all in a short span just before Xmas.

But this Christmas does bring some unique challenges that studios are preemptively working around for their titles that are not “Dune” or “Avengers.” Both of those films have had tickets on sale for months, and both are locked in a fight for premium large format screens that distributors would be lying to say they didn’t want, even if it’s for a family film that doesn’t need it. Warner Bros. and Legendary’s “Dune: Part Three” specifically will exclusively be on IMAX screens, which has famously left “Doomsday” without them, leaving Disney to create its Infinity Vision certification to drum up excitement.

To compete, “Angry Birds 3” is still opening in 3D if on otherwise standard format screens. “Werwulf” won’t have IMAX as Focus did for “Nosferatu,” but it has pre-sold select 35mm screenings of the film that have already done quite well (they went on sale on the full moon last month). The hope, too, is that titles like “Jumanji” and “Mr. Irrelevant” appeal to crowds that are distinctive from the male, fanboy-heavy audiences for “Dunesday.”

One source IndieWire spoke with argued that even though this Christmas is top heavy, it’s arguably lighter in sheer quantity than we’ve seen in recent years. What we’re not seeing is a movie like “Marty Supreme” or “Uncut Gems” getting a run in a more mid-size or limited number of screens. Universal doesn’t have a movie opening in that window, nor does Amazon MGM. Other awards titles like “The Debut” from A24 are going earlier in the month and aren’t doing the limited, Christmas day, qualifying run before going wide in January (GKIDS’ “Look Back” may be an exception, opening December 30).

There are some potential holdovers that could generate money well into Christmas. Rival studio execs are keeping an eye on movies like Disney’s animated “Hexed” or Universal’s “Focker-in-Law,” and Focus’ “Elsinore” will also be going wider shortly before the holidays.

The hope now is that all of these films get their flowers and collectively put an exclamation point on a stellar 2026, with the box office now projected to finish far above $10 billion domestic, a number that might’ve been a pipe dream this time in 2025. That’s reason for holiday cheer, indeed.

#3369. Three Ways to Avoid CAPTCHA Prompts When Using a VPN

VPNs make it harder to track your online activity across websites, but it also makes them suspicious about your origins. When you borrow an IP address that hundreds of other people are also using for any number of reasons, you’re much more likely to get repeat verification requests from online firewalls.

CAPTCHAs are simple puzzles that websites use to filter out bots and spam. They’re supposed to be easy for people but hard for robots, such as simple object recognition tasks or audio-visual challenges. However, they can still disrupt your browsing experience if they happen too frequently.

Most modern CAPTCHA providers, like Google's reCAPTCHA v3 or Cloudflare Turnstile, start working long before they give you a puzzle to solve. It usually starts with a risk score that studies your IP address, browser and device signals, or recent online activity.

If the CAPTCHA provider can’t confidently identify your request as human based on those signals, it requests that you complete a puzzle before deciding if the request should be blocked. That means when you get repeat CAPTCHA requests, there’s something affecting your browser’s risk score. For example, popular VPN servers spread the same IP address across any number of users, which can easily make a website mistake you for a bot farm. If you change your IP address frequently by switching servers often, that might look suspicious too.

Luckily, there are ways to deal with frequent CAPTCHA requests using tools and services available with your browser and VPN. Cloudflare has already cut its CAPTCHA requests by 91% using its Managed Challenge platform. Apple has also been shipping token-based verification on devices since iOS 16 and macOS Ventura. In June 2026, Cloudflare even announced a joint effort called the Private Access Control Tokens (PACT) standard with Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Shopify.

While there’s no direct off switch for CAPTCHAs, you can use different fixes to improve your browser’s trust signals when using the internet. That way, you’re less likely to be hounded by verification requests.

The easiest fix for repeat CAPTCHAs is to stop connecting to whichever server your VPN app picks automatically. Proton recommends choosing servers with lower traffic load. In fact, its apps display load as a percentage to help you avoid the most crowded options. I'd also skip big traffic hubs like New York or London, since that's where most traffic originates from. Servers in smaller cities located nearby are often just as fast but never as populated.

You should also avoid changing IP addresses too frequently, which can look suspicious on its own. Pick a server that seems to behave well, then continue using it for at least one session. Also remember you’re more likely to get premium server options if you’re on a paid VPN plan. Major platforms like ExpressVPN, Surfshark, Proton, and Nord are particularly likely to have a larger server collection to pick from.

Costs nothing more than your current subscription

Hopping between servers often can backfire

Private Access Tokens (PAT) let you verify the authenticity of your request using your device rather than an IP address. Apple calls it Automatic Verification, where an Apple server validates your device and Apple Account to assign you an anonymous token.

To enable Automatic Verification on an iPhone or iPad, go to Settings > [your name] > Sign-In & Security > Automatic Verification. On a Mac, open System Settings > [your name] > Sign-In & Security > Automatic Verification.

Unfortunately, there’s no equivalent feature for Windows, Android, and Linux users. That said, Cloudflare offers the Silk extension for Chrome, Firefox, and Edge that serves a similar function. A quick look at the ratings will tell you it’s not as effective, but Cloudflare’s upcoming cross-browser standard called PACT seems promising once it is released.

Doesn’t share personal details with websites

Chrome and Firefox extensions can be unreliable

If you pay a bit extra for a dedicated IP add-on, VPN providers can assign you a unique IP address that isn’t shared with anyone else. For example, NordVPN offers dedicated IPs in 30 countries for $2-5 a month and Surfshark charges $3.75 a month for it.

There are also dedicated providers like Private Internet Access, which charges $3.99 per month for a zero-trust setup so not even their employees know which IP address is assigned to you. On the other hand, Proton VPN offers dedicated IPs only to business plan users, so you’ll need to be on the Workspace Standard, Premium, or Enterprise plans to get one.

That said, there is a trade-off here too. NordVPN itself admits that a dedicated IP makes it easier to link online activity back to a single user. Also, many websites can still tell that the IP address originated from a VPN data center rather than a consumer’s device.

Get unique IP addresses with pristine reputation

Works across desktop, mobile, and even smart TVs

Also functions as an allowlisted address for work

Add-ons cost more on top of the VPN subscription

Offers less anonymity than shared VPN servers

#3364. watchOS 27.3: Three new features coming soon to Apple Watch

watchOS 27.3 will launch to all users next month and introduce these three new Apple Watch features.

Siri AI keeps getting new features and also expanding to more languages. And in watchOS 27.3, the assistant will improve in both categories.

watchOS 27.3 upgrades Siri AI with new app actions across built-in apps like Calendar, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, and Weather. With these capabilities, Siri on your wrist can do more than ever.

There are also four new Siri AI languages supported in watchOS 27.3: Chinese (traditional), Norwegian, Turkish, and Vietnamese.

For the latest Apple Watch models, watchOS 27.3 adds a new Audio Intelligence feature called Live Rewind. Per Apple’s website:

Live Rewind recalls what was just said in the last 15 seconds by showing a text snippet on your Apple Watch when you double-press the Digital Crown, so you can catch something you missed or are less familiar with. You can ask Siri about the content of the snippet or simply save it to the Siri app.

I’m curious to see how useful this proves in everyday life. When Apple demoed the feature in September, it showed Live Rewind being used at a restaurant when an Apple Watch user missed part of the server’s menu explanation. Asking the server to repeat what they said seems like an easier solution, but perhaps there are other occasions Live Rewind will come in handy.

It won’t be for everyone, but I’ve been testing watchOS 27.3’s new Siri Recap feature and really love it.

Siri Recap only works on Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, and it’s off by default. But if you have one of those models and enable the feature, Siri can create automatic logs of what’s happening in your day-to-day life.

Most of the time, you won’t need to reference any of the recaps and they’ll be automatically deleted after a week. But based on my experience with the feature, Siri Recap definitely comes in handy at times when trying to remember key details from conversations.

Which of watchOS 27.3’s new features are you most interested in? Let us know in the comments.

Nine years after its October 2017 debut, and five years after episode #170 went off the air in March 2021, Studio Pierrot’s seasonal overhaul is finally giving Yuki Tabata’s shonen epic the universal acclaim it always deserved.

That newfound respect is showing up across every major metric. Black Clover currently sits at #6 on IMDb’s global Most Popular TV Shows chart, standing completely alone near the top while the next closest anime, Attack on Titan, trails way back at #50. On top of dominating viewership on Crunchyroll, season 2 also delivered the highest-rated anime episode of 2026 after episode #5, “The Highest vs. the Lowest,” scored a near-perfect 9.9/10 on IMDb.

However, the anime is burning through the manga so quickly that a traditional season 3 might not make sense. Tabata’s eleven-year manga run officially ended in May 2026 in Jump GIGA with chapter #392, leaving just 122 chapters between the end of season 1 (chapter #270) and the finale.

With season 2 reportedly planned for 24 to 26 episodes across two cours, the first cour is already adapting the 61-chapter Spade Kingdom Raid arc. By its end, the anime will be ready to enter the final 61-chapter Ultimate Wizard King saga. Whether Cour 2 covers the Land of the Sun and Judgment Day battles in 2027 or reaches the showdown against its next major threat, Asta's journey may wrap up in a completely different format rather than a traditional season 3.

On paper, Black Clover season 2 adapting four to five manga chapters per episode makes it look like Studio Pierrot is racing through the remaining story. However, that breakneck pace has more to do with how Yuki Tabata structured the Spade Kingdom Raid arc. Most of those chapters are packed with massive double-page spreads, fast fights, sparse dialogue, and shorter 13-to-15-page counts. Five chapters of nonstop action might sound like a lot, but they don't necessarily translate into five times the usual amount of animation.

That should change as the anime moves into the final Ultimate Wizard King saga, which begins with chapter #332. The story shifts towards heavier lore, character development, and longer conversations, especially during the Land of the Sun training arc with Ryuya Ryudo and the Ryuzen Seven.

Black Clover also moved to Jump GIGA in late 2023, where chapters became longer, often reaching 20 to 25 pages. With all that in mind, the adaptation rate could naturally drop to two or three chapters per episode. If Cour 2 follows that pattern, season 2 could end around the peak of the Judgment Day invasion, leaving the final stretch for a separate finale.

Even then, there won't be enough chapters left to fill a traditional 12- or 24-episode season 3. A canon theatrical movie could be one way to finish Asta's story. With Demon Slayer: Infinity Castle, Jujutsu Kaisen 0, and Chainsaw Man – The Movie: Reze Arc showing the box-office potential of anime films, Studio Pierrot has plenty of reason to consider it.

The studio also has experience with the format. Its 2023 film, Black Clover: Sword of the Wizard King, was directed by current season 2 director Ayataka Tanemura and became a hit on Netflix. A theatrical finale could give the series the grand send-off its long-awaited return deserves.

A theatrical movie isn't the only way Studio Pierrot could wrap up Asta's story. If the studio wants to keep the finale on television, it already has the perfect blueprint in Bleach: Thousand-Year Blood War. Pierrot worked with Tite Kubo to expand the manga's rushed final arc with new fights, extended backstories, and never-before-seen Bankai reveals. Yuki Tabata could take a similar approach with an expanded final cour for Black Clover.

With the manga officially ending, the final war against Lucius has finally revealed the absolute strongest mages.

Tabata struggled with health issues towards the end of his Weekly Shonen Jump run and had to condense several side battles during the Judgment Day war. An anime adaptation could finally give those moments the time they deserve, whether by extending the Magic Knight Captains' fights against upcoming threats or adding more material after chapter #392. So, while Black Clover might not get a traditional season 3, that doesn't mean Asta's story is ending with season 2. Between a theatrical finale and an expanded final television event, the series still has plenty of ways to give its fans the ending they've waited years for.

Asta and Yuno, orphans with a shared dream of becoming the Wizard King, follow distinct paths: Yuno with natural magic abilities, and Asta through determination despite his lack of powers.

#3362. I Played Wendy's RPG, and It's Actually Worth It for the Free Food

November is a huge month for video games. Nintendo dropped its remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Switch 2 last week, and the long-awaited Grand Theft Auto VI is right around the corner. But the game we've been waiting for most of all also launched this month: WendyQuest, the free RPG from Wendy's. (No, this is not a joke.)

Despite the absurdity of a hamburger chain making a full video game (complete with Wendy's-themed puns), the thing is, this game is pretty solid—even if it is a promotion at the end of the day. WendyQuest's main purpose is to offer customers coupons they can use toward purchases in real life, though it's a bit of a commitment. It took me just under an hour of gameplay before I earned my first coupon, and Wendy's says it takes roughly 15 hours to beat. All that to say, this is a pretty unique marketing campaign.

I was surprised booting up WendyQuest on my iPhone. This doesn't necessarily feel like a thrown-together product. On the flip side, the production quality is quite high. The music is solid and very much traditionally RPG; there are even three save slots, in case you plan to return to this RPG again and again.

There's even a story, albeit cheesy (no pun intended): As the game explains, the "Four Great Spirits of Flavor" created Savoria, "a food-rich paradise." All was well until Mech Corp, led by the evil Dr. MechBorg, built robots to take over Savoria. The plot is far from compelling, and the writing can be a little over the top, but hey, I'll give them credit: They thought through a full story here.

You play as Wendy, the "representation of true culinary excellence and taste as dictated by the four ancient spirits of flavor." Wendy (or The Wendy, as some call her) is tasked with saving the world, traveling between villages and picking up new characters along the way. The game world even has "real" Wendy's locations you can visit. These act like inns and shops in other RPGs, giving you a chance to heal while also buying equipment.

Like other RPGs, WendyQuest uses turn-based combat. You have to charge up your attacks, but stop before they hit 100%, or you'll miss. (It took me a while to master the timing.) I'm pretty impressed with how challenging some of these battles can be, though you are quickly given the option of an amulet that gives you a huge leg-up in combat. You don't have to take it, but it makes fights easier if you're only in it for the coupons. That, combined with the spatulas the game encourages you to buy, lets you mow down enemies. You can also utilize your companions here: "Frygor," for example, can either attack enemies with a barrage of fries, or use those fries to build a shield to protect you.

While there are tons of enemies to fight, the key baddies are the "mechs." There are five in total, and after you defeat each, you get a coupon. Spoiler alert: The first mech drops the "Fry Stone," which nets you a coupon for a free order of medium fries—though you need to buy something in tandem, as well as use the Wendy's app. While I stopped my gaming here for this article, the other four coupons are:

Free biscuit or croissant (I didn't even know Wendy's sold biscuits and croissants)

Again, it's wild that WendyQuest has a 10+ hour campaign, with over 1,000 lines of dialogue to boot. I'm not sure this is a game I'm going to see through to the end, but I'll admit, it's a fun marketing approach from Wendy's. Sure, they could have run a promotion in the Wendy's app to give people coupons, but instead, they built an entire RPG. I respect it. You can download the game for iOS, Android, or Steam.

#3361. Taylor Sheridan’s Hit Western Series Officially Dominates Streaming Worldwide

From Mayor of Kingstown and The Madison to Lioness and Landman, Taylor Sheridan's impact on modern television through his pantheon of shows cannot be overstated. Currently, the fourth season of Tulsa King is the latest to dominate the streaming charts, as viewers remain gripped by Sylvester Stallone's Dwight "The General" Manfredi and his fight "to legitimize his empire while facing corrupt politicians and new enemies."

As Season 4 continues weekly, Season 5 of Tulsa King remains in production in New York. Erik Palladino, Glenn Fleshler, Anthony Skordi, and Nickola Shreli have already been added to regular series roles, with it confirmed that Girls and Ironheart star Manny Montana has also joined the growing ensemble as "Gilberto Torres, a gangster with a strong presence, though he doesn’t have to advertise it." The good news continues for Sheridan fans, as the most important series in his catalog has returned to the global streaming stage.

At the time of writing, Yellowstone is one of the ten most-watched shows on Paramount+ in the world, a list featuring the aforementioned Tulsa King in second place. Sheridan's flagship series ran for six years, five seasons, and 53 episodes, rarely missing a beat as it helped pioneer a Western renaissance on the small screen. The show's impact cannot be overvalued, as the current landscape of 21st-century streaming simply wouldn't have been the same without its major pop culture impact.

The show that claimed the most of your answers is the world you were built for. If two tied, both are shown — you're complicated enough to straddle two Sheridan universes.

You are a Dutton — or you might as well be. You understand that some things are worth protecting at any cost, and that the modern world's indifference to history, to land, to legacy, is not something you're willing to accept quietly. You lead from the front, you carry your family's weight without complaint, and when someone threatens what's yours, you don't escalate — you finish it. You're not cruel. But you are absolute. In Yellowstone's world, that combination of ferocity and loyalty doesn't make you a villain. It makes you the only thing standing between everything that matters and everyone who wants to take it.

You thrive in the chaos of high-stakes negotiation, where the money is enormous, the margins are thin, and the wrong word in the wrong room can cost everyone everything. You're a fixer — the person called when a situation is already on fire and needs someone with the nerve to walk into it. West Texas oil country rewards exactly what you are: sharp, adaptable, unsentimental, and absolutely clear-eyed about what people want and what they'll do to get it. You're not naive enough to think this world is fair. You're smart enough to be the one deciding who it's fair to.

You are a Dwight Manfredi — someone who has served their time, paid their dues, and arrived somewhere unexpected with nothing but their reputation and their wits. You adapt without losing yourself. You build loyalty through respect rather than fear, though you're not above reminding people that the two aren't mutually exclusive. Tulsa King is for people who are still standing when everyone assumed they'd be finished — who find, in an unfamiliar place, that they're more capable than the world gave them credit for. You don't need a throne. You build one, wherever you happen to land.

You carry the weight of a system that is broken by design, and you do it anyway — because someone has to, and because you're the only one positioned to do it without the whole thing collapsing. Mike McLusky's world is for people who are comfortable operating where there are no good options, only less catastrophic ones. You speak every language: law enforcement, criminal, political, human. That fluency makes you invaluable and it makes you a target. You've made your peace with both. Mayor of Kingstown belongs to people who understand that keeping the peace is not the same as being at peace — and who do the job regardless.

Yellowstone might've been off-air for two years and counting, but its impact on the streaming charts hasn't faded. This is thanks to the ever-expanding Yellowstoneuniverse, with one of the most dramatic spin-offs currently mid-season.Marshals, the neo-Western police procedural that is both a spin-off and sequel to Yellowstone, is now five episodes into its second season, with last weekend's installment, "Secret Explosion," picking up in the aftermath of Rudy Carpenter's (Braxton Hale) suicide explosion. The synopsis for the upcoming Episode 6, "Roughstock," reads:

"With Cal away in Utah seeing a cancer specialist, Andrea steps up as team leader and is instantly tested when Kayce ventures outside Marshals jurisdiction to help Mo track down his missing nephew."

Yellowstone is one of the ten most-watched shows on Paramount+ in the world. Make sure to stay tuned to Collider for all the latest streaming stories.

#3360. Google Gemini for CarPlay now available

Google’s Gemini AI chatbot app for Apple CarPlay is now available. The company confirmed that it is bringing the full Gemini Live conversation experience to CarPlay on Wednesday, and the app update arrived on Thursday.

Google bringing Gemini to CarPlay is especially notable for one reason. Gemini was the last major AI chatbot holdout.

CarPlay has supported AI chatbot apps and other conversational apps for a while now.

iPhone apps including ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude, Copilot, Meta AI, and Grok all shipped CarPlay support already. Siri includes a standalone app in iOS 27, which also supports CarPlay.

Google has previously supported Gemini features through Google Maps on CarPlay, but not the Gemini Live experience through the dedicated chatbot app.

“Gemini on Apple CarPlay is rolling out globally starting today to all Gemini users on iOS across every supported Gemini Live language,” Google says.

“To get started, make sure you’ve updated to the latest version of the Gemini app on your iPhone, enabled microphone permissions, and used Gemini Live on your phone at least once. The next time you connect your phone to your car, tap the Gemini icon on your CarPlay display, then start a new conversation or pick up a recent one.”

Google Gemini for CarPlay is now available through the iPhone App Store.

#3359. IndieWire Honors Film Celebration to Fête John Turturro, the ‘Artificial’ Cast, Los Javis, and More

IndieWire, the definitive outlet for creative independence in film and TV, announced on Friday, November 13 the lineup for the Winter 2026 edition of our IndieWire Honors event, featuring our largest lineup yet of film honorees. Curated and selected by IndieWire’s editorial team, IndieWire Honors is a celebration of the filmmakers, actors, and artisans key to crafting some of the most exciting cinematic works this year.

The event will take place on Thursday, December 3 in Los Angeles, starting with an intimate cocktail reception and awards ceremony. IndieWire will also begin rolling out exclusive editorial content, including honoree profiles, on Friday, November 27 through the lead-up to the awards night. Throughout the ceremony, into the next day, IndieWire will publish photos and exclusive social content from the event as well. The ceremony’s host will be announced at a later date. Related Stories ‘Fatherland’ Wins Golden Frog at ToruńCAMERIMAGE 2026 — Full Winners List After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies

“It’s thrilling to be able to recognize the artists behind so many of this year’s most exciting and compelling films,” said Brent Lang, IndieWire’s editor-in-chief. “They dazzled us with their talent, inspired us with their willingness to take risks, and left an indelible mark on cinema. We are excited to celebrate their accomplishments.”

“It’s exciting to celebrate such an eclectic group of film talent for this year’s IndieWire Honors,” said James Israel, IndieWire’s SVP and Publisher. “We are also pleased to continue to celebrate top craft artisans in entertainment.”

The Winter 2026 IndieWire Honors honorees are:

The fact that he is known for being a frequent collaborator of both Spike Lee and the Coen brothers conveys just how expansive an actor Turturro is. The Brooklyn native is quintessentially New York, as most recently proven in Sony Pictures Classics’ acclaimed Sundance premiere “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,” written and directed by Noah Segan. Yet, a filmmaker can still drop the performer into the corporate dystopia of sci-fi series “Severance,” or have him go on a Southern odyssey in “O Brother, Where Art Thou?,” and he just as well hits it out of the park.

With nearly five decades of film work under his belt, starting with an uncredited role in “Raging Bull,” Turturro manages to be one of the few veteran actors who continues to best himself year after year.

The pair of Madrid-based directors colloquially known as Los Javis are not shy about cluing the audience in on the shoulders upon which they stand on. They cast Penélope Cruz and Lola Dueñas, two muses of auteur Pedro Almodóvar, as the most important women within their epic adaptation of an unfinished play by Federico García Lorca, another one of Spain’s queer artist forefathers. That reverence is balanced by the confidence in their own eye for new talent, weaving together three different timelines led by three relative unknowns, including most notably, indie musician Guitarricadelafuente, who also contributed the poignant original song “La Nieve” to the project.

Made outside the Hollywood system and chosen to represent Spain in the Best International Feature Oscar race, the Netflix release “La Bola Negra” is a film of immense scale. If viewers knew nothing of the director duo before seeing the film, they come away with a crash course in everything they are about. Considering how they won both the Best Director Award at Cannes, and the coveted People’s Choice Award at TIFF, it seems to be an experience most cinephiles enjoy.

“Tallgrass” is the code word that unlocks what makes the creative collaboration between “Paper Tiger” writer-director James Gray and star Adam Driver such a feat. Though the Neon release, which premiered at Cannes, is their first time ever working together, the filmmaker imbues the two-time Oscar nominee with such a specific vision of what it feels like to realize one’s time has gone by. Though the film is another deeply personal work in the oeuvre of the Queens-born auteur, Driver adds a more broad portrait of a figure wrapped up in crime, slowly feeling the overwhelming situation constrict and constrict.

“Josephine” was not made to be an easy watch, but boasts the rare feat of winning both the Grand Jury Prize and Audience Award at the Sundance Film Festival. Written and directed by Araújo, and starring Gemma Chan and Mason Reeves as mother and daughter, the drama is a bold exploration of how little control parents have over their children being confronted by certain horrors in life that there’s no guarantee of avoiding.

An early release for new distributor Sumerian Pictures, “Josephine” has only felt more necessary as the year has gone on, and news stories like the Cornell rape case have come to the forefront. It is a conversation piece about a subject many wish to evade, that puts forth the effort to reach meaningful discourse.

The most bold artistic choice in “Artificial,” the latest film from prolific director Luca Guadagnino, is to not proffer any romance in becoming one of the Promethean figures. The repeated refrain of “Feel the AGI” rings as a benevolent threat by the time the two hours and 20 minutes of the Neon release are over. Garfield, Borisov, Barbaro, and Barinholtz, all four playing key figures in the genesis of OpenAI, play incredibly off of each other as tech titans forcing a smile as they convince their audience artificial technology is inevitable. Join or die. Their joint efforts to invoke a common sense of humanity would be funny if the reality of the situation weren’t so uncanny.

Re-teaming with her “Secret Sunshine” director Lee Chang-dong almost 20 years later, the “Possible Love” star is unmissable as a woman caught in a class divide between her blue collar, out-of-work husband, and the couple that hosts them as a means to interview them for a documentary. It is a role that she said uses “the whole entirety of her body” to push back against the weight of capitalism. The Netflix film chosen to represent South Korea in the Best International Feature category at the 2027 Oscars offers a feast of ideas, with Jeon’s layered turn as Mi-ok alone being enough fodder for many conversations to come.

All sorts of biopics enter theaters each year, but few task their leads with the difficult job of playing someone still actively in the public eye. In Peter Farrelly’s “I Play Rocky,” from Amazon MGM Studios, newcomer Ippolito deftly captures the distinctive look and sound of a young and hungry Sylvester Stallone. But what is more impressive than that form of transformation is how the 27-year-old actor captures the spirit of the unlikely star and scribe of the 1977 Best Picture winner. How some of his best moments come when he himself plays Rocky is a meta element we are still unpacking, but add it to the overwhelming evidence that Ippolito is one to watch.

There is a standout moment in Oscar winner Siân Heder’s “Being Heumann” in which Madeley, as trailblazing disability rights activist Judy Heumann, asks a well-meaning congressman what he means by calling her “inspiring.” “Inspired to do what?,” she says. It is a moment that clarifies that the film about Heumann leading the successful protest to get the government to sign Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act is not standard fare about a woman in a wheelchair overcoming odds, but a film about her refusing to let those odds overcome her.

Madeley embodies a fight against circumstances that applies to more than just the disability community. May casting directors take notice of the limitless potential she offers as part of any type of ensemble.

As the President and CEO of Laika Studios, Knight has spent over 20 years educating audiences on the artform of stop-motion animation. And still, in his latest film “Wildwood,” a fantasy epic taking place in the forests outside Portland, Oregon, Knight directs scenes that seem inexplicable. It is hard enough to animate one bird flying, using that technique, yet the Fathom Entertainment release sees whole flocks fly off toward a war between species. The film’s commentary on parents and children is as heartrending as the craft behind how the film was made is genuinely inspiring to filmmakers of all types.

Talk about legacy. Decades after his father, noted documentarian William Greaves, hosted a party for the surviving members of the Harlem Renaissance, “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” co-directed finished the film, one of the gems of Sundance 2026. To listen to Black luminaries from the ‘20s speak about how their work has endured into the ‘70s, with the dramatic irony of watching the film through a modern lens, is a singular cinematic experience. In a year where there is so much conversation around what pushes the documentary artform forward, the Neon release delivers both necessary context and innovation.

There is humor in having puppetry, one of the world’s oldest artforms, at the center of a conversation around innovation, but come on. Ortiz’s performance as Rocky in “Project Hail Mary,” supported by the work of visual effects team leaders Scanlan, Lambert, and Sarnowska, made us fall in love with a spidery alien rock that has no mouth or face. Puppetry’s forebearers would have still found that to be an insurmountable challenge. Hence, why the artist behind the fan favorite character opposite Ryan Gosling in the Amazon MGM Studios blockbuster deserves their flowers for helping viewers go beyond their earthly imaginations.

If you’re building a new cordless tool set, or updating your battery system, getting a cordless tool set can save you some money because these combos usually include batteries and a charger, which can be the most expensive part of your tool set. Here are a few of the best early Black Friday deals on cordless tool sets.

The set comes with a drill, an impact driver, a circular saw, a sawzall, an oscillating multi-tool, a work light, a 1.5-amp-hour battery, a 4-amp-hour battery, a charger, and a tool bag. This is a great starter set because it has the first two tools you need for a cordless kit and it comes with batteries so you can expand your set for cheaper as you develop your skills.

This set is handy for DIY projects that require fine detail, like wood carving, craft projects, or framing pictures.

The DeWalt drill and driver combo set is on sale for $149, 38% off its regular price on Amazon. This set includes a drill, an impact driver, 2 1.5-amp-hour batteries, a charger, and a tool bag. This is a good deal on a trusted brand for drills and drivers, and a good start for a cordless DIY tool set.

If you have a cordless tool set already and you want to expand your kit, or if you have a DIYer in your life who already has a particular brand of battery and you want to get them something they can use, a single tool deal can be just the thing.

The DeWalt 20-volt compact drill/driver is on sale at Home Depot for $99, 45% off its usual price. This tool comes with a 20-volt, 2-amp-hour battery and a charger, so it’s ready to use out of the box. It’s a good first tool for a set.

The Milwaukee 18-volt impact wrench is on sale at Home Depot for $199, 68% off its typical price. This tool comes with two 5-amp-hour batteries and a charger, so it’s ready to use out of the box. This is a good tool for driving bolts through tough materials and for automotive projects.

#3356. Apple offers a military discount, here’s how to get it

If you’re a member of the U.S. military, Apple offers an easy way to save 10% on eligible products and accessories. It’s available to current and veteran members of the U.S. military and their immediate family members living in the same household. While you’ll need to verify your eligibility to access the discount, the process is simple. There are also a few limitations you’ll want to know about before placing an order. Here’s everything you need to know.

A 10% discount is available to current and Veteran members of the US Military, National Guard and Reserve. Immediate family members who reside in the same household are also eligible.

Verification is handled through ID.me. Creating an ID.me account is free, and current military members can verify their service using their .mil email address. Veterans can enter details of their service information for ID.me to verify, or upload images of official documents (such as a DD-214) for ID.me to review and confirm their eligibility. Once you’re verified, your ID.me account can also be used to access military discounts from other retailers and services that support ID.me verification.

Once verified, you can start shopping by visiting Apple’s Store for Veterans and Military. The discount only applies to Apple products and accessories (including Beats) so third-party products aren’t eligible. Apple services, such as Apple Music and iCloud+, are also excluded. Orders can be shipped directly to you, or you can choose in-store pickup if the product is available at a nearby Apple Store.

This is probably the biggest catch. Apple specifically says ACMI isn’t available when shopping through the Veterans and Military Store. You can still earn 3% back in Daily Cash with Apple Card, but you lose the option to finance your purchase at 0% interest over several months. Apple Upgrade also isn’t available when purchasing through the military store.

The only way to get the military discount is to make your purchase through Apple’s website in a browser. The Apple Store app isn’t an option, which means you also can’t take advantage of Apple’s “Get Ready” feature to select your iPhone model, color, storage capacity, and carrier ahead of pre-orders opening. Instead, you’ll have to navigate Apple’s website on launch day, when demand is high and server traffic can make checkout more challenging. Whether the 10% savings is worth giving up the convenience of a potentially quicker checkout is ultimately up to you.

The military discount can’t be combined with carrier promotions or discounts on iPhone purchases. You can still trade in your existing iPhone through Apple and receive the applicable trade-in value, but you can’t take advantage of carrier-specific trade-in offers, like promotions that give you a larger credit when you trade in an eligible device and activate or upgrade a line.

These purchase limits reset on January 1 each year.

Apple’s military discount is a useful perk, especially if you’re buying a product at launch and want to save 10% right away. However, it’s worth comparing prices with other retailers before you buy, since sales and promotions can sometimes beat Apple’s discount. The military store also comes with a few limitations, so you’ll want to weigh the savings against the features and payment options you’re giving up. Even with those caveats, 10% off can make a real difference on an expensive Apple purchase.

#3355. Pokémon Colosseum Is Officially Coming To Nintendo Switch 2

Over the years, Game Freak has brought Pokémon fans all kinds of different games in the franchise, from sprawling open-world adventures all the way back to the original raft of Game Boy releases that started the whole journey. Along the way, there have been some arrivals that are markedly different from just about anything else.

Pokémon Pokopia is a solid recent example, applying the cute creatures we all know so well to a survival crafting formula. Back in the day, though, the examples that spring to mind most readily would be Pokémon Stadium and Pokémon Colosseum, both of which had been relegated to the annuls of time for the last couple of decades.

Pokémon Stadium has been available to Nintendo Switch 2 players for a while now, but Colosseum has remained noticeably absent, despite being the better game in the eyes of many. That was scheduled to change, but things have gone frighteningly quiet, leaving many wondering what exactly is going on.

In case you missed it, Nintendo announced a bunch of iconic GameCube titles would be coming to the Nintendo Switch as part of the Classics Catalogue (as long as you have the Expansion Pack). Those included games like The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker, F-Zero GX, and SoulCalibur 2, as well as Super Mario Sunshine, Fire Emblem: Path of Radiance, Pokémon XD: Gale of Darkness, Super Mario Striker, Chibi-Robo!, and, crucially, Pokémon Colosseum.

The interesting thing about that is that all of those titles are now available for Nintendo Switch 2 players to enjoy, apart from the conspicuously absent Pokémon Colosseum. Neither Nintendo nor The Pokémon Company have commented on the reason why, though the length of the gap between the initial announcement and its still pending arrival would suggest that there may be some kind of issue.

As much as it's hardly the very best of the series to date, it really was a lot of fun to play back then, and returning to it in the cold light of 2026 would likely be a nostalgic experience, if nothing else. It would also come along at the perfect time, as the vast excitement around the 30th anniversary starts to die down and we wait to see what's coming next for the series.

What we do know in that regard so far is that the first games of the tenth generation will be Pokémon Winds and Waves. Within those, players will be exploring an archipelago of sorts, based on certain portions of South-East Asia.

As with all games that debut a new generation, we'll have a whole fresh roster of 'mons to track down and add to our dex. The last couple of generations haven't really managed to be as memorable as they were likely intending, so they could really do with a set of releases that managed to nail down a handful of iconic designs.

The next Pokémon games could also do with more than a subtle evolution in terms of the gameplay as well, with the last few efforts feeling like they were treading water more than anything else. If they can get it all right though, the games easily have the potential to recapture the magic of those first few iconic releases.
