#3354. Production Designer Ruth De Jong on How to Build (Ancient) Worlds for Auteurs

From the misty seaports of Massachusetts seaports to the otherworldly town of Twin Peaks and even the distant shores of Troy, Ruth De Jong has spent the past twenty years transporting audiences into the unforgettable worlds created by auteur directors like Paul Thomas Anderson, Terrence Malick, Kenneth Lonergan, David Lynch, Jordan Peele, and Christopher Nolan.

“My goal in my work is to always paint the most authentic pictures,” De Jong shared with IndieWire at the Virginia Film Festival, where the production designer received the festival’s Craft Award. The town of Charlottesville has a special place in De Jong’s heart.

It’s here where legendary production designer Jack Fisk, father of De Jong’s high school friend Schuyler Fisk, suggested she forgo attending the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts for grad school in favor of working on the set of Paul Thomas Anderson’s 2007 Oscar-winning film “There Will Be Blood” instead. Recalling that fateful conversation, De Jong said that Fisk told her he saw the younger version of himself in her, sharing, “I think what the world continually needs are mentors [like Fisk] showing up.” Related Stories ‘Fatherland’ Wins Golden Frog at ToruńCAMERIMAGE 2026 — Full Winners List After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies

De Jong fell in love with filmmaking as she continued to work with Fisk on Anderson’s “The Master,” and a handful of films by Terence Malick, including his Palme d’Or winner “The Tree of Life.” Eventually she spread her wings and took on her first film as production designer: Kenneth Lonergan’s “Manchester by the Sea.” Looking back on these early days and everything she learned on those sets, De Jong said that she believes “a body of work like that is built upon itself. I think I’m constantly pulling from the past, but also pulling from the future.”

Whether designing a fishing village in modern-day Gloucester, recreating the White House Oval Office, or crafting the iconic Trojan horse, all of De Jong’s work comes in service of the characters and story being told. While crafting a film’s world, De Jong asks herself, “How do I make this tangible and alive and real and authentic?”

To capture undertones of the real working-class people in the fishing community at the center of “Manchester by the Sea,” this meant spending time with local fishermen. “We asked if we could go into their houses. We asked if we could use their fishing boats. We asked if we could use their lobster cages and rope everything, and then we would,” De Jong recalled. All of this research helped De Jong nail the subtle nuances and layers of the region. “You’re always striving to not make it cliché,” De Jong told IndieWire.

The first step involves breaking down the script. At this phase of her process, De Jong attaches an image to each scene. “It may be a piece of art. It could be a photograph. It could be a texture. It could be a piece of cloth. It could be anything,” she shared, adding, “Then from that, I add physical locations, and we start putting the whole thing together and seeing our film.”

Sometimes these images come from the director themselves. While working on “Twin Peaks: The Return,” David Lynch gave De Jong some of his own artwork for inspiration. “He would hand me some of his paintings, his drawings, his work, and say, ‘Here, this is this set. Build that,,’” De Jong revealed, adding that even if it was “a flat 2D painting, the colors were wild and it’s textural.” These came in handy for the new worlds of the series, like the landmark Episode 8 (also known as “Gotta Light?”), in which De Jong designed the radio station and other eerier riffs on the atomic age 1950s.

For the more iconic aspects of “Twin Peaks, ” De Jong also dug up the original plans for the Red Room from the 1990s. “David remembered in his mind’s eye,” De Jong said, “and I’m there to continue to be David’s conduit on the new work. It was just a beautiful, beautiful dance.”

Along with reviving iconic sets from pop culture’s past, De Jong herself has created work that has become part of the entertainment firmament. The set she created for the “Jupiter’s Claim” theme park in Jordan Peele’s “Nope” has been added to the Studio Tour at Universal Studios Hollywood, a unique feat for an aspect of filmmaking that is often binned as soon as a production wraps. On the honor of her set being preserved in such a way, De Jong said, “It’s pretty incredible, because in the act of doing it, you aren’t thinking about what this is going to turn into.”

After receiving her first Oscar nomination for her work on Christopher Nolan‘s Best Picture-winning biopic “Oppenheimer,” De Jong re-teamed with the writer-director this year for his ambitious take on Homer’s epic poem “The Odyssey.” For this film, her process began at Nolan’s home, where she spent hours reading the script. Afterwards, De Jong asked for the parameters. “He said, ‘There are none,'” De Jong recalled.

This allowed the designer the freedom to “take the audience on the same journey that Odysseus (Matt Damon) was on,” she said. Starting with seven countries, De Jong and Nolan began searching for the film’s faraway locations, the only edict being that Nolan wanted the film to start in the Mediterranean and end in the Mediterranean. Without the barriers of realism, De Jong found inspiration in locations across the globe. “We didn’t care that we were shooting the Laestrygonians in Scotland. It didn’t matter. It just had the topography we were interested in. Same with Iceland and the same with Morocco,” De Jong said. Once the locations were determined, then came building sets that reflected the characters who inhabit them.

For the ominous stone house owned by Circe (Samantha Morton), who beguiles Odysseus’ men and turns them into pigs, De Jong shared that Nolan “was very clear about not wanting Circe’s home to be a Hansel and Gretel in the woods type cottage. She’s so peculiar and unique and bizarre and a witch.” With this in mind, the duo decided she should live on the edge of a cliff, finding the perfect craggy rocks in Scotland. Soon, a whole backstory informed the building of her dwelling. “She formed her house out of those craggy rocks,” De Jong said, adding, “We just made up all these stories and created the sets from there.”

The same attention to character informed the creation of the iconic Trojan horse, an imposing image of which opens the epic film. Nolan envisioned a rearing horse, telling De Jong that “it has to be iconic and it has to be larger than life.” For Nolan, De Jong said, the question at the center of this opening scene is, “Are the Trojans going to accept the gift?” Thinking about what kind of horse would be accepted, Nolan wanted their horse to be “the antithesis” of the one in Wolfgang Petersen’s 2004 film “Troy.” “We didn’t want the clunky wheels,” she said, adding that “these were master shipbuilders.”

“They’re master craftsmen,” De Jong insists, “If they collected all this wood, why don’t we shiplap the entire body, shiplap the tail? They hand-carved the legs and the head. That leaves the body all hollow like a ship, so all the men could all go inside and cut a trap door.” Once they agreed on the backstory for the building of the horse, the next step was figuring out how to make multiples out of fiberglass (and later out of plastic as one of the summer’s hottest collectible popcorn buckets).

As “The Odyssey” marches its way into awards season, De Jong is looking towards her future – and her next gig. With every project she takes, De Jong is looking to push herself as an artist. “It’s that space of being uncomfortable that is how you know you’re in the right place,” she said, adding, “The minute I find comfort, I realize I’m in the wrong place. So I’m always pushing to get back into that area of discomfort.”

Thinking back to her conversation with Fisk all those years ago, De Jong feels that what he taught her was “The act of physically doing and going and staying in momentum,” adding, “That’s something that Christopher Nolan has. All of these directors; They don’t stop producing work. They don’t do it in vain. They do it because that’s their language and their medium. They’re all artists at heart.”

Although De Jong looks back at her past fondly, she doesn’t regret forgoing art school to join the movie business. What she learned after all these years is that, “You need to go forward, and even if you go forward and you hit a wall, then just keep pivoting a little bit. Stay open and don’t be fearful. You can’t fear. I’d rather screw up royally and have tried than not tried at all.”

#3351. FX’s Best Breakout Series Is Officially Changing Its Formula in Season 3

Giovana Gelhoren is a High-Trending Topics Writer at Collider, covering the most-talked-about stars, movies, and TV shows. Before joining Collider, she was a Digital News Writer at People Magazine and served as Associate Editor at SheKnows, where she honed her expertise in celebrity coverage and entertainment journalism.

A proud Latina from Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, Giovana graduated from Northwestern University with a degree in Journalism and International Studies. She has interviewed countless celebrities, including Anne Hathaway, Halle Berry, Pamela Anderson, Jamie Lee Curtis, and Brenda Song, and is known for her encyclopedic knowledge of film, TV, and pop culture.

From shows like Not Suitable for Work and Overcompensating, the young adult comedy genre (not to be confused with YA shows) has seen several exciting new additions lately. But as Overcompensating's long-awaited Season 2 gets ready to release, FX's beloved addition to the genre, Adults, is getting more support than ever.

After premiering Season 2 of Adults on August 27, 2026, the series, which follows five young adults dealing with the ups and downs of life, love, and friendships as they live in a house in Queens, just got the green light for Season 3. While the new installment has yet to have a release date, creators Ben Kronengold and Rebecca Shaw confirmed to Variety that Season 3 will consist of 16 episodes, double the eight episodes inits first and second seasons. The extra room not only shows the studio's commitment to the series and how successful it's become, but sets the series up to become an all-around comedy classic.

The Season 3 renewal of the series was confirmed by Variety on November 11, 2026. “We started working with FX over six years ago, back when Paul Baker was but a twinkle in all of our eyes,” said Kronengold and Shaw of Jack Inannen's now viral character. “In the years since, John [Landgraf] and the rest of the team have taught us everything we know about how to lead, produce, and tell stories that make people feel like part of a community. They’ve become family, and we’re so glad to make it official — and to start yelling at them like we do our parents.”

Four of the largest communities on the planet, and four completely different reasons to belong to one. Here is yours, what it would give you, and the argument you would be having within a week.

You belong to the fandom that is really about comfort. Hogwarts works on people because it is a place rather than a plot, and the pull is not the wizard war so much as the corridors, the food, the weather and the sense that somebody is expecting you.

You belong to the deepest fandom on this list, the one where somebody has always read further than you and is quietly delighted to say so. Middle-earth rewards patience more than any other world in popular culture.

You belong to the loudest and largest tent of the four, the one where three generations are all watching the same thing and none of them agree about any of it. That disagreement is not a flaw in this fandom, it is the main activity.

You belong to the thinking fandom, the one that turns up for the argument rather than the explosion. Trek has always been a series of ethical problems in space, and the people who love it love being asked what they would have done.

Of course, the renewal isn't exactly a surprise. On Rotten Tomatoes, the sophomore season of the series scored a flawless 100% from critics and a still very impressive 96% from the audience. In Collider's review, Taylor Gates stated that the second season continued what made Season 1 so great, and delivered even sharper, funnier storylines. "In Season 2, the group interacts with everything from K-pop to viral man-on-the-street interviews, making it feel new and resonant," Gates wrote. "In addition to the sharp dialogue, there's an impressive amount of well-executed physical comedy, and the cast goes all in with the slapstick vibes."

All those features together meant that Season 2 showed how production honed in on the magic of Season 1 and delivered an increasingly funny series to viewers. "With better, more refined writing and performances that feel even more confident and lived-in, Adults achieves something that few shows do by improving in its sophomore season," Gates concluded.

Now that the third season of Adults is renewed and is confirmed to be longer than its previous installments, the series has almost unmatched potential. After all, one of the biggest advantages of a longer third season of Adults would be the opportunity to let its central friend group grow at a more natural pace. With 16 episodes, the comedy could embrace the kind of everyday storytelling that made older ensemble sitcoms, like Seinfeld or Friends, so enduring. The seemingly insignificant conversations, unlikely character pairings, running jokes, and low-stakes misadventures that gradually make a fictional world feel like home. More time spent inside Samir’s (Malik Elassal) house would allow viewers to become even more invested in the rhythms of the group, not just their biggest moments.

A longer season would also give the characters room to make mistakes, experience setbacks, and figure out adulthood without having to rush through those experiences. Their messy relationships, professional frustrations, and sometimes unhealthy dependence on one another are all part of what makes the show's portrayal of being young and figuring things out feel recognizable. Rather than resolving conflicts within a handful of episodes, 16 episodes could allow those tensions to build and evolve organically.

Ultimately, Adults is the kind of comedy that could benefit from spending more time with its characters. While the short seasons so far have been a hit, a longer season could hit the sweet spot, proving that sometimes an ensemble sitcom isn't always about where the story ends up, but about the small, familiar moments along the way. Giving this friend group more episodes to simply exist together could make the show even more rewarding to follow. Fans are surely in for a treat.

Adults: A 2025 film exploring the journey of a group of codependent housemates navigating the complexities of adulthood. As they attempt to be good individuals, they grapple with their shortcomings and growth, reflecting the challenging transition from youth to maturity.

#3350. After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies

With Cannes entry “Bitter Christmas,” Oscar-winning Spanish auteur Pedro Almodóvar (“Talk to Her”) is back making movies in his native language. Since his debut “Pepi, Luci, Bom and Other Girls Like Mom” in 1980, Almodóvar has written singularly identifiable, heightened, rhythmic, and mellifluous Spanish dialogue.

While Tilda Swinton and Julianne Moore adeptly wrangled his translated English in Golden Lion-winner “The Room Next Door,” which deployed his usual bright Almodóvar colors and exacting mise-en-scène, the director did not enjoy dealing with the unions in New York. “In Spain everything is much more immediate, and also it is my language, it’s my culture,” he told me during the New York Film Festival. While he doesn’t rule out making another English-language movie, it would have to be small-scale. “I don’t find myself, anymore, capable of dealing with a production that is chaotic with a lot of people and a lot of characters.” Related Stories ‘Fatherland’ Wins Golden Frog at ToruńCAMERIMAGE 2026 — Full Winners List Production Designer Ruth De Jong on How to Build (Ancient) Worlds for Auteurs

Now he’s back in Spain in self-referential, meta autofiction mode in full force. The results are exhilarating. “Bitter Christmas” offers a movie within a movie, as writer-director Raúl (Leonardo Sbaraglia) crafts a script that lifts some key story points from his friends’ experiences. Even though Almodóvar considers the movie one of his riskiest, it’s the filmmaker’s biggest hit in Spain since “Volver.”

Almodóvar considers “Bitter Christmas” to be “twins” with Oscar-nominated “Pain and Glory,” which starred his old favorite Antonio Banderas as his alter ego. “‘Pain and Glory’ is more about the physical pain, right?,” he said. “The character [Raul] has had a lot of surgeries, and his fear is about that the fact that he’s not going to be physically able to to handle another another film shoot. Whereas in this film I deal with a different pain, which is the pain of writer’s block, of the blank page, or writing something that doesn’t quite come together for you. The character of Aitana in the film says to Raul, ‘you know we are all losers, you have lost grace.’ And by grace it means inspiration, something that is equally painful to that writer-director as the physical pain was to the writer director in ‘Pain and Glory.'”

Mostly when Almodóvar sits down to write, he’s making things up. He’s gotten into trouble in the past for raiding his friends’ stories. “There is not any law that creates the limits of the autofiction,” he said. “There is no law that’s going to define the limits of what you can appropriate and what you can’t appropriate. But if I’m inspired by the life of someone who’s close to me, who’s going through a difficult time, as a writer, you are selfish, because what propels you is the idea, even if it means going against the relationship. I don’t feel comfortable the two or three times that I did it. This is the limit: not to hurt anyone. But it’s normal that writers are influenced by everything in life you see, you talk to with others, you read, you see movies. So it’s impossible to renounce the influence of the life of others.”

And he’s passionate about making movies. As Raúl says in the film, “This is all there is to my life.” But Almodóvar has never suffered writer’s block. “I inspire myself because this is the profession that I know better than anyone, than any other,” he said. “The only thing that separates me from this alter ego is that I never lived a creative crisis. The experience I have had is more scripts that have taken me a long time to find the solution and to get them to gel together. But I’ve always succeeded ultimately.”

And he only recently discovered panic attacks, which took him by surprise. “I hadn’t previously experienced panic attacks, but now I have,” he said. “At that moment I was unconscious, and it was something awful, awful.”

Needless to say Almodóvar spends most of his days sitting at his desk at the computer. (Hence his legendary bad back.) Mostly he enjoys writing but also feels the clock ticking. “You always feel like time is lacking, right?” he said. “Especially that moment when you get that idea that’s going to become the motor of your story, you feel like there’s no time to breathe, because you want to get it all down as fast as possible. They’re quite intense days as we’re trying to get this. And then once I’ve started the story, my process is to get up in the morning and start writing. Those are some of the most pleasurable days in my life because you know where you’re going. But also, I have to pay attention to everything, because in that moment that you are possessed by the idea, you experience everything in your life filtered through the sensibility of the story that you’re writing.”

Listening to music feeds his creative beast. While he was writing “Talk to Her,” he listened to Caetano Veloso’s “Cucurrucucú Paloma,” a song that he had heard thousands of times, “but then it was like an epiphany. I discovered the song, and you feel it in a different way.” And in “Bitter Christmas,” his two actresses in the movie-within-the-movie listen to “Weeping Woman” from the filmmaker’s longtime muse, Mexican chanteuse Chavela Vargas.

Finally, the filmmaker had fun making himself the bad guy. “This was a new structure for me,” he said. “What I liked about it was that I could talk about myself as a writer-director, but mostly I also enjoyed the part of becoming the villain in a sense of that story. But the spectator does have to pay a lot of attention because if they go to the bathroom for two minutes, they’re going to miss something and be lost.”

In one scene, the filmmaker offers a close-up of the cursor on the computer screen. “Even though the cursor itself is not a very cinematic thing to see,” he said, “it’s his call to creativity, right? It’s the thing that calls him and pulls him in to have to tell his story. So it’s autofiction.”

Going forward, Almodóvar has no plans to put himself at the center of another film. “I promise not to talk about me anymore,” he said. “I was interested since the beginning of my career about the origin of creation and the relation with reality. Inspiration and life together, like the two sides of a coin. This mysterious question that so fascinates me is about not just where does creativity come from, how does it come, when does it come, how does it manifest? I have reached the end of my exploration around this.”

Up next: He’s writing, he said. “This is almost the opposite of this one. The new one will be very different.”

A Sony Pictures Classic release, “Bitter Christmas” is now playing in theaters in New York and Los Angeles. It expands nationally on November 25.

#3349. Update Your iPhone to Prevent People From Seeing iMessages They Shouldn't

Has this ever happened to you? You add someone new to an iMessage group chat, and wonder, "Huh, can they see any of the messages from before they were added?" The answer to that question is supposed to be "no." By design, new iMessage group chat members are only privy to texts that arrive after they were added. When they join, it's essentially a blank slate, as if you just created the group for the first time. At least, that's how it's intended to work.

As it turns out, there's a bug with iMessage that may allow new group chat members to see texts from before they were added to the chat. That's a problem, and not just for the iPhone users out there talking smack about people before inviting them to join the group chat. It means iMessage, and Apple's platforms in general, aren't working like they're supposed to be. You don't have to be talking behind people's backs to not want new members seeing existing chats. Maybe you're planning a surprise party for someone, and add them to the group once everyone's in on the plan; maybe the texts in the chat aren't relevant to the current group, and the person joining simply does not need to access them.

That's not all: There exists another security flaw that could allow remote hackers to join an iMessage group and receive new messages. You might add a new user to a group chat and inadvertently invite them to read all existing messages, while at the same time being attacked by a bad actor who can then intercept all future messages. Not good.

Luckily, there's currently a fix for these problems. Apple patched (and revealed) the bugs, along with seven other security flaws, with a series of software updates on Monday for iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, and Vision Pro. Not all of the updates include patches for these two iMessage flaws—specifically, some of the updates for older Apple devices. But the rest, including iOS 27.2.1, macOS 27.2.1, macOS 26.7.3, macOS 15.8.3, watchOS 27.2.1, and visionOS 27.2.1, include the iMessage patches.

Each update includes its own list of patches, but, for this article, I'll take a look at the nine patches in iOS 27.2.1. You'll find the two iMessage bugs, plus seven other patches, in the list below:

AirPlay: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113968: Apple

App Intents: Impact: An app may be able to access sensitive user data. Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113963: László Várady

Bluetooth: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to corrupt process memory. Description: A use-after-free issue was addressed with improved memory management. CVE-2026-113970: Apple

brotli: Impact: Processing maliciously crafted input may lead to memory corruption. Description: An out-of-bounds write issue was addressed with improved input validation. CVE-2026-111497

CoreUtils: Impact: A malicious Bluetooth device may be able to establish a pairing without user interaction. Description: This issue was addressed with improved checks. CVE-2026-113965: Apple

CoreUtils: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts and pair with a device without user interaction. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113964: an anonymous researcher

Messages: Impact: A remote attacker may be able to join an iMessage group chat and receive its messages. Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved validation. CVE-2026-113961: an anonymous researcher

Messages: Impact: A user added to an iMessage group may be able to access messages sent before they joined. Description: This issue was addressed by removing the vulnerable code. CVE-2026-113960: an anonymous researcher

Rapportd: Impact: An attacker on the same network may be able to bypass the rate limit on AirPlay pairing code attempts. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113969: Apple

For a full accounting of the patches included in the other security updates, check out Apple's official security releases site.

To install Apple's latest security updates, you'll simply need to update your device as you usually do. On iPhone, iPad, Apple Watch, and Vision Pro, head to Settings > General > Software Update; on Mac, go to System Settings > General > Software Update. Here, follow the on-screen instructions to download and install the latest version of your device's software.

#3347. Brand New Day Was Great, But Marvel Still Hasn't Done 1 Thing With Tom Holland's Spider-Man

As impeccable as Spider-Man: Brand New Day is, there’s still one thing the Marvel Cinematic Universe hasn’t achieved with Tom Holland’s Web-Head. Tom Holland's Spider-Man has undergone one of the most interesting journeys in the MCU timeline. Introduced as an enthusiastic teenager desperate to prove himself, Peter Parker has gradually become a more experienced, emotionally complex crime fighter. His story has also been closely connected to some of the MCU's biggest events.

Holland's natural charisma, excellent comedic timing, and ability to convey Peter's insecurities have made him one of Marvel's most consistently entertaining leads. More importantly, the character has finally reached a point where the consequences of his decisions can meaningfully shape his future, rather than simply serving as another stepping stone towards becoming an Avenger.

Spider-Man: Brand New Day is an exciting new chapter in that development. Director Destin Daniel Cretton’s thrilling blockbuster allows Holland plenty of opportunities to explore a different side of Peter Parker, while maintaining the spectacular action and humor audiences expect. It is arguably the strongest installment of Holland's Spider-Man series so far. However, despite its success, Marvel still needs to explore one particular direction if it wants to get the absolute best out of its web-slinger.

One of the defining characteristics of Holland's Spider-Man has been his relationship with the wider MCU. Unlike Tobey Maguire and Andrew Garfield's interpretations, who largely operated independently of other superheroes, Holland's Peter Parker was introduced as part of an already-established superhero community. His first appearance in Captain America: Civil War established his connection to Tony Stark, with the billionaire becoming Peter's mentor throughout Spider-Man: Homecoming and Avengers: Infinity War.

Tony's influence provided an interesting alternative to the traditional Uncle Ben relationship, allowing Marvel to explore Peter's desire for approval from somebody he considered a genuine hero. However, it also meant that Peter's introduction to superhero life was heavily dependent on another character.

Spider-Man: Far From Home brought Nick Fury into the story, while Spider-Man: No Way Home featured Doctor Strange and a swathe of legacy Spider-Man characters. It was an enormously entertaining cinematic event, but it also meant that Holland's third solo movie was arguably his least independent adventure.

Brand New Day continues the tradition, albeit with a different assortment of familiar faces. Frank Castle, AKA the Punisher, is an important part of Peter's latest adventure, while Mark Ruffalo returns as Bruce Banner and Florence Pugh appears as Yelena Belova. These characters certainly have defined narrative purposes beyond simply showing up for the sake of recognition.

Nevertheless, the pattern is difficult to ignore. Across four solo movies, Holland's Spider-Man has shared significant screen time with numerous established characters. While he's garnered might be an impressive collection of guest appearances, it’s hard not to wonder if Spider-Man will ever get a truly solo adventure.

Importantly, this isn't necessarily a criticism of Brand New Day. If anything, Destin Daniel Cretton's movie proves that Marvel can incorporate its wider universe without allowing established characters to overwhelm the story. It certainly makes considerably better use of its supporting superheroes than No Way Home, which occasionally struggled to balance its emotional narrative with the excitement of bringing together so many familiar faces.

The difference is that Brand New Day has a much clearer understanding of what Peter's story needs. Following the events of No Way Home, everybody has forgotten Peter Parker exists, leaving him without the relationships that previously defined his life. His isolation is central to the narrative, and Holland gets plenty of opportunities to explore the emotional consequences of sacrificing his personal happiness to protect the people he loves.

That makes the inclusion of the Punisher particularly effective. Rather than introducing Frank Castle simply because audiences recognize Jon Bernthal's character, the narrative establishes an entertaining dynamic between two fundamentally different approaches to superheroism.

Bruce Banner's inclusion in Brand New Day is similarly appropriate, with Peter experiencing changes to his physiology. Banner's scientific knowledge and personal experience with an uncontrollable alter ego make him a logical person to consult. Yelena's appearance is comparatively brief, but Florence Pugh brings plenty of personality to her scenes without demanding that the movie divert attention towards the wider MCU.

The important distinction is that these characters contribute to Peter's development rather than simply reminding audiences that they're watching another installment of a larger franchise. Despite its extensive supporting cast, the most compelling material involves Peter, MJ, and Ned.

There's no reason Marvel needs to abandon crossovers altogether. The interconnected nature of the MCU is one of its greatest strengths, and Spider-Man's comic-book history is filled with memorable team-ups involving other superheroes. Peter Parker has fought alongside the Avengers, teamed up with Daredevil, and developed friendships with characters occupying completely different corners of the Marvel universe.

Those relationships are worth exploring, but they shouldn't be an obligatory feature of every solo adventure. The ending of No Way Home created an especially interesting opportunity to change direction with Peter is now completely alone, without Tony Stark's technological resources, the Avengers' support network, or even his closest friends knowing who he is.

That opens the door to a more grounded story built around Peter, a compelling villain, and the people closest to him. Rather than another world-threatening crisis, Marvel could explore the pressures of balancing superhero responsibilities with Peter's ordinary life, with several quintessential aspects still missing.

The Daily Bugle, J. Jonah Jameson, the citizens of Queens, and the neighborhoods Peter regularly protects are all essential parts of Spider-Man's identity. His relationships with MJ and Ned, meanwhile, offer a particularly rich source of drama following the events of No Way Home. There's plenty to explore without needing to introduce another superhero to explain the stakes.

Brand New Day proves that Holland can carry a compelling Spider-Man story while sharing the screen with other MCU characters. His next challenge should be doing so without them. Marvel has spent four movies establishing Spider-Man's place in its interconnected universe; now it should give him the freedom to occupy his own corner of it.

#3346. This AirPods Feature Fixed My Biggest Problem With Listening to Podcasts to Fall Asleep

We're highlighting the small changes—from useful new gadgets, to fresh productivity techniques, to efficient hacks—that are improving our lives on a weekly basis.

There's lots to recommend about podcasts (and lots of podcasts to recommend), but one of their biggest benefits—for me, anyway—has little to do with what a particular show is about or even who hosts it: They're great for dissociating. I often have a podcast playing to distract my anxious brain from whatever I'm worried about (which, in 2026, is usually slightly less than everything).

Any time I don't want to be alone with my thoughts (say, when commuting or doing mindless chores), I can put on a podcast and be entertained by a couple of goobers talking about movies rather than spinning my wheels about my son's middle school applications. And there's no time I want to disassociate from reality more than bedtime.

For years I've used podcasts as a non-pharmaceutical sleep aid, and few things are more effective at helping me drop off quickly. Unfortunately, for years this also meant that once I fell asleep, the podcast kept playing. I have my podcast app set to delete episodes once finished, so if it was a show I cared about, I'd need to do a lot of redownloading and scrubbing through to find where I left off—that is, until I upgraded my earbuds to the AirPods Pro 3.

The AirPods Pro 3 launched alongside iOS 26 in the fall of 2025 with flashy features like vastly improved noise cancellation, Live Translation, Heart Rate Sensing, and hearing health settings, all of them quite welcome on a set of $250 premium earbuds. But the best new AirPods feature was one I didn't even know about when I decided to upgrade my four-year-old Beats Fit Pro.

In the AirPods settings (accessible via your iPhone's Settings app), if you tap Audio & Routing and scroll down, you'll see an option to turn on a setting called Pause Media When Falling Asleep. I don't think I need to tell you what this setting does. I can tell you that it works great.

According to Apple, the feature works by sensing when you're drifting off using the earbuds' built-in accelerometer to track your movement (or lack thereof). Once your earbuds have determined that you're falling asleep, they will pause your audio for you. And it isn't just the 2025 AirPods Pro 3 that support it—it also works on the second-generation AirPods Pro as well as the AirPods 4 and the AirPods 5.

I'll admit that I don't really understand how the AirPods Pro 3 can tell I'm falling asleep versus just lying very still, but I've never had them pause accidentally during active listening. Conversely, whenever I go back to the podcast I was listening to the night before, I'll find that the audio paused within a minute or two of the last part I remember hearing.

The AirPods Pro 3 aren't the only earbuds with a feature like this, but you'll most often only find it in dedicated "sleep earbuds" designed specifically for the purpose. While many of those offer extra health features like the ability to track your sleep cycles, I'm not really interested in that (my Apple Watch does most of it, and I don't look at that data anyway). Pausing my audio when I'm asleep is really all I need, and the AirPods Pro 3 do it well enough that I don't need to bother with a pair of dedicated bedtime buds.

#3345. Apple reportedly met with Thai officials over spyware alerts sent to politicians

Bloomberg reports that Apple has met with Thai government officials in the wake of its recent wave of iPhone alerts about mercenary spyware attacks. Here are the details.

Last week, The Financial Times and TechCrunch reported that Apple had sent a fresh wave of threat notifications to potential spyware targets in 99 countries, warning them that they may have been targeted by mercenary spyware attacks.

At the time, the FT focused on German lawmakers who had received the warnings, while TechCrunch highlighted recipients in other countries, including Beirut-based filmmaker Radwan Mortada.

Today, Bloomberg reported that “Thailand held meetings with Apple Inc. officials” over the notifications, adding that the warnings raised questions about “who may have targeted [Thai politicians] and why.”

Receiving an alert doesn’t necessarily mean a device was successfully compromised, Digital Economy and Society Minister Chaichanok Chidchob said after meeting Apple representatives Wednesday, Krungthep Turakij and other media reported. Thai authorities also have no evidence so far that the latest attempted attacks involved Pegasus, the spyware developed by Israel’s NSO Group, he said.

As Bloomberg explains, Pegasus was “allegedly used against pro-democracy campaigners in 2022.”

The recent wave of alerts, which were sent out on October 29, followed another round in August, when Apple notified potential targets in 110 countries. As always, Apple declined to disclose what triggers these notifications to prevent attackers from evading detection in the future, but recommended that recipients enable Lockdown Mode and seek expert security assistance.

Bloomberg added that Thai authorities are expected to meet with other technology companies on Thursday to discuss potential countermeasures, including risks to Android devices.

With the end of ToruńCAMERIMAGE 2026, the world’s premier annual celebration of cinematography has come to a close. Poland’s largest film festival prides itself on shining the spotlight on directors of photography, saving each film‘s final introduction and the biggest round of applause for the artist who shaped its images. Post-screening Q&As are filled with discussions of lenses, aspect ratios, and shutter speeds as the artists gleefully get technical about the choices that give each film its distinct look.

Inevitably, the festival’s awards focus on cinematography as well. Nicholas Hoult is headed back to Hulu. He's set to star with fellow Hulu alumnus Daisy Edgar-Jones in the new dramedy series Mosquito. Now, that series is buzzing to life; production has started, and a swarm of new cast members have been added to the call sheet.

Hoult previously starred in the Hulu historical drama series The Great as Peter III, the wife of Russian tsarina Catherine the Great; that series was created by Poor Things screenwriter Tony McNamara, who's reuniting with Hoult for Mosquito. They'll be joined by Edgar-Jones, who starred in the hit Hulu drama Normal People. In Mosquito, Hoult and Edgar-Jones will play Ed and Kate, a recently married couple whose lives begin to crumble as their dark secrets are revealed...all because of one annoying, blood-sucking insect.

Now, we know that they'll be joined by a bevy of recognizable faces. Kyle Soller (Andor) will play Hunter, Ed's half-brother and business partner; Phoebe Fox (Task) will play their cousin and co-worker Gail; and Francis Magee (Game of Thrones) will play Viktor, a long-time employee with a simmering grudge. Belinda Bromilow (The Roses) will play Kate's boss, Agnes, while John Macmillan (Surface) and Liv Hill (The Serpent Queen) will play her coworkers Brian and Georgie. Akshay Khanna (Murderbot) will star as Kate's university friend Will, with Phoebe Campbell (House of the Dragon) as his wife, Cressida. Bamshad Abedi Amin (Kill Jackie) will play Gail's PhD supervisor, while Den Rasaq (Criminal Record) will play Kate's work rival. You belong in the North, where the weather does most of the arguing and nobody is impressed by a title. The Starks are the only great house on this list who genuinely believe that being right matters more than winning, which is exactly why the show spent eight years punishing them for it.

You belong to the house that worked out early on that gold moves faster than armies. Casterly Rock runs on leverage, reputation and the certainty that everybody at the table owes you something, and you are perfectly comfortable with all three.

You belong to the house that conquered a continent and never quite got over it. Targaryens do not ask for a seat at the table, because in their version of events the table was theirs to begin with, and that certainty is either magnificent or catastrophic depending on the week.

You belong to Highgarden, where nobody raises their voice and everybody gets exactly what they came for. The Tyrells feed the realm, charm the realm and quietly steer the realm, and they have never once needed to win a battle to get their way.

#3339. 8 Best Survival Drama Series Of All Time

The survival genre has produced many great shows, often with a sci-fi or action bent. Lost might have been about a group of castaways on the surface, but it soon became much less straightforward — the show needed extra explainers because the Lost timeline became so confusing. Regardless of sub-genre, though, all survival dramas are about characters doing their best to stay alive in circumstances they rarely, if ever, expected to find themselves in.

Many of the best survival dramas feature small groups of people suddenly forced to work together after disaster strikes, causing beliefs and personalities to clash. Others involve so many characters it’s hard to keep track of them all, with numerous conflicting factions springing up. Some begin immediately after the event that changes everything, while others start their stories years down the road. Whichever way a survival show structures its characters' challenges, there's something for everyone in TV's best survival dramas.

Very loosely based on a Belgian comic book series, Jeremiah aired on Showtime and starred Luke Perry and Malcolm-Jamal Warner. Set in 2021, the series follows two people living in a world where, 15 years earlier, a virus known as “The Big Death” wiped out almost everyone over the age of 13. The leads meet by chance when they’re imprisoned by a warlord and recruited by a guy to help a mysterious organization. Their journey leads them to discover Thunder Mountain and the Valhalla Sector, both organizations trying to rebuild the world in very different ways.

While some survival dramas focus on people's fight to stay alive, Jeremiah took a different approach. People had already learned to survive because it was set 15 years after a pandemic. This series was more concerned with what came next — the rebuilding of society and the new systems and institutions that underpin it. It also explored what kinds of communities would spring up in a new world originally led by children. It was somewhat hopeful for such a depressing premise, though; Jeremiah wasn’t so much about what was lost, but about what humanity could do better the second time around.

AMC’s The Terror is an anthology series that explores real-life historical events through a fictional (and supernatural-tinged) lens. The Terror season 1 follows the doomed crews of HMS Terror and HMS Erebus as the ships become stuck in the ice while trying to make their way through the Northwest Passage in the Arctic Ocean. Based on a book inspired by the 1845 expedition led by Captain Sir John Franklin and Captain Francis Crozier, season 1 is a bleak, haunting look at men trying to survive in impossible conditions (while eventually being hunted by a monster).

Watching these sailors try to stay alive in a land of nothing more than snow and ice is harrowing, and not surprisingly, some of the men turn to cannibalism. However, while the harsh conditions might be most likely to kill them, they aren’t the only threat to survival; violence between the factions that occurs in the crew also springs up and leads to some pretty gruesome moments. The Terror season 1 isn’t for those who enjoy people actually surviving in survival dramas, as there’s little hope.

When Netflix released The Society, critics praised it for its social commentary and storytelling. However, the show only lasted one season; the second season was canceled during the COVID-19 pandemic. Unfortunately, that means there’s no resolution, but The Society is still one of the better survival dramas around. When a group of teens returns home from a school trip to find that every adult in their town has disappeared — and they’re now mysteriously cut off from the rest of the world — they have to learn to survive on their own.

Thankfully, these kids aren’t starting totally from scratch. They have resources, and they end up creating a society based on communal living. However, teenagers will be teenagers, and it isn’t long before power struggles, hormones, and total anarchy threaten the tenuous situation. The mystery of what put them in this scenario in the first place adds an extra layer of depth to the story. Lord of the Flies was a major influence, but it was also compared to The Leftovers and Lost.

Imagine growing up on a space station because the planet your people originated from suffered a nuclear apocalypse a hundred years ago, only to be thrown back down to that planet with 99 other juvenile prisoners to see if it's habitable once again. That was the premise of The 100, a survival drama that saw a group of teens forced to learn how to survive in a place they never could have imagined.

As if finding food and resources wasn’t hard enough, the group eventually learns that people survived the dangerous radiation levels all those years ago, so the planet is actually inhabited. Though The 100 had its moments of controversy and flaws, it also featured all the hardship and drama expected in a survival show. Each season turned into a different kind of fight to keep living; it became a story about how far people will go to survive.

The Walking Dead began as a comic book series, became a hit television show, and then branched into numerous spin-offs, creating a monster franchise. While it’s a horror show about zombies, its main premise is the survival of those who weren’t immediately killed or turned in the initial outbreak. During its long run, the show evolved from following the original group of survivors as they learned to exist in this new world to different human factions rising and clashing.

The Walking Dead franchise has expanded far past the original show, and this means that there is more than one way for viewers to watch the series.

It’s one of the ultimate survival shows, and while it went off the rails at times, it showed how great the human spirit can be in the face of adversity (even if that adversity is the walking dead). The series also proved that when the world as we know it ends, humanity is the scariest monster around.

Before Yellowjackets, there was The Wilds, a survival drama about a group of teen girls on their way to an empowerment retreat whose plane crashes, leaving them stranded on an island. The girls must learn to work together to survive and find a way off the island — only, as it turns out, they’re actually unwitting participants in a social experiment, so getting off the island will be harder than expected.

The second season adds a group of teen boys to the mix, as their plane also crashed on the island as part of the experiment. This brings even more tension and terrifying drama. Featuring flashbacks and flash-forwards, The Wilds explores how surviving an ordeal like this can change a person and who they become when it's all said and done.

When it comes to survival dramas, there are few better than Lost. A plane crashing into a mysterious island and a group of survivors working together to get off that island is the epitome of survival setups. The introduction of the polar bears, the Smoke Monster, the Others, and so much more allowed the show to develop a rich mythology and added an edge to the group's survival story, turning it into one of the most popular TV shows ever made.

While survival shows existed before Lost, this series set the blueprint for many shows that followed. With glimpses into the past and future, Lost turned this survival story into a deeply emotional, highly philosophical saga that still resonates with viewers.

Yellowjackets is one of the most recent offerings in the survival drama genre, and to say it's made a splash would be an understatement. Like Lost, the show starts as a fairly straightforward story about a girls’ soccer team whose plane crashes in the wilds of Canada. However, as the series goes on, things take a dark turn, and something supernatural constantly lurks in the background.

The showrunners wanted to explore how trauma can shape lives and interpersonal dynamics within social hierarchies, and they managed to do that with Yellowjackets. Those eventually rescued from their plight were drastically changed by what they experienced. The cannibalism and ritualistic elements give the show a horror edge as well. The final season premieres on November 20, 2026. It's time to find out how Yellowjackets ends.

#3338. 10 Hacks Every Waze User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Waze is a crowdsourced navigation app designed to help you get where you're going as quickly and with as much information about your route as possible. Where Google Maps and Apple Maps offer relatively straightforward directions, Waze tries to outsmart these alternatives by integrating real-time community feedback about hazards, speed traps, road closures, and more. If you are switching to Waze or using it alongside your other navigation tools, these are the hacks to help you maximize everything the app has to offer.

If you find yourself losing track of time or running late for events, Waze can notify you when it's time to leave—based on your current location and live traffic—so you arrive on schedule. You can set up "Time to leave" reminders in advance for individual planned drives, or you can sync your calendar to receive notifications for scheduled events. Calendar sync connects to your device's default calendar app, but you can change this to a third-party alternative if you prefer. Calendar events must include a navigable address to trigger reminders, and you must select Plan a drive in Waze for the event.

Waze has a feature called "child reminders," which are notifications to check for children before you get out of the car. This is clearly an incredibly important use case, but you can also use these alerts for custom messages, like "Don't forget the groceries!" In Waze, tap the menu button > Settings > Reminders > Child reminder and select Custom message.

Variable speed limits, especially on unfamiliar routes, can result in you speeding when you don't mean to. But Waze can alert you if you exceed a customized speed threshold so you aren't caught by surprise or at higher risk of being ticketed. From the menu, go to Settings > Speedometer and turn on Show speedometer. Tap Speeding threshold to select what limit you want to trigger alerts, and turn on Alert at threshold if you want Waze to play a sound.

Waze offers a wealth of information on routes to help drivers navigate obstacles and hazards, but this can clutter your map and distract you from the most critical information, especially in congested, high-traffic areas. Waze says it limits and prioritizes alerts automatically, but you can actually customize which alerts you see based on what's most important to you. From the menu, go to Settings > Alerts and reports > Reports and select the relevant alerts.

In the same Alerts and reports menu, you can enable Alert while driving, which will give you an audio warning and an onscreen pop-up about your selected hazards. This allows you to run navigation via a different map app (like Google Maps or Apple Maps) in the foreground while still getting Waze data in the background.

Waze integrates with toll road and HOV lane passes, so if you have an express or fast lane subscription, your route will optimize for it. If you don't, Waze can still account for HOV lane eligibility if you tell it how many passengers are in your car. From the menu, go to Settings > Toll and HOV passes and tap the plus icon to add your pass(es) from the list. If you need to add your passenger count instead, you can do so from View routes and enable the HOV option.

If you're driving through an unfamiliar, highly congested, or poorly designed area, you can ask Waze to help you avoid tricky maneuvers, such as crossing multiple lanes of traffic or turning left at intersections without lights. This prioritizes ease over speed using protected green arrows, roundabouts, and right turns. From the menu, go to Settings > Navigation, Avoid difficult intersections and select Always. You can also ask Waze to avoid toll roads, ferries, freeways, and unpaved roads.

Waze has a built-in audio player that syncs with your preferred listening platform—such as Spotify, YouTube Music, and Pandora—so you can control your music without having to navigate between apps. (As Waze is a Google product, Apple Music isn't included.) Simply tap the music icon on the map to select your audio player and hit Accept. If you don't see the icon, go to Settings > Audio player and turn on Show on the map.

If you want to make audio directions more interesting, you can select a celebrity or character voice to help you navigate. Recent appearances include Bill Hader's Cat in the Hat and Ziggy Marley. Tap the speaker icon > Current voice to search for the voice or language you want to use. You can also record directions in your own voice.

#3337. Binance warns iPhone crypto holders of security flaw researchers say remains unpatched

Crypto exchange Binance has warned iPhone users about an iOS vulnerability that could allow malicious apps to access sensitive data stored by other apps. Here are the details.

In a post published on X (via AppleInsider), Binance says that a vulnerability called worse_query could allow “malicious apps to read local files from other apps, putting seed phrases, private keys, and login credentials at risk across the entire ecosystem.”

Binance says the flaw affects iOS 26.7.1, iOS 27.0.1, and iOS 27.2. However, a Community Note points out that researchers describe the vulnerability as an unpatched zero-day and that Apple’s latest security updates, including iOS 27.2.1 (the current version at the time of writing), do not mention a fix.

A vulnerability (worse_query) affecting iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and 27.2 allows malicious apps to read local files from other apps, putting seed phrases, private keys, and login credentials at risk across the entire ecosystem. This is an iOS-level issue, not unique to Binance.…

That said, in addition to updating their devices, Binance recommends that iPhone crypto holders take the following immediate actions:

The vulnerability was disclosed by security researchers @0xjohnny and @forcequitOS, who published a proof of concept on GitHub demonstrating how it can be used to bypass iOS sandbox protections, which normally prevent apps from accessing each other’s files.

Researcher @forcequitOS also noted that neither iOS 27.2.1 nor iOS 27.3 beta 1 patches the vulnerability.

Just as a general statement so there isn’t any confusion about it, worse_query is *not* patched in iOS 27.2.1 and 27.3 beta 1. I’ll update version support on the readme when it’s patched.

Although the researcher describes the code as intended for developers and not useful on its own, other developers have already built apps using it, including a file manager that can access, modify, and delete data belonging to other apps without requiring a jailbreak.

According to The Hacker News, neither Binance nor the researchers have reported any attacks or cryptocurrency thefts involving the vulnerability so far.

#3336. Box Office: ‘Ebenezer’ Opens to Modest $19 Million, Showing Johnny Depp Is Still a Draw for the Right Price

If Johnny Depp was hoping that “Ebenezer” would mark a glorious return to mainstream movies, he may need to hold out for another vehicle. The Christmas fable, released long before Thanksgiving, let alone the holidays, topped the box office this weekend with $19 million domestically and $42 million globally, a solid but unremarkable debut. It shows that enough moviegoers are able to look past the scandals that led Hollywood to remove Depp from their call sheets for the better part of a decade, but also exposed the limitations of his popular appeal.

The fact is that Depp was always something of a dicey commercial proposition. Put him in a “Pirates of the Caribbean” movie and you were guaranteed to earn $1 billion even if the script sucked and the plot seemed designed at the end of a wine bottle. Team him with Tim Burton, as he was quite successfully with “Sweeney Todd” ($153 million gross, $50 million budget), “Charlie and the Chocolate Factory” ($475.8 million gross, $150 million budget), and “Alice in Wonderland” ($1 billion gross, $200 million budget), and you were likely to have a big hit. Well, unless they were looking to reboot “Dark Shadows.” Related Stories ‘Fatherland’ Wins Golden Frog at ToruńCAMERIMAGE 2026 — Full Winners List After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies

But the rest of Depp’s track record was spotty. “Public Enemies” ($214.1 million gross, $100 million budget) and “Black Mass” ($100 million gross, $53 million budget) did well considering they were R-rated adult dramas, but struggled to break even because they cost too much to make and Depp commanded his full $20 million salary. Then there were the costly bombs, a litany of duds that includes “Mortdecai” ($47.3 million gross, $60 million budget), “The Lone Ranger” ($260.5 million gross, $250 million budget), “Transcendence” ($103 million gross, $150 million budget), and “Alice Through the Looking Glass” ($300 million gross, $170 million budget), the latter a return to Wonderland sans Burton. Many of these seemed like paycheck gigs rather than an attempt to burnish Depp’s star power. There was a private island to pay for and a pirate-themed wine cave to keep stocked on Depp’s sprawling French estate. But the promise of another Jack Sparrow adventure meant that Hollywood was able to look the other way, confident that there was more plunder to be found by allowing the actor to follow his idiosyncratic muse.

Depp could have kept going like this, but his messy personal life interceded. Depp’s reputation took a hit in 2020 when he became embroiled in a costly, two-continent legal battle against ex-wife Amber Heard, in which he was accused of domestic abuse. He denied the allegations, and later lost a U.K. libel suit against The Sun, when the court found an article calling Depp a “wife beater” was “substantially true.” Depp would go on to defamation trial against Heard in the U.S., after she wrote an op-ed in the Washington Post, calling herself a domestic abuse survivor. By that time, he’d been fired from the “Fantastic Beasts” franchise (it would be canceled after a non-Depp-led installment bombed), and was consigned to appearing in straight-to-streaming schlock or barely seen indies. But it wasn’t just the reputational damage that made major studios skittish about Depp. They had grown tired of his antics. There were reports he would show up late and unprepared, even as his salary demands and requests for perks escalated. That’s fine when your movies are making lots of money, it’s less charming when they are losing it.

So a lot is riding on “Ebenezer.” Depp looked a little uneasy on red carpets promoting the movie and Paramount, which is backing the film, wisely kept him from doing profiles with harder-hitting journalists who might ask him a probing question. He also cut his salary, reportedly receiving a $5 million paycheck to play one of his dream roles — Ebenezer Scrooge, and with it a chance to wear fright makeup and talk in a weird voice. But unlike most of Depp’s recent films, “Ebenezer” is poised to be a modest financial success. The film skewed older, with 59% of its domestic audience over the age of 30, and was slightly more female, as only 48% of ticket buyers were men. Paramount said it over-indexed in the South. One warning sign is that family crowds didn’t turn out in force for the PG-13 movie, comprising just 9% of opening weekend crowds.

However, the $38 million budget is low enough that if the film continues to draw crowds through the holidays and performs well overseas, where it has earned $23 million, it will turn a profit. But that points to a new reality — Depp is a sound bet, for the right price. Maybe that was a lesson that studios should have taken long ago. Depp’s taste is rococo, but Hollywood kept treating every one of his outings like potential blockbusters when a little more caution was warranted.

Next up for Depp is “Day Drinker,” an action thriller that seems to play into the star’s libertine image. Lionsgate will release the film in March. Will it be the vehicle that puts the 63-year-old Depp back on top, or will it, like “Ebenezer,” confirm that there’s still a smaller, but committed audience for his antics? Budget accordingly.

#3334. iPhone Duo one week later: The future, or not for me?

My iPhone Duo arrived last Thursday, so I’ve had a week to use it as my daily carry. My early experience has been mixed, so I keep asking myself an important question: is this the iPhone’s future and I just need to adapt, or is the Duo simply not for everyone?

After a week using the iPhone Duo, in some ways I have a lot of clarity about the product, and in other ways my thinking is very clouded.

To put it simply: I’m not having a great time with the Duo, which makes me wonder if the problem is me, not it.

I’ve seen countless social media posts from Duo owners proclaiming how much they love the product. And I absolutely believe them. The iPhone Duo is a remarkable innovation for the iPhone. It’s cool, weird, and wonderful in all sorts of ways. But for me and my needs (preferences?), it’s been more frustrating than enjoyable.

And that frustration mainly boils down to one thing: I almost never want to open it.

I’d estimate at least 90% of my iPhone Duo usage involves the front display. And when I unfold it the remaining 10% of the time, it’s often because I force myself to do it in the hopes of discovering what I’m missing out on. Like, I know I should be unfolding it more, so I do. But it doesn’t add any real value for me.

Because I rarely want to open the iPhone Duo, I’m left using the outer display all the time. In that mode, the Duo is too heavy for extended use, too wide to comfortably reach, and the UI in most apps is an adjustment.

Are these dealbreakers? No. I could live with the Duo’s outer display if I had to, but it’s definitely an inferior experience to my iPhone 18 Pro.

If I was opening the iPhone Duo more, and actually taking advantage of the key value proposition of foldables—that you can unfold them—I doubt the outer screen would bother me much.

But what I’ve found, at least so far, is that one-handed iPhone use is very important to me, which rules out using the inner display. I use my iPhone mostly for quick interactions, and often with a child in one hand (I have three very young kids). In situations when I do have two hands free to open the Duo, I’m probably sitting in front of my iPad Pro with a Magic Keyboard attached and would rather use the iPad instead.

So again: is the problem with the Duo, or with me?

I think foldables and slab phones will obviously coexist as there will be fans of each.

I’m absolutely already converted however and am loving my duo.

Considering the Air was my favourite phone up until this it’s surprised me. I love proper one handed use again on the outside screen and unfolded it’s much nicer than my old mini 7.

I get it’s not for everyone but those that click with it like myself have a superb device!

I think it’s the latter, but I’m not sure “problem” is the right word. I just don’t find myself using it the way it’s meant to be used. And that’s fine.

I want to love the iPhone Duo, because I see how much fun other people are having with it. And maybe given more time, something will click and I’ll start to use it “as intended.”

If iPhone Duo is the future of the iPhone, I’ll adapt and move on with my life. But one week in, I think it’s probably just not for me. And if it’s not for me, maybe there are a lot of people who will continue preferring non-foldable iPhones for many years to come.

What’s your iPhone Duo experience been like? Are you loving it or struggling? Let us know in the comments.

#3333. Ring's New $250 Indoor Camera Drone Sounds Terrifying

Ring made its name with its smart doorbells with built-in cameras, and now sells more indoor cameras than any other company, capturing more than 40% of the market. When you've already moved tens of millions of devices (enough to raise serious concerns about their use as part of the surveillance state), you always need to keep innovating, and today, the company announced a product it has been working on for a decade: an indoor camera drone powered by artificial intelligence. I got a chance to check it out during a media event yesterday, and I can report that, as harbingers of our dystopian future go, it is only mildly terrifying.

The drone camera is one of two products in the company's new Ring Robotics line, alongside a "rover cam" that looks kind of like the canister of a vacuum cleaner attached to an iPad. While the Ring Rover Cam is priced at $999.99 and targeted at businesses, the Ring Drone Cam is a much more affordable $249.99, reasonable enough that it will appeal to consumers looking for another way to keep (robot) eyes on their stuff.

The drone camera records 2K video and has a 148-degree field of view and the ability to rotate 360 degrees. It works with existing Ring cameras, doorbells, sensors, and alarms, as well as the Alexa Home Map. It has a flight time of eight minutes, and once it returns to its base station, it takes around an hour to fully recharge (eight minutes on the dock will give it one minute in the air).

As Ring founder Jamie Siminoff explained during the preview event, the company has been trying to build a workable camera drone for around a decade, but couldn't overcome certain design challenges until the advancement of AI models that allow the device to handle most of the computing—from route programming to threat detection—via the cloud, so the drones can be smaller and lighter.

According to Ring, when setting up the Ring Drone Cam, you carry it around your house, allowing it to map the interior. It will "intelligently identify rooms and suggest patrol points: spots worth extra attention." When sent out on "patrol," the drone's AI pilot will travel between hotspots, sensing and avoiding furniture and other obstacles along the way.The Ring Drone Cam works with other Ring cameras, so if an alert is triggered somewhere in your home—say, a window opening unexpectedly—the drone will take off to investigate. It has a built-in security light that will make its presence known, so it can also act as a deterrent, though the screaming sound of its spinning propellers will accomplish that just as well.

According to Ring, the drone camera can deliver peace of mind whether you're home or away, and admittedly I do like the idea of being able to check on my pets or make sure no pipes have burst while I'm at work or on vacation (though admittedly you can get the same sort of monitoring without involving an AI device that looks like a mini version of the flying robots from The Terminator).

I admit that the Ring Drone Cam seems pretty cool, provided I don't think about it too much. I don't know that I really feel the need to have every inch of my home covered in security cameras, but I do like the idea that the drone could, for example, go to check out what's going on if one of my smoke alarms' temperature sensors reports that one spot in the house is all of a sudden hotter than it should be.

If you're ready to enter this brave new world of security, you'll have to wait a bit longer: The Ring Drone Camera isn't expected to ship until January 2027, but you can sign up to be alerted when it is available for preorder now.
