#3332. Nicholas Hoult’s New Heist Thriller Almost Had a Much Darker Ending

When it comes to the action-comedy genre, few directors are as accomplished and inventive as David Leitch. The former stunt performer/coordinator-turned-filmmaker returns with another high-octane action-comedy, How to Rob a Bank, which releases only in theaters this weekend. The director of thrilling romps such as Deadpool 2, Bullet Train, and The Fall Guy brings an extra punch this outing, as How to Rob a Bank tackles pressing and topical issues dominating the national discourse, particularly the wealth gap and the health care crisis. The 2026 film, starring Nicholas Hoult, Zoë Kravitz, Anna Sawai, Rhenzy Feliz, Pete Davidson, and John C. Reilly, was screened as part of Collider's Screening series, with a Q&A featuring Leitch and his wife and producing partner Kelly McCormick, moderated by Steve Weintraub.

After the screening of How to Rob a Bank, Leitch and McCormick discussed their long creative partnership and the challenges they faced while filming their latest project, as well as getting candid about the state of America's political revolution in the wake of the recent midterm elections. The two reflect on the most difficult stunts they've pulled off throughout their career in Hollywood, with Leitch discussing his time as a co-director of the original John Wick. Leitch and McCormick share the creative process behind How to Rob a Bank, working on a constrained budget, obtaining music rights, blending crowd-pleasing entertainment with biting social commentary, and the film's alternate ending.

Below is a full transcript of the conversation between Leitch, McCormick, and Weintraub, with the full video of the Q&A available above.

STEVEN WEINTRAUB: For people that have not seen The Fall Guy, do you want them watching the extended cut or the theatrical cut?

DAVID LEITCH: I actually ended up liking the theatrical cut. I'm that rare director that goes through the process, and then realizes, “You know what? This is actually the best version of the movie, and most people will enjoy it.” When I sit back and watch the extended cut, it's like, oh, there's a lot of unicorns that we're missing! I don’t think you can go wrong with more unicorns. I enjoy them both, but I do like the theatrical [cut].

Going back into your stunt career. What's a stunt performed where you look back now and think “I cannot believe I did that?”

LEITCH: There was a time on The Bourne Ultimatum, and it's not the one you're thinking of. There was an explosion in The Bourne Ultimatum, where I'm standing in front of a car and it's like ten feet away. We were on some really long telephoto lenses, so everything feels compressed. I’m at a safe distance, and I'm hooked up to this wire rig, and you're just facing the car, and I literally just got off a plane that day because Dan Bradley [stunt coordinator] had called me to come in and double. I walk onto set, I go through makeup, and I stand in front of this thing that's all rigged. I haven't met this effects crew. It was one of those things where you don't have control over it–you're a passenger, and you haven't seen rehearsals. When I think of that, sometimes you have trust in all the people that make movies, but sometimes it's like as a stunt performer, you have to have a lot of trust. Watching that thing blow up, I'm like, “God, I hope the ratchet takes me away.” And it all worked out, but it was one of those ones where you're like, “Yeah, I signed up for this. That was a bad idea.”

So you spent a lot of time doing stunts and working with a lot of gifted filmmakers. I'm just curious, was there one or two things on a movie set that you sort of said, “I'm stealing this”? This is something that you now use on a daily basis or some lesson that you have applied to your own life from those early days working on all those sets.

LEITCH: There's a ton that gets absorbed. I don't have a lot of specifics that rush to mind, but there's one phrase that [James] Mangold gave me when we were working together on the first Wolverine. He knew I was aspiring to direct, and we had a lot of conversations about directing while I was on that film. I shot a lot of second unit on the first Wolverine. He always said, “You know what? It’s really important to cast the man. Cast the man. If they're halfway to the character already, you're golden.” I thought that was really smart. I think you look at your actors and if you can see something in them, that they could personify that character. There's something in their personality that you think they could pull out and make bigger. It is a good rule of thumb: Cast the man or the woman.

I definitely want to touch on Atomic Blonde just real quick. The stairway sequence [is something] people still reference and still talk about. For people that aren't familiar with what really went into that sequence, talk a little bit about how daunting that thing was from a producer standpoint. Did you ever think, “we can’t do this based on our schedule or budget.” What was it like behind the scenes putting it together?

LEITCH: Well, it was actually the opposite in the sense that it was a really small budget movie. Kelly, being the incredible producer that she is, challenged me and she said, “Look, you need to find some distinctive action. You need to figure out what's the moment in this film that makes it stand above all these small-budget action films.” In the past, we’d choreographed oners [shots in one take] and presented them to directors and it. You thought it was logistically hard, but it was really a challenge. I think we went to the stunt team and, ironically, Sam Hargrave, who was the second unit director and stunt coordinator on that.

He was like, “No, we'll never. It's going to be too hard. The actors will never be able to do it, and it's going to be these long takes. I don't want to do this. We're not going to be able to pull it off in the amount of time we have. It's going to take too much training,” and I'm like, “You guys will figure it out.” The choreography team went after it. Kelly and I went in and made a lot of adjustments. And then I had a great production team. Jonathan Sela, who really understood how we could light it and shoot it, and we put together a really amazing sequence for not a lot of money in Budapest. I think it was seven days for that sequence, all in with the car into the water. He didn’t want to do oners, and now that’s his thing. You see the Extraction movies, and the opening scenes are like 30 minutes long.

What do you wish more people knew about being a producer and being a director in Hollywood? I think a lot of people would like to do what you're doing, and what do you maybe wish more people knew or anything you want to share?

KELLY McCORMICK: I don't think anybody wants to be a producer! [Laughs] I don't think I wish anybody anything, to be honest. I do think that one of the things that I do as a producer is that I’m film forward. I can sort of navigate the studios needs, the director's needs, and everybody else's needs based on what the movie needs, if that makes sense. My goal is always everybody signing on to be making the same movie for a moment, go and really sussing out if people aren't on the same page about that as early as possible, to try to get people to understand the movie that we're all making, and then once you do that, then the film will tell us what it needs. We make a lot of different types of things. Movies need a lot of different things, different sizes, budgets, different directors. David's movies are all different in a sense. Following the film as the North Star is one of the things that I do that I think is specifically how I explain the job.

LEITCH: I think that's right, because I think producing is a title that can encapsulate a lot of different things, and everybody makes it their own and can make it their own profession in a way. Kelly has a unique way of working with multiple filmmakers, working with different size budgets, building a company, and then also managing our big films together. There are very few producers in Hollywood that have the ability to do that. Being in the business for 30 years, I haven't seen a producer that's that flexible.

LEITCH: Being a director is awesome. You get to have all these great artists working for you and you get to take their ideas and curate something great. I think the best part about it is being able to create art, entertain people, and then also start a conversation and I hope that's what we did with this film. This was really exciting for me to have this conversation that we're all having in America right now, and we had last Tuesday [Midterm Elections], and it feels like people want change, and so the challenge for me was like, “how can I embed that conversation in a fun action movie?” As a director, I get to do that stuff. I get to take on that challenge and make the art that I find interesting, and then you guys get to take it, enjoy it, comment on it, and go have conversations about it.

McCORMICK: I will say, on hard days, David's like, “okay, you know, do I get a decision today?” It's usually him really handling everyone else's needs the whole day and like trying to get his manipulating everything into what he needs as well.

LEITCH: Yeah, directing is the art of compromise as well. It totally is. You have a vision for something, and it's like a bag of marbles that you hold at the beginning of the day, and they just dump them on the table, and then the rest of the day, you're trying to keep all the marbles. That's directing really, essentially.

Kelly, I am a huge Weezer fan, and you are producing something called The Weezer Movie. What the f is The Weezer Movie?

McCORMICK: I cannot speak about The Weezer Movie! [Laughs] Not really. If you know Weezer, you know the movie is going to be very “Weezer-y.”

McCORMICK: I hope it's aiming for next year, Steven.

What's been the most difficult sequence of your career, and how close did it come to being like, “we can't do this?”

LEITCH: There were a lot of those on The Fall Guy. There were just a lot of practical stunts in that film. We were challenging ourselves to do them for real. We took a lot of time and a lot of prep to get it right. The car jump was scary in the sense that you were making that land on the ground. We were landing it ramp to ramp, but then when you actually put it up two stories in the air and do the same jump, you're just kind of like, “oh.”

McCORMICK: They were testing it near where we were shooting. There was this ramp to ramp, and they kept getting the ramps higher and farther apart as they succeeded every day, basically. The set was actually manmade, but it was also filled with dirt and stuff, and I was just really worried that the wind, the rain, or even the sun would be pushing one side or the other differently than we were expecting. It needed to be exact. I made them do that survey that they do on the streets all the time. Every day, I was like, “Do the survey; just tell me that it's not eroding leading up to it." The crazy part with that stunt was that it was really the speedometer that ended up being problematic. It tripped up and stopped working while he was taking the ramp. It was very programmed exactly how fast he had to go in order to make sure he got to the other side ,and it was wrong, and he was slow, and he felt it, and he punched it, and he got over. In the movie, you can see it.

LEITCH: He clipped the front of it and he hit more of the set than the ramp.

McCORMICK: You can see the set just flying in the movie. That's him barely making the ramp. That one was really intense. That one's one where, if it goes sideways, it's not a good thing. Honestly, some of How to Rob a Bank was stuff that I was like, “Are we going to be able to get it done?” David puts 800 pounds of genius and a 2 pound bag, like no matter what size he's doing. And in this case, it was a modest budget. The needs were still really high. It was all of our guys who worked on, three times, four times the size budget that this was. The film is shot on 35 millimeter, and then on Prosumer, and at the end, it's on digital. There are only 230 extras, which is for the riot, which is like not a lot considering what we're doing. They came up with the most genius ways of stacking the extras. If you saw the shot where John is racing and trying to get to Nick, that's like the way that they shot it, made it look like there were tons of people. There were not tons of people! Some of the scariest parts to me is not being able to have the resources. Weirdly, that's scarier than a stunt to me.

I actually have a question about that. You mentioned you have a limited amount of extras. With the way technology is now, how much do you think about [not using AI], but using technology like CGI to add more people in or do you want real people?

McCORMICK: I mean, it depends on the movie, probably.

LIETCH: CGI wouldn't have looked great, you know. The top shot, at the end, where we crane up, it's the drone shot where Nick is laying out on the pavement. I'll be honest, I added a few people in CGI because we had less extras, and so we made it look like there was more of a group, and CGI worked great there.

McCORMICK: By the way, this movie couldn't afford much CGI either.

You guys are offered a whole bunch of stuff at this point. What was it about this one that said, “We have to do this”?

LEITCH: The script really spoke to us. What's been going on in the last couple of years and reading this script, it just felt really timely and really relevant. Actually, we passed on it, because of the size, and we were going to look and go into some bigger things, and we just couldn't let it go. A couple weeks later, we reengaged and said, “you know, we really want to do that.” Again, I really wanted to just address the elephant in the room. We have this massive disparity of wealth with young and old. Could I tell that story and be part of the conversation using sort of the 87 North Engin–the David Leitch engine–of action and comedy, and be a little bit more message forward than I normally am, but also make it an entertaining ride and have people enjoy it, but then at the end of it, feel something and maybe there's a call to action for you in your own life to do something for your neighbor or go out and vote and hold your politicians accountable. This originally was going to come out on Labor Day, and I think Amazon had wished for it to go out on Labor Day, and I think the timing wasn't right for marketing, and we found a great slot at the end of the year or so. Every week it gets more timely. It's not like the movie's lost its timeliness. After Tuesday, it’s even more timely. That was the goal with this film. It was to do something provocative and dangerous, but also entertaining.

McCORMICK: It's a subject we're really passionate about, and we wanted to use our platform to join the conversation and to be part of it like a [time] capsule film. There were two other aspects that were really exciting to us. I think David always bends genres or at least adds to the conversation of the genre, and heist movies aren't like this movie, right? The robbers are hiding. They're not trying to hide in plain sight. The message is so forward in this movie in the coolest way that’s almost done with this bravado that they're going to get away with it. It's so Gen Z in that way. They do it for longer than they probably even think, but it's worth it for the message because they're that devoted to what they want people to hear. To try to make change, which was what was cool about it. The second part was to try to find a way to connect with social media and creator storytelling in an authentic way. Everybody’s watching. These creators have such connectivity to their followers. What's the difference? How can you play in both formats? How do they meet? Where do they meet? How do they connect? How do they answer and question each other? We thought that that would be a really fun opportunity for David to play in that space. I haven't really seen a movie that does it in the same way, and I think it's one of the achievements of the film.

I really love the way you did the YouTube stuff with Nick talking to the camera. Talk a little bit about putting together those YouTube clips, because they're very effective and they're dropping truth bombs on the audience. You’re not lying with these numbers.

LEITCH: No, not at all. I think that was one of the fascinating things about the script initially. You read those first numbers. Then you do a little research and you're like, “wow, really?” I think people will be shocked by it. It’s a real motivation to want to rob a bank. The first video was scripted, and there were other videos along the way, but they were really more like The Anarchist Handbook. It was very grounded. Social media doesn't feel like that to me. I mean, the things that I watch are really entertaining and they're engaging and they're crazy. I started to rework those sequences and created the persona of The Wolf that wasn't in the script. We created the gang wearing these colorful masks. The whole social media thing became its own life in the pre-production process. I started to write those edutainment videos so I could drop them in at different places in the scripts to carry the story forward, but also keep the energy going and, again, combine these two storytelling styles. You see in the middle of the second act when they get caught and there's the interrogation scene, those two styles come together, and that's where life really meets social media. Nick is breaking the fourth wall on film, and we're using graphics over film and there's a song playing like you would [hear] if you were watching a YouTube thing, but it's like carrying you through the whole piece. That was an intentional thing. How can we, like Kelly said, bring these to make a modern piece about social media and its power? It’s still grounded in these people's real traumas that have led them to wanting to rob banks.

I know you guys made this on a budget, so how the f did you get Radiohead and Billie Eilish? You have some real needle drops in this movie, and they're big songs.

LEITCH: Kelly is always good with me at the beginning when there's a budget and we're looking at line items and you look at your spreadsheet. You realize, “How much am I going to need for Dave’s musical appetite?” We usually set that aside, and it's like, “Wait, that's two days of shooting?!” But we do it because I know it's going to make the film. I know for me, as a storyteller, that's an emotional cheat code. It's shameless, but it's premeditated. I go through the script and there are needle drops that come to mind, and 99% of them stick. And then I formulate my shot sequences around that music. That sequence in the interrogation scene, I knew we were going to use Lily Allen and we were going to use “Fuck You.” I'm shooting it in that way. It’s shot to the music and we know how we're going to edit it. At the end of the movie, with the Billie Eilish song, that did change. That was Lewis Capaldi for the longest time. It used to be “Someone You Loved,” which is also beautiful. We changed it at the last minute, but I still shot that section like a musical piece intentionally.

McCORMICK: We loved it so much, and then it was exactly what happened with the playability of that song. Everybody overplayed it, and so did we. Young women actually were testing really high in the film, and they would literally write like, “is there any way to change out that Lewis Capaldi [song]?” They're our biggest lovers of the movie. We got to take care of the ladies!

Billie Eilish works pretty well. Radiohead is pretty selective with what they allow. How tough was it to actually get “Karma Police”?

McCORMICK: We work with this music supervisor named Susan Kent, and she's really awesome. I don't know how she gets the deals that she gets. I just say, “is there any way to get it lower?” And then she says, “yes!” There are times where we write love letters. David wrote a love letter to Billie Eilish. I think you wrote something to [Radiohead] as well. We show them clips of the movie sometimes to show them where it's going to play, which works really well for our films because it's usually a pretty good use, and that sometimes brings the budgets down, but it also just gets you the song sometimes, too.

LEITCH: You know, people believe in it. I think this was a special piece where they knew the material. This movie has a little bit of a message.

McCORMICK: The Billie Eilish [song] I learned is a toxic breakup song. I thought there was something so cool about it in the sense that it's kind of a toxic breakup from the system. We added that component to it, even though it is kind of their love story. At the same time, there's such sorrow to it that I think it kind of works for everything you need to feel.

This isn't really a question. It's more like a statement. I just want to make sure I say out loud that the health insurance industry in America is out to fuck you, and anything that we can do, especially in your movie to get more people talking about this, is very important. That's all I got. I give credit to Amazon for being behind it. It's a huge corporation pointing out some of the bullshit.

McCORMICK: Everybody inside of Amazon is really passionate about the movie. They were so incredibly supportive. You've seen the work that they're doing on social media, especially. These trailers are out of this world, and you could just feel that this is hitting us all, even when you're working there too, you know? It’s pretty interesting to see how much everybody who's been a part of it galvanized around it. One of my favorite stories [was] when we were shooting in the streets of Pittsburgh. If you've ever shot with extras, you know that they barely stick around for lunch, let alone stick around for the full day, let alone if you're shooting nights. They don’t stay all night or come back the next night, forget about that. We shot two weeks of nights in downtown Pittsburgh, and every night there were five more people! They came, and then they brought five friends, and we ran out of masks, costumes, and everything, because it just became this movement in Pittsburgh while we were shooting it. They all came to party. It was like a rave. They made their own signs. It was just so cool and it made us feel like this is what we want people to feel coming out of the movie, too. You don't have to riot, per se, or rob a bank, but together you're stronger. Find your communities, say your truth, let's make a change.

I need to talk about editing, because you guys know I'm fascinated by editing.

McCORMICK: Elisabet Ronaldsdottir crushed this.

LEITCH: The Icelandic genius. She edited the first John Wick and all of our films. She's amazing.

Everyone in this audience knows that I love John Wick. A lot of people don't remember that it was possibly going straight to DVD or straight to Blu-ray. I could be wrong about this, but then Lionsgate picked it up and then it became a thing.

McCORMICK: It’s more complicated, but we should talk about the editing on How to Rob a Bank.

What is it like when you guys are in the editing room and you're putting together the assembly cut, because you've worked on a number of movies. When you're making your assembly cut, which is where you take all the footage and put it together, have you ever wanted to, like, jump out the window when you have an assembly cut? Or do you always have something?

LEITCH: That's a great question, Steve. Wow. You should do this for a living! Sometimes, you see it, and you're like, “what have I done?” I hide it really well! I do try to walk in with positivity, but there are times where I'm like, “oh, my God!” I trust Elisabet, who's amazing, and I trust Kelly. Elisabet has seen a lot of material over the years, and she's really brutally honest, and she pulls no punches. She can look at you and go, “we have a great movie.” If she looks at me like, “we got some stuff to figure out,” and then I’m like, “oh shit, now we really got to go to work.” Post[-production] has become a passion for me. During the first Wick, I didn’t love it. I didn’t understand that letting go amplifies another scene, and as I’ve grown as a filmmaker, post has become one of my favorite places to play. We were meticulous about the editing in this film. We got to play with those video sequences that were edited in a different house, but then [they were] brought in and we re-edited them. Getting the timing just right, playing with the music, adjusting the sound, having a scene in, having a scene out, watching it again. I love that process. I've become really comfortable with letting things go to make for the greater good. I would be bad on an island where you have to pick somebody to go and be like, “it's the greater good. You got to go out.”

For people that don't realize how, how long does it typically take for you guys to edit a film? I don't think people realize that it’s a battle. You are working long hours for many months to put something together.

McCORMICK: We have a pretty short editing schedule. I think it's 27 or 28 weeks.

Tell the people, is that like a Monday through Friday? Is it 9 to 5?

LEITCH: Yeah. It's more like a 9 to 7. There’s a lot of things going on. You have your editor who's working on scenes you may be watching, you divide the movie into different reels so you can actually digest it in a way so that you're not rewatching everything all the time. I might be watching a reel doing notes, Elisabet might be working on a second reel. We may have an assistant editor looking for sound or a different take.

McCORMICK: You’re working with your composer, you're working with your visual effects team, you're having meetings all the time on iterations of either music or effects. It’s a lot.

LEITCH: It’s kind of endless. There's so much to do that the day just gets consumed.

McCORMICK: There’s a 10-week period that’s contractual with the DGA. I think people really think that that's a ton of time, and then they run out of time. That happens so often that they didn't have the discipline in those ten weeks, and things go off the rails because it feels like you've got all the time in the world, and then you are out of time so fast.

LEITCH: What I like to do now is to get my first six weeks. I'm super intense and I try to get to the strongest version of the movie that I'm feeling at the moment. I try to get a really strong assembly cut, reduce it down. I bring Kelly in for fresh eyes and then it's like dropping a hand grenade on it! “Damn it, it was good for a second!” Then I have another four weeks to take those ideas and shape them. The movie ultimately becomes better the more you put it under pressure.

McCORMICK: David's director's cuts are really mature, so it's nice, because then the studio can see what the movie is. You're basically testing that cut. He's pretty accepting of notes, if they’re really good, at the director’s cut phase, to do his first preview so that, again, we're making the same movie with the studio. It's not like a split where it's like it's his cut versus theirs. We've never really done that. Then it’s testing it again and really listening to the audience for confusion, for pacing, for jokes, for songs, and then finishing it, which takes forever, too, because it's like three weeks of mixing. It's the slowest process in our high-tech world to have AI taking over our jobs. They have to mix a reel and then match the reel to the edit, and the conforming. It takes forever. I go, “Isn’t there a way to do this faster?!”

LEITCH: You're sliding things around frame by frame to get the sound back to where it was when you make an edit.

McCORMICK: It’s like three weeks of that, going back and forth and then listening again and going back and forth, then it's color.

LEITCH: You can see how much Kelly loves post!

McCORMICK: I actually do! I like it more than production!

Every time I hear from people about what goes on behind the scenes, in terms of making some of these movies, and the bigger the film, the longer it can take and the more meticulous, it's crazy. What was the last thing you cut out before you picture-locked [on How to Rob a Bank]?

LEITCH: Let me say this, because I would be more like the last thing I put in because we were toying with the ending. If you were having the real feels when he's laying on the ground and the camera's moving up, we could have gone to black. That was my first ending of the movie, but I shot all the other endings.

LEITCH: It leaves a very, very different feel. I wanted this to be a call to action, and I wanted this to be about hope. At the end of the day, I thought it was better to go with the original ending that we shot. I kept watching the film, and I was really moved by that moment.

How did you decide on how to escape prison? When you do something like that, are you in the back of your mind, like, “well, we might want to continue the story”? Or is it like, “we're just going to have fun with this”?

McCORMICK: It actually stemmed from just wrapping, and the hope. Wrapping up Renzi, it worked so well that you knew that he was still doing stuff and like going to hack his way into some more fun videos, and it wrapped up Anna Sawai’s character so well, and then it gave you hope. It wasn't about a franchise play at all. It was just about hope in this case.

LEITCH: Exactly. It was really more of just wrapping up this movie, because I think it was really a one-off about this message.

The best movie title of 2027 is you guys. You own the best title of next year. They made another movie and the title is…

McCORMICK: It’s definitely a palate cleanser from tonight.

You've done a lot of second unit [directing]. How much do you lose your mind having a second unit director on your movie? Because I would imagine you want to shoot absolutely everything, or maybe I'm wrong about this.

LEITCH: I don’t have a lot of second units on my set. I don't push a lot off to the second unit. When I do, I generally have great people that I trust that have been with me for years. On this film, Greg Rementer directed all the heist stuff, and that was the stunt team dressed as the actors, because we're using masks. I just let them go wild.

McCORMICK: There were like a thousand cameras on everyone, prosumer cameras, the drones, and he shot them like they were a play.

LEITCH: We shot it like it was just real life. You're capturing it like a content creator would, right? There's just cameras everywhere, and you're seeing the cameras. There’s a lot of trust with me and the stunt teams, because we go way back, and I've been in that world for so long.

I could ask you guys a million other things, but I'm going to get killed. I've already gone way too far and so on. I'm just going to stop there and say, congrats on the movie.

LEITCH: You’re already going to get killed by the health insurance industry!

Fuck the health insurance industry! I hate them so much. No one should go bankrupt in America for having to go to the doctors.

#3331. Box Office: ‘Club Kid’ Scores Best Limited Expansion of the Year as Younger Audiences Embrace Jordan Firstman’s Oscar Hopeful

Jordan Firstman’s “Club Kid” was the belle of Cannes. Critics raved about Firstman’s feature directorial debut, as well as his sensitive performance as a party promoter turned unlikely dad, and A24 swept in to buy the film for $17 million after a bidding war. But plenty of movies have been embraced at film festivals only to face rejection when they hit the wider world. Would “Club Kid” be another “Dope” or “Begin Again”?

Well, based on a very limited sample size, “Club Kid” seems to be performing just fine, thank you very much. Those raves and A24’s imprimatur of cool are paying off as the film enjoyed the best limited expansion of the year this weekend, grossing $756,060 across 27 screens. That translates into an impressive $28,002 per-screen average. Since opening in six screens on Nov. 6, “Club Kid” has earned nearly $1.5 million. But this very New York story has mostly played in major cities and liberal bastions like the Big Apple, Chicago, Austin, San Francisco, and Los Angeles. Will audiences across the country embrace the story of a drug-taking, sex-positive gay man and his adorable 10-year-old accidental son? We’ll find out on Thanksgiving when it goes wide. Related Stories Box Office: ‘Ebenezer’ Opens to Modest $19 Million, Showing Johnny Depp Is Still a Draw for the Right Price ‘Fatherland’ Wins Golden Frog at ToruńCAMERIMAGE 2026 — Full Winners List

In order for “Club Kid” to be a financial success, it will need to more than double the $17 million that A24 shelled out for the rights, because theaters keep half the ticket sales. That could happen if “Club Kid” generates awards buzz and positive word-of-mouth spreads, something that seems plausible given how funny, touching, and life-affirming Firstman’s film is (seriously, audiences have been applauding as the credits roll). Plus, A24 is on a heater this year, releasing hits like “You Can See Everything” and “Backrooms” that have it rivaling the market shares of much larger studios like Warner Bros. and Paramount.

There are certainly a lot of other Oscar hopefuls out there. Searchlight’s “Wild Horse Nine,” which is seen as a near lock for a Best Picture nod, earned $4.6 million domestically in its second weekend. The film about two CIA agents up to no good in Chile has earned $28 million globally. Then there’s “La Bola Negra,” a multigenerational gay epic from Netflix. It’s earned $3.5 million domestically over five weeks in theaters. And “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,” which is generating Oscar buzz for John Turturro, picked up $322,830 to bring its domestic haul to $4.7 million after four weeks in theaters.

“Wicker,” with its story of a fisherwoman who becomes romantically entangled with a wicker man, may be too weird to generate a much love from Academy voters, but it has done well for its distributor, Black Bear, earning $1.5 million in North America last weekend. Its global total stands at $36.7 million after four weeks of release.

As for “Club Kid,” A24 thinks its trajectory mirrors that of other recent arthouse hits, with ticket sales pacing alongside those of “Moonlight” ($67 million gross) and “Anora” ($59.3 million gross) at this point in its expansion. Exit scores are among the best in the studio’s history and the film is connecting with young audiences as 80% of ticket buyers were under the age of 35. Next weekend will be another test for “Club Kid” as it expands to 200 screens across the top 50 markets. If it keeps drawing crowds, Firstman and A24 will have a lot to celebrate.

#3330. How Oz Became The Most Controversial Magazine Of All Time

Oz magazine is remembered today as one of the most notorious counterculture publications. Launched on April 1, 1963, by Richard Nevile, Richard Walsh, and Martin Sharp in Sydney, Australia, it was a satirical, psychedelic provocateur whose legal battles still feature in free-speech debates, and whose archives historians and designers now study.

Pre-Oz, Western society heavily operated on traditional post-World War II values. In other words, the status quo was staunchly conservative and rigid, with substantive dissent either intolerable or criminalised.

Staying deferential wasn’t merely a choice for the mainstream press; it was driven by routine censorship. It’s a climate that saw Britain’s Lord Chamberlain vet stage plays before they could be performed, Australian customs officials screening books and films, homosexuality outlawed, and obscenity trials happening as late as 1960.

Despite this hostility to the underground press, Oz thrived for a decade (1963-1973), and across continents. It proved that a market existed for anti-establishment satire.

The first step toward controversy is to stand out, and in media the surest way to do that is to publish what everyone else avoids. Long before Oz became famous for psychedelic London posters or the “Schoolkids” trial, it built its notorious reputation in Sydney, Australia, by printing what polite society only whispered about.

The debut April 1963 issue tackled the largely avoided subject of illegal abortion head-on, exposing underground abortion clinics and the corrupt police system that protected and profited from it. Included in the mix were incendiary takes on homosexuality, then both criminalized and deeply sensitive, along with provocations such as bodily tattoos, chastity belts, and Australia’s White immigration policy.

Oz added deadpan hoaxes that mocked public authority and symbols of sacred cultural status, such as a report of the Sydney Harbour Bridge collapsing. That was the equivalent of Parisians waking to (fake) news that the Eiffel Tower had crumbled, or New Yorkers reading on the front page of The New York Times that the Brooklyn Bridge had fallen.

If that doesn’t seem audacious enough, consider the cover of Oz’s Issue No. 6 in February 1964. It featured a photo of editor Richard Neville and two friends pretending to urinate into a newly unveiled wall fountain designed by prominent sculptor Tom Bass, a work that had just been inaugurated by Prime Minister Robert Menzies.

Oz’s early work in Sydney set the tone for its shock-and-satire identity. It also showed readers that public authorities and the mainstream press could fool them just as easily as the magazine did with its hoaxes.

Unsurprisingly, the reaction was as polarized as it was immediate. Newsstand bans did nothing to dissuade buyers who cleared all 6,000 debut copies. Establishment institutions hit back fast: advertisers pulled their contracts, writers’ jobs were threatened, and the editors were evicted from their government-owned Sydney office.

Oz had jolted Sydney’s readers, but more than 10,000 miles away in London, its 1967 relaunch as Oz London hit even harder. And it was a huge success: circulation doubled from Sydney’s 40,000 peak to 80,000 copies.

Much of the credit goes to Martin Sharp, who harnessed photographic offset lithography, freeing designers to experiment with neon colour, spiral layouts and collage. In modern terms, it was like leaping from a plain-text newsletter to a neon, meme-saturated TikTok feed.

Rather than arguing solely in neat columns as in Sydney, Oz London utilized countercultural provocations, especially with revered art and public faces. Nothing moves mouths quite like a magazine with the Mona Lisa smoking a joint, Bob Dylan as a swirling psychedelic portrait, or Vincent van Gogh as a modern hippie on its cover. That’s exactly what Oz London did.

For the average 1960s British youth, the radical art was bedroom wall poster-worthy. And a copy in hand (laden with topics such as feminism, drug laws, and the Vietnam War) became tantamount to being the cool, rebellious mind the age grade so relished.

Audacious as it was, the May 1970 issue of Oz was downright impudent. Bored with their own output, editors Richard Neville, Jim Anderson, and Felix Dennis handed the reins of an entire edition to under-18s, to test the limits of the rawness and rebellion of British adolescence. Pitch that to a modern magazine today, and the legal department would hyperventilate.

Predictably, the teenagers’ finger and mind prints were all over the resulting 48-page Issue No. 28. However, the nude cover and explicit personal ads in the back were entirely the adults' idea.

The juveniles aired their grievances, attacking the British school system’s authoritarian headmasters, corporal punishments, uniform rules, and exams. Alongside these critiques were their unfiltered views on teenage sexuality, contraception, recreational drugs, and countercultural music. Far from an orderly debate, their confrontation was chaotic and deliberately juvenile. It peaked with what is now infamously known as “The Rupert Bear incident.”

In that same issue, 15-year-old Vivian Berger made a notorious collage: she pasted the cheerful head of children's icon Rupert Bear onto a sexually explicit body of an X-rated comic by American underground cartoonist Robert Crumb, with the nursery rhymes clearly still visible underneath.

Vivian Berger’s shattering of the innocence associated with Rupert Bear (the ultimate symbol of wholesome, middle-class British childhood) was rude at best. To British authorities, though, this crossed an unforgivable line. By indulging teens in the magazine's production and publishing Berger’s explicit collage, Oz had committed cultural sacrilege in a deliberate attempt to corrupt Britain’s youth.

The police, who had hitherto restricted their raids to Oz’s offices, arrested Neville, Anderson, and Dennis and confiscated all printing materials at the Oz headquarters. This set the stage for the historic 1971 Old Bailey obscenity trial.

Anyone in London (the wider British public and International counterculture inclusive) who hadn’t heard or been bothered by Oz did so following the “Schoolkids Issue.” And the few still unbothered couldn't ignore the resulting trial that began on June 23, 1971, inside Court No. 2 at London’s Old Bailey.

This six-week trial was the longest obscenity trial in British legal history. And it was a public affair, so much so that thousands rallied in support outside the courthouse and John Lennon and Yoko Ono recorded a charity single, "God Save Us,”

Even with such a high-stakes trial, including a “conspiracy to corrupt public morals” charge that carried a life sentence, the defendants did what underground counterculture did best: mock authority. They arrived at court rocking psychedelic shirts, in schoolgirl uniforms, and having Richard Neville defend himself in court while wearing a long, flowing velvet jacket.

More importantly, it was a cultural clash between the British establishment, wielding the 1959 Obscene Publications Act under which the defendants were tried, and counterculture, represented by defendants Richard Neville, Jim Anderson, and Felix Dennis. In the end, both sides won and lost, though to varying degrees.

Neville, Anderson, and Dennis lost when they were acquitted of conspiracy but convicted of publishing and posting an obscene article, receiving sentences of 15, 12, and 9 months respectively. This was not before they were remanded for psychiatric evaluation and their signature hairs shaved.

The law’s victory was short-lived and pyrrhic. Following intense public outrage, the convictions were overturned on appeal in November 1971, and the trio walked free. Subsequently, the British justice system lost the political appetite to prosecute obscene publications, even as Oz itself buckled in 1973 under the weight of legal debt.

In the end, though, the real winner was Oz. They emerged as free-speech folk heroes whose legal victory permanently broke the back of British print censorship and paved the way for modern media freedom. Wealth flowed from it too: lessons learnt from Oz were vital in Dennis establishing a publishing empire.

#3328. 10 Shows Like 'Minimum Wage' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Spinning off of a popular web series, Netflix's Minimum Wage is currently in the middle of a 28-episode first-season run. If that sounds like a lot of episodes for a show in 2026, keep in mind that they're generally less than 15 minutes each, which is perfect for your overloaded to-watch list—especially when they go down so easily. This cringe workplace mockumentary follows the crew of teenagers running a failing pizza place and making (you guessed it) minimum wage; they're under enormous pressure from their boss (Randall Park) to save the business and their one dumb source of income.

The punchy episodes will leave you plenty of time to explore other streaming shows dealing with the utter ridiculousness of the modern workplace. Here are 10 to get you started.

Workplace comedies usually revolve around white-collar office environments (The Mary Tyler Moore Show, 30 Rock, Parks and Recreation, etc.). Like Minimum Wage, Superstore instead follows the staff of Cloud 9, a generic big-box retailer. The show’s deep bench and diverse cast are largely focused on the jokes, but much of that comedy involves the relatable situation of working a job that demands commitment and a smiley attitude in the face of both entitled customers and obnoxious bosses. It's a different venue and age bracket, but a nutty workplace is a nutty workplace. Stream Superstore on Hulu and Peacock.

We're moving away from the workplace and aging things up a bit, but no worries: the name is a little ironic given that the codependent, co-habitating twenty-somethings of the title are hardly mature. Five friends are cohabiting in the childhood home of Samir (Malik Elassal), and dealing with the uniquely Gen-Z humiliations around dating, work, and even health insurance. Only one member of the group has an actual reasonably good job, while career paths for the others include being a temp, waiter, and a part-time ballet instructor. Stream Adults on Hulu.

This offbeat workplace comedy kicks off with a fabulous premise: Jeong Bok-dong (Kim Byung-chul) was a high-level director in a major corporation until one bad meeting saw him demoted. To president! ...of the company's failing Pegasus Mart offshoot. Bok-dong makes it his mission to get revenge by bankrupting the store, hiring eccentrics to execute eccentric, entirely whackadoo plans and accidentally getting Pegasus noticed by customers, who quickly make it more popular than ever. Think The Producers, but in retail. Stream Pegasus Market on Tubi.

It might sound a little (or a lot) niche, but we’ve seen enough headlines about the working conditions at many video game production houses to understand why a workplace comedy set against such a backdrop would make for a dark and juicy comedy. Charlotte Nicdao and Rob McElhenney are the leads, playing a brilliant workaholic and an unsociable egomaniac, respectively, and the chemistry between them gives the show more than enough spark. There's also a four-episode spin-off called Side Quest. Stream Mythic Quest.

A half-hour comedy-drama with an emphasis on the comedy, Gentefied follows three Mexican-American cousins who have built lives in Los Angeles, only to be faced with a new challenge: the looming gentrification of the neighborhood they helped to build via their family's taco shop. Gentefied has a baked-in sense of place and culture and a lot of heart; the second season is even better than the first. Stream Gentefied on Netflix.

Perhaps there's a bit of counter-programming in this dramedy about a couple of scrappy New York City outsiders, but there's a fundamental goofiness to this show about a couple of nice guys who are great at getting themselves into trouble, and equally good at talking themselves out of it. Bryan Greenberg plays Ben Epstein, a quiet guy with any number of big ideas, while Victor Rasuk plays the outgoing, often shameless Cam Calderon; together they manage a startup clothing business with the benefits of neither money nor experience, amiably hustling their way to success, maybe. Stream How to Make It in America on HBO Max and Netflix.

Debuting at the beginning of the Obama administration before getting a surprise revival just a couple of years ago, Party Down is an acclaimed cult sitcom for the ages—lots of laughs, low ratings, and always worth rediscovering. A group of six (or so) struggling LA actors and writers work as cater waiters for a fancy company, with every episode into a new and wildly absurd situation, even as their aspirations far outstrip their actual lives. Stream Party Down on Prime Video and Netflix.

A legitimate sitcom that just happens to be set in Northern Ireland during the violent Troubles of the 1990s, when clashes between nationalists and unionists frequently resulted in violence. It’s a fascinating contrast, brought to life by a writer and creator (Lisa McGee) who lived it. It’s also laugh-out-loud funny—though it doesn’t make any allowances for audiences unaccustomed to Irish accents, so don’t feel bad if you need subtitles until you get the hang of it. Erin, Orla, Clare, and Michelle are joined by James, the only male student at their Catholic girls' school, dealing with normal growing-up stuff in absurd times. This world is a far cry from that of Minimum Wage, but Lisa McGee's sense of the absurd connects both shows—if the setting is a bit more dramatic, the comedy is just as wonderfully silly. Stream Derry Girls on Netflix.

Not a comedy! But about as good an indication of where we are in the modern global workplace as you're likely to find. Hyuk‑jun is a young guy saddled with debt who signs on for some part-time work at a job agency...at 50x the going rate, no less (should've been a red flag). Each new assignment places him in new and increasingly horrific situations, with increasingly arbitrary-seeming rules. But, hey, in 2026, it's a living. Stream Dead-End Job on Netflix.

It's an office (obviously) and not a pizza joint, but the point here is kinda that white-collar jobs in the 21st century can be at least as soul-killing as working customer service. The Office inherited some of the finer tropes of the workplace comedy (mostly involving tossing together a group of weirdos overly invested in their jobs) while also launching a million mockumentary-style shows, running for nine seasons, and becoming one of the most popular shows of its era. Stream The Office on Peacock.

#3327. There’s a Good Reason the NYC Marathon Winners Wore These Watches

Over 60,000 runners crossed the finish line at the New York City Marathon last week. When you think of the elites fighting for a spot on the podium, you might expect to see only the priciest, most feature-packed GPS watches money can buy—historically, this meant the most premium Garmin Forerunners. Looking at the wrists of this year's New York City Marathon podium finishers, though,  you’ll see that Garmin—the name most recreational runners reach for by default—was far from the only brand on the course.

Here are the watches I’ve been able to confirm among the top NYC Marathon finishers:

Men's winner, Andreas Almgren: Coros Pace 4 (sponsored)

Men's runner-up, Yemaneberhan Crippa: Amazfit Cheetah 2 Pro (sponsored)

Women's runner-up, Jessica McClain: Garmin Forerunner 570 (sponsored)

Women's third place, Hellen Obiri: Coros Pace 4 (sponsored)

Nonbinary winner, Ryan Montgomery: Suunto Race 3S (almost certainly sponsored, since this watch was released last month)

An important disclaimer: I haven't spoken with any of these athletes. What follows is my opinion, based on what I know running watches offer the people who wear them.

"Garmin" has long been the default answer to "what running watch should I buy?" It earned that spot with reliable GPS, excellent software, and a huge ecosystem. And on this podium, it's represented by a Forerunner 570—a great watch, but at a price tag most runners would struggle to justify.

Of course, sponsorships muddy the water, since athletes wear what their sponsors put on their wrists. But that's exactly the point: Other brands are investing in elite runners because they believe their products can stand next to Garmin's, and it looks like they’re making the right bet.

It's fair to ask whether Garmin's grip is loosening. The company has increasingly pushed toward the fanciest watches with the most features at higher and higher price points. The Forerunner 570 starts north of $500. Meanwhile, COROS, Amazfit, and others are proving that a perfectly solid, competitive watch doesn't need to cost that much. Is Garmin still the best running watch overall? For ecosystem, polish, and depth of features, it's still a strong contender. But "best" no longer means "the only serious option," and the gap between Garmin and the field is narrower than it has been in years. Sponsored or not, seeing two Coros Pace 4s and an Amazfit Cheetah 2 Pro among the top finishers is worth noting.

You don’t need an expensive watch to be elite—just look at the cheap running watches worn by the men who broke the sub-two-hour barrier at the London Marathon this past spring. Training load scores, recovery metrics, maps, music, and smart notifications are nice, but they're extras. If you're shopping for a watch, spend your money on the basics being done right, and don't feel pressured to pay for features you'll never use. Everything besides your time and pace is icing on the cake.

Whichever brand you choose, focus on these basics in your running watch:

The New York City Marathon podium shows a running-watch market that's a bit more competitive and intriguing than the era of "just buy a Garmin" suggests. Garmin is still excellent, but now we’re seeing proof that Coros, Amazfit, and Suunto are all making watches good enough for the fastest humans on the planet. If they can trust those watches on their biggest days, the rest of us can probably trust them with our Saturday long runs.

#3326. Gentler Streak 6.0 adds a new wellbeing timeline and customizable dashboard

In an update rolling out today, Gentler Streak is introducing new ways for users to track their wellbeing and personalize the app’s guidance based on how they feel. Here are the details.

One of my favorite exercise-tracking apps got even better today with an update that expands its functionality beyond workouts and fitness metrics to better reflect how users actually feel.

Starting today, Gentler Streak will let users log how they feel each day, including their mood, symptoms, and other factors that may not be reflected in their health and fitness data.

Some days, the way we feel isn’t reflected in what the data says, no matter the data quality. “How I Feel” captures the part that devices can’t grasp: personal context. And how you feel is not only a mood: it is also a sore throat, heavy legs or a poor night’s sleep. The feature was inspired by the Gentler Streak community, including people living with chronic fatigue, fibromyalgia, ADHD, and those not wearing their Apple Watch at night. Without overnight signals, their guidance has less to work with.

According to the team behind Gentler Streak, these new features are aimed at users whose health and fitness data may not accurately reflect how they feel, including those dealing with chronic conditions, menopause, stress, or poor sleep.

In practice, the app will now feature four tabs: Today, Health, Workouts, and Insights. In the Today and Health tabs, a new “Anything to add?” field will let users rate how they feel, from Great to Off, and add context about what might be affecting their well-being, including fatigue, feeling calm, or custom tags.

You decide when the prompt appears. Go to Profile > Settings > Self-Evaluation Prompt and choose one of three options: only when your vitals or sleep are off, always on, or never.

Gentler Stories notes that the self-assessments will override the app’s wellbeing estimates for that day, with its daily guidance adjusting accordingly.

The Today tab will also feature an expanded 10- or 30-day timeline showing logged workouts, wellbeing estimates, potential symptoms, poor sleep or vitals, and the first day of a menstrual period, while Health will introduce an interactive chart showing users how their wellbeing changes over time, with the ability to filter by symptoms.

Users can now also customize which information appears on their Today screen, including vitals, sleep, steps, menstrual cycle, VO₂ max, and workouts, which is a nice touch.

For users who are sick, injured, or taking a break from exercise, the app’s hallmark Activity Path will make way for a new Wellbeing Path, which lets them track their wellbeing on a daily basis.

For users with Active status, a new colorful wellbeing line will appear beneath the Activity Path, reflecting how they feel each day. This information is logged automatically for those who wear their Apple Watch overnight, or based on self-assessments for those who don’t.

Importantly, Gentler Stories notes that all information entered through the new feature remains on the user’s device, with no accounts or company-operated servers involved.

#3325. This Actively Exploited Chrome Vulnerability Is Putting Your Browser at Risk

If you've seen an uptick in security updates as of late, you're not alone. AI models have become very good at finding new security vulnerabilities throughout 2026. Researchers and hackers alike are increasingly relying on these models in their individual pursuits: Hackers want to find these flaws to exploit them, while researchers want to block hackers from doing so. Microsoft's latest Patch Tuesday update included more than 1,400 patches; meanwhile, Apple's latest security update fixed two iMessage flaws that let both bad actors and innocent parties alike access texts they shouldn't.

Whether you use a Mac or a PC, you probably browse the web with Chrome, or a Chromium-based browser. As it happens, Google's web browsing platform is the latest to receive an important security update—but it's far from the first important Chrome update of the year.

As reported by The Hacker News, Google released a new update for Chrome on Monday that patches nine security flaws. While all vulnerabilities are important to patch, one in particular is more serious than the rest: CVE-2026-125350, a use-after-free bug in Chrome's XML component.

Use-after-free vulnerabilities happen when the system frees up a memory location, but a program tries to access it anyway. It's a glitch in programming, but it offers bad actors an opportunity to break into your system. At worst, it allows arbitrary code execution, or, in other words, gives hackers the ability to run their own code in the app or system.

That's bad enough on the surface, but, unfortunately, Google confirmed that CVE-2026-125350 has an active exploit in the wild. The company is keeping other details close to the vest, but it's dangerous nonetheless. At least someone, somewhere, has used this flaw against a target, which puts all Chrome users (as well as users of Chromium-based browsers) at risk.

What's more, this isn't Chrome's first active exploit of the year—this is its eighth. The company is playing catch-up with hackers looking to target users of its browser, which makes sense, seeing as Chrome is by far the world's most popular browser.

If you're using Chrome on your computer, you'll want to update it as soon as possible. Make sure you're running at least versions 157.0.8103.50/.51 on Mac or PC, or 157.0.8103.50 on Linux. To check, click the three dots in the top-right corner of your Chrome window, then go to More > Help > About Google Chrome.

Other Chromium-based browsers may not have the update yet, but they are affected by this flaw. If you use browsers like Microsoft Edge, Opera, or Brave, keep an eye on your updates to install any of the latest patches.

#3324. High-Protein Packaged Foods May Not Be As Healthy As They Look

Of the three major macronutrients—protein, carbs, and fat—protein has the best reputation, and it’s fairly well deserved. We need significant amounts of protein in our diet, and nothing particularly bad happens if we get too much. Dietary protein helps you build muscle, and if you’re trying to lose weight it helps stop you from losing too much muscle along with the fat. It also helps to make meals feel filling. Great! But.

Once the general public gets the idea that something is good for you, the companies that make packaged food start putting it in everything. Or, they make products where the good-for-you thing features prominently on the label, whether or not there is very much inside. So a lot of packaged food now boasts protein on the label. Here’s what you should ask yourself about those foods:

Take a close look here—sometimes a food will boast of a certain amount of protein per package but the package contains two or three servings. Other times, the protein per serving is correct, and we're supposed to be excited to have, say, 7 grams per serving. That's just not very much—and certainly not worth paying extra or choosing a less-delicious food just for those few added grams.

It’s good to know how much protein you need in your diet. If you’re not gaining or losing weight, and not doing very much exercise, a 150-pound person only needs about 54 grams of protein a day. (I've done the math for various body weights here.) If you’re working out a lot, or if you’re trying to gain or lose weight (yep, either way), that same 150-pound person will need more like 81 to 95 grams of protein per day. More is OK, but not necessary.

So if you’re trying to get 90 grams per day, 30 grams per meal is a reasonable amount to shoot for. Coincidentally, 30 grams is the amount of protein that tends to make a meal feel satisfying. You can do the math to figure out whether a protein-added product is going to be helpful in your day’s diet.

I think this is the most important question about protein-added foods. It’s not hard to get protein in a meal; meats, dairy, tofu, beans, and grains all tend to supply plenty. So what is this protein-added thing you’re considering, and are you eating it instead of a traditional meal?

Here’s an example. If I’m heading straight from the gym to run some errands, and I need something to substitute for a meal—yeah, this isn’t great planning, but sometimes it happens—a protein bar with 20 grams of protein is a step in the right direction. Much better than a candy bar, anyway.

But then there are things like this "protein mix" trail mix: 7 grams of protein with 200 calories. A double serving would be 400 calories and only 14 grams of protein. Hardly a great choice if your goal is just to add to your protein intake for the day.

And then there are the chips that my kid, for a time, couldn't stop eating. He loves Doritos and such; on a whim, we bought him some protein chips (yes, these are a real thing). Are they better for him than the equivalent amount of Doritos? Arguably, sort of yes. But then he started arguing that since they have protein, he should be able to eat them in place of dinner. We nixed that, but admit it: Are you having that same argument with yourself, feeling better about a snack food because it contains extra protein? If so, the marketing is working—you’re feeling good about your supposedly healthy choices, even though you’re just eating a bag of chips.

#3321. Netflix’s 10/10 School Drama Is The Exact Opposite Of Euphoria

The best comfort show on Netflix proves not all school dramas have to be the same. HBO’s Euphoria became a defining pop-culture phenomenon thanks to its bold take on teenage drama and its breathtaking visual style. Creator Sam Levinson injected hypnotic cinematography and Labrinth’s gospel-infused score into a tense story about addiction and growing pains, elevated by Zendaya’s Emmy-winning performance as Rue Bennett and a large cast of talented stars. Euphoria famously refuses to soften the messy realities of teens and twenty-somethings to create a sensory-heavy portrait of modern anxiety.

While not strictly the first of its kind, Euphoria is the most famous series to tackle its themes. Over a decade before Euphoria premiered, British pioneer Skins pioneered chaotic substance-fueled teen ensemble storytelling in mainstream media. Parallel to Euphoria, HBO also experimented with We Are Who We Are and Genera+ion, which explored queer youth and identity. In the years leading up to Euphoria's premiere, Netflix had already tapped into this genre. First, two years prior with the social media phenomenon 13 Reasons Why; and just a year later in 2018, with the Spanish hit Élite, which had a similar impact on Spanish-speaking audiences before Netflix expanded its reach.

It's clear that series like Euphoria strike a chord with audiences, but that doesn't mean every show with the same setting has to have a similar plot and tone.

In an era dominated by high-stress teen dramas, The Fragrant Flower Blooms with Dignity is a soothing sanctuary. Modern series like Euphoria and Élite base their edge-of-your-seat appeal on toxic relationships and psychological dread, whereas CloverWorks' adaptation of Saka Mikami's manga focuses on school students developing genuine empathy and care for each other. The plot follows the towering Chidori High student Rintaro Tsumugi, who conceals a tender heart beneath his intimidating appearance; and the petite scholarship student Kaoruko Waguri, who comes from the prestigious and rivalrous Kikyo Girls' Academy right next door. Their first meeting inside Rintaro’s family bakery sparks an immediate connection that quickly develops into wholesome love.

Instead of stretching out contrived misunderstandings and bitter love triangles, The Fragrant Flower Blooms with Dignity celebrates Rintaro and Kaoruko's honest communication. Whenever social class friction and the lingering prejudice between their rival schools threatens to pull them apart, Rintaro, Kaoruko, and their loyal circle of friends talk through their feelings and stand up for each another with remarkable grace. CloverWorks’ soft sunlit animation and expressive characters turn a remarkably low-stakes story into a pure dose of comfort television filled with mouth-watering pastries and adorable interactions.

CloverWorks’ first season of The Fragrant Flower Blooms with Dignity barely scratches the surface of Saka Mikami’s manga. Having debuted in Magazine Pocket in October 2021, the original series has grown past two hundred chapters and more than twenty collected tankōbon volumes, meaning the initial thirteen-episode anime run only covers roughly the first forty chapters, or about a quarter of the overall story. Given that Mikami’s pacing lets every emotional milestone breathe naturally, future seasons can continue adapting the manga at the exact same unhurried pace.

Netflix has some of the best romance anime series around, but only a handful are so good that they can be considered near perfect.

As the plot continues beyond the anime’s finale, Rintaro and Kaoruko’s relationship from the manga evolves into an official couple as they progress in their high school life. They eventually meet each other's families, balance part-time jobs, and confront the looming pressure of university entrance exams and post-graduation career paths. Alongside Rintaro’s own quiet growth in self-confidence and culinary passion, The Fragrant Flower Blooms with Dignity also explores their tight-knit friend groups from both Chidori and Kikyo, complete with side romances and deep bonds formed when the two once-divided worlds learn to trust each other.

Which series would you describe as your comfort show?

Black Friday is always the day after Thanksgiving. This year, Black Friday starts at midnight on Nov. 27. Cyber Monday is the Monday following Black Friday, which starts at midnight on Nov. 30.

The major retailers doing sales are the usual: Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, Home Depot, and many others. Currently, Walmart has publicized its plans already and has early deals available. Best Buy is offering one of the largest Black Friday and Cyber Week sales, with multiple events and early deals. Target has a three-day event. Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Cyber Monday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026.

Black Friday used to be bigger for major retailers and more expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was better for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Nowadays, though, the distinction is almost meaningless. Every major retailer will offer sales on both days, and the smart move is to know what you want, do your research, or refer to guides like our Black Friday and Cyber Monday coverage that have done all the vetting for you.

Unlike Spring or Summer sales, Black Friday doesn't focus on specific categories, which means everything is fair game for discounts. In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Prime Day and Black Friday are the two best times of the year to get the best deals on most purchases. Of course, depending on what you're shopping for, you might find other opportunities throughout the year, but in general, Prime Day and Black Friday have the best sales.

Srouji has led one of the most successful in-house silicon programs in the industry, overseeing the custom chips that power the iPhone, Mac and other Apple devices. His track record gives him deep credibility on chip design, product integration and long-term technology roadmaps. But much of his experience has been built inside Apple’s tightly controlled ecosystem, and he hasn’t been tested in the kind of high-profile salesmanship which Huang is famous for.

Given the urgency, my money is on Nvidia announcing Kress as at least interim CEO, if not a permanent replacement. It seems exceedingly unlikely that Srouji would be appointed at this time, given the in-depth negotiations and discussions that would need to take place.

As to whether he’s a potential candidate following an interim appointment, it still seems unlikely. There was an earlier report of his claimed dissatisfaction at the company, but it seems a stretch to imagine him jumping ship so soon after his promotion to chief hardware officer.

#3317. Why Websites Show the Wrong Server Location When You Use a VPN

There are many reasons why someone might use a VPN, but most often, it’s to conceal your real geographic location or prevent websites from tracking your online activity. It can also be a way to get around location-based restrictions that stop you from accessing certain websites or platforms.

When you connect to a VPN server in the United States, websites are supposed to detect that your online traffic is originating from the U.S. That way, you can access online platforms that use IP filters to block non-U.S. traffic or circumvent regional censorship when travelling outside the U.S. But if you connect to a VPN server in the United States while you’re vacationing in Mexico, and a website thinks your IP address is from Brazil, that might not solve your problem and may even add unnecessary complications.

If you’ve encountered something similar with your VPN provider, there are several fixes you can try. Depending on why your IP location is being misinterpreted, one of these should help you access the internet from the server location of your choice.

IP geolocation isn’t infallible. Websites rely on third-party IP databases to look up your location based on your current IP address. Maxmind, which has one of the largest such databases in existence, claims that its GeoIP products have a 99.8% accuracy. Lesser-known providers with smaller IP databases may be far less accurate.

Websites can also use more than just your IP address to estimate your location. For example, they can send WebRTC requests to your browser or directly query your device’s GPS. Moreover, VPN providers often have physical servers in one country while their IP addresses are registered to another country, and this discrepancy can also create issues. Let’s take a closer look at each of these problems individually, so you can find the fix that works best for you.

WebRTC is an open-source technology that lets your browser reduce latency when engaged in high-bandwidth tasks like streaming or video calls. Based on the IETF standard RFC 8828, it lets a website choose between your VPN server and your real IP address so it can establish the quickest path to transmit large amounts of data and reduce wait times or buffering.

But the catch with WebRTC is that it exposes both your VPN server and ISP-assigned addresses to websites, which can reveal your real IP location and cause websites to reject your VPN server country. Firefox now comes with built-in protections to prevent WebRTC leaks, while Chrome and Edge support third-party extensions like WebRTC Control that you can use to eliminate these issues. To check if your browser is leaking your real IP address during WebRTC requests, you can use a free tool like BrowserLeaks.

Even when a browser isn’t leaking your real IP address, DNS resolvers may fetch inaccurate location information if their nearest servers are too far from your current location. For example, a user in São Paulo may be geolocated to Chile when using Google Public DNS because that’s where Google’s nearest resolvers are located.

If you toggle on DNS leak protection in your VPN app, this will force websites to use your VPN’s resolver to perform DNS lookups. That often solves the problem, but, again, you can confirm the fix worked through a service like BrowserLeaks or IPLeaks.

Websites rely on IP databases like Maxmind, IP2Location, IPinfo, etc. to look up your exact location, but these databases get outdated quickly and need constant updating. Most of these databases also correct errors on request, but that takes some time. Also, each website has its own rules for how often it queries IP databases for updates.

Even when locations are updated in the actual database, a website may be sitting with outdated information unless it actively has refreshed it recently. MaxMind recommends doing this at least twice a week, but that’s ultimately up to the specific website.

VPN providers often rely on virtual servers that use IP addresses registered in a different region than the server’s physical location. For example, ExpressVPN notes that it serves IP addresses in Bolivia, Ecuador, Peru, Uruguay, and Venezuela through servers located physically in Brazil.

While this is usually to help with the lack of local infrastructure or strict surveillance laws in the region, many databases and analytics tools will flag the discrepancy for websites, leading to confusion and inconsistency regarding your actual server location. In these cases, your best bet is to switch your VPN server or use a dedicated IP address by signing up for a paid add-on for your VPN.

Before investing in a specific solution, it’s better to do a thorough lookup to make sure why your IP address is pointing to the wrong location and whether a WebRTC or DNS issue, virtual servers, or something else is the cause. Here’s how I’d go about it, step by step:

We’ll start by recording your baseline IP address, country, city, and ASN. With your VPN disconnected, navigate to IPConfig.co on your browser to grab your default IP details. I like this tool because it’s free and uses echoip to pull your location data straight from Maxmind. If you prefer using Terminal instead of your browser, you can also run curl ifconfig.co/json to grab these details in plain text format.

Now connect your VPN server. Then visit IPConfig.co again to note down the changed details.

Make sure the Country and Timezone fields match your current VPN server location. Also make sure the ASN (organization) field does not list your home ISP.

In case these details do not match your VPN server, run a WebRTC leak test and a DNS leak test using BrowserLeaks. If either of these tests doesn’t return your VPN server’s IP address, you’ve found your culprit.

If both the leak tests come back clean but a specific site still gets your location wrong, the issue is likely originating from an outdated database or virtual server.

There’s no surefire way to solve IP location mismatches for good. But if it happens often enough to disrupt your internet use, you can consider switching to a different VPN server and getting a browser add-on that prevents WebRTC leaks. If that doesn’t work, I’d consider buying a dedicated IP address that isn’t based on a virtual server. While many IP databases like MaxMind or IP2Location also have ways to request a location correction, that takes a while to go through and isn’t worth the effort unless it’s a permanent IP address registered through your ISP.
